We discuss how class-based pressures and shifting ideologies, as well as policy incoherence, institutional fragmentation, and dysfunctional governance have driven transport decision-making and outcomes, and have led to the contemporary crisis in which transport investments increasingly favour capital-intensive, image-driven projects that serve higher-income groups, at the expense of equitable accessibility and mobility. We conclude by arguing for integrated, multi-modal transport planning rooted in accessibility and equity, and for unified governance mechanisms and a renewed focus on pedestrian accessibility and mass transit, in Mumbai. Our article hopefully provides valuable insights and lessons for other cities in the Global South.

title: Examining inter-county border effects on daily population mobility in China's metropolitan area: The case of Jinan
Toward age-friendly housing: Everyday practices of older women in common spaces of collective housing in Santiago, Chile
Teleworking and residential sorting in polycentric cities: A model of rent gradients and travel response
Intended versus experienced benefits of urban blue-green infrastructure: Lessons from Ōtautahi Christchurch, New Zealand
abstract: Urban blue-green infrastructure (BGI) has become an increasingly common method of urban stormwater management. It has the potential to deliver multiple bio-physical and socio-cultural benefits, but BGI design teams often lack awareness of the socio-cultural dimensions of these infrastructures. These practitioners may consequently have a limited understanding of how BGI is valued amongst urban communities, and of how BGI might best be designed to provide the socio-cultural benefits most desired by these communities. Against this background, this research explores the relationship between the intended and experienced benefits of urban BGI. It does so in the context of Ōtautahi Christchurch, a city of around 400,000 in New Zealand, through an examination of four BGI sites. Our work shows that although urban BGI projects have conventionally been driven by stormwater practitioners and interests, in these sites community members primarily valued their ecological and health promoting dimensions. The communities also identified opportunities for BGI to enable other socio-cultural benefits. We argue that future BGI projects would benefit from more holistic consideration of socio-cultural outcomes, enabled by transdisciplinary design approaches and co-design with local communities and Indigenous groups.

title: Designing urban agriculture for climate resilience: Socio-psychological impacts and policy lessons from Mashhad, Iran
How does transport poverty affect subjective well-being in China: Mechanisms analysis, and urban-rural disparity
Delivered to distress: The impact of online food delivery emergence on depressive symptoms among older adults in China
Tourism and the commodification of rural space: A grounded theory study of peri-urban villages
Intercity mobility networks and urban economic output: A cross-national comparison of commuting versus migration
Out of business: design constraints and financial burdens in repurposing dead shopping malls
abstract: The paper explores adaptive reuse options for abandoned shopping malls amid the so-called retail apocalypse, defined as the widespread closure of brick-and-mortar retail stores, largely driven by the rise of e-commerce and shifting consumer behavior. The research question deals with returning dead shopping centers to productive use through technically feasible and financially viable conversions. The focus is on repurposing rather than demolishing-and-rebuilding solutions, to reconcile functional obsolescence with substantial residual structural life. The four-stage methodology includes: identification of alternatives and criteria through a literature review; alternative ranking using multi-criteria evaluation, specifically the Analytical Hierarchy Process; concept design and cost appraisal; economic valuation using Discounted Cash Flow analysis and Monte Carlo simulation. The method is tested on a case study identified with a survey of Italian dead and dying malls. Out of nine potential repurposing options, multi-criteria evaluation prioritizes a data center, followed by senior housing and a medical facility. Concept design tests suggest minimal invasive works for a data center, versus extensive reconfiguration for the residential and healthcare options. Base-case cash-flow analysis yields net present values and internal rates of return of €12.8 M/7.7% for the data center, €3.4 M/5.3% for senior housing, and €2.2 M/4.4% for the medical facility. Economic viability ranking is sensitive to changes in the discount rate. Results are also strongly affected by changes in revenue fundamentals. Simulation analysis shows that, depending on those fundamentals, the probability that the net present value exceeds zero is 75%, 85%, and barely 50%, respectively. Property book value hinders the feasibility of repurposing.

title: Toward safer micromobility: Identifying urban e-scooter crash severity factors through automated machine learning and crash narrative analysis
Uneven resilience: Constructing a climate environmental vulnerability index for South Africa's urban core
abstract: Urban areas in developing countries are increasingly exposed to climate risks, yet vulnerability assessments often remain generalised and fail to capture intra-regional disparities. This study addresses this gap by developing a Climate Environmental Vulnerability Index (CEVI) for municipalities in Gauteng Province, South Africa, over the period 2010–2024. The CEVI integrates 17 standardised indicators across three dimensions: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct sub-indices and a composite vulnerability measure. The results reveal significant spatial and temporal variation in climate vulnerability across municipalities, highlighting the multidimensional and uneven distribution of risk across geographically proximate areas. While some municipalities exhibit persistently high vulnerability due to limited adaptive capacity, others demonstrate relative resilience despite similar levels of climatic exposure. The findings show that differences in adaptive capacity are the primary drivers of variation in vulnerability across municipalities, with improvements in socio-economic conditions playing a more decisive role than exposure alone. These results underscore the importance of spatially differentiated and multidimensional approaches to climate risk assessment. From a policy perspective, the study highlights the need for targeted, municipality-level adaptation strategies rather than uniform provincial interventions. The CEVI framework provides a practical and replicable tool for urban planners and policymakers to support evidence-based resource allocation and enhance climate resilience in rapidly urbanising regions, thereby enabling more targeted and effective urban climate adaptation policies.

title: Fusing spatial and text semantics: A social semantic representation framework for coupling urban functions with their social attributes
Tourism pressure and tourism-relevant urban quality for spatial decision support in data-scarce cities: The case of Tunis metropolis
Influence of multilevel and polycentric governance structures on climate change mitigation and adaptation in 209 German municipalities
abstract: Studies have identified municipalities as key actors in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. However, the level of municipal engagement in these policy areas varies widely, and little is known about how different multilevel and polycentric governance structures affect their performance. To address this gap, we examined the mitigation and adaptation commitments, plans and ambitions of 209 German municipalities until the end of 2022 and scored them using an updated and revised assessment framework. We then used one-factor ANOVAs and linear regressions to analyse how their scores relate to a municipality's location in a federal state, its belonging to a county, and its function in Germany's ‘central places’ system. Our results show that belonging to certain federal states can have both positive and negative effects, and belonging to a county is a significant negative factor for local adaptation, while the central places system exerts very little influence. Based on these findings, we suggest that more coordinated multilevel governance structures—as opposed to more fragmented polycentric arrangements—are more likely to trigger local climate action. As such, we call for further and more targeted support for municipalities, and a (more) active role for the federal states in supporting municipal policymaking.

title: Can polycentricity lead to co-prosperity? The impact of polycentric urban structure on urban-rural integration: The evidence from China
Changing residential preferences in the digital age: Evidence on teleworking and online shopping from the Netherlands
abstract: Teleworking and online shopping, as two ICT-enabled behaviours, are reshaping everyday routines and raising questions about how digital practices enter long-term housing trade-offs. This matters for urban planning because changing preferences may alter spatial demand and land-use and transport needs. This study investigates how teleworking and online shopping are associated with residential location choices in the Netherlands and how these relationships vary across demographic groups and life stages. A stated choice experiment was designed to capture forward-looking housing decisions under varying levels of teleworking, online shopping, and anticipated life events. Data were collected from 1064 Dutch participants and analysed using tenure-specific discrete choice models: a covariate-dependent Generalized Mixed Logit model for homeowners and a mixed multinomial logit model for renters. The results show that teleworking eases homeowners' penalty for 20 km commutes, but not for 35 km, while analogous patterns among renters are more limited. Online grocery shopping is associated with supermarket-distance preferences, although this relationship should be interpreted cautiously because it may partly reflect income-related and locational differences. Higher online non-grocery shopping remains associated with stronger preferences for very close retail access, especially among homeowners. Anticipated life events, such as expecting a child, also reshape utility. Scale parameters indicate substantial individual variation in choice consistency. Overall, both ICT-enabled behaviours are associated with housing trade-offs, with stronger and more direct evidence for teleworking. These results have implications for housing policy, accessibility planning, and land-use and transport modelling in increasingly digital urban contexts.

title: More-than-human governance: beyond top-down and bottom-up logics in disaster risk management
Unraveling the dynamics of urban park visits: Daytime visitation patterns and behavioral determinants derived from mobile phone data
Urban climate actions: connecting city characteristics to planning responses
abstract: Cities, recognized as complex adaptive systems and epicentres of both climate vulnerability and innovative solutions, are increasingly adopting Climate Action Plans (CAPs) to navigate climate change. While considerable literature explores how various urban characteristics (climatic, physical, socio-anthropological, environmental) influence climate vulnerability, exposure, adaptation and mitigation responses, there is a gap in empirically understanding which of these distinct characteristics most powerfully drive the selection and prioritization of specific climate actions and interventions. This research aims to address this issue by systematically analysing the planned actions within the CAPs of twenty diverse global cities in relation to their unique urban fingerprints. Using multivariate statistical analysis to cluster cities by their characteristics and natural language processing to classify CAP actions, we empirically investigate the relationships between distinct urban profiles and the resulting climate action choices. Our analysis reveals that while cities facing severe, immediate climate pressures often prioritize community-level adaptation, mitigation and hazard awareness measures, cities with higher economic development tend to integrate climate action more broadly within economic restructuring and advanced policy frameworks. This study offers an in-depth understanding of how urban context translates into tangible climate actions, from a global perspective, aiming to inform more effective and tailored climate strategies for urban resilience.

title: Good(s) planning in cities — A review of urban planning scholarship on large freight generators
abstract: Urban freight transportation is both a traffic concern and a spatial issue. Yet within urban planning, freight remains overlooked. To advance the interface between urban planning and urban freight, it is important to understand how planning scholarship approaches urban developments with significant freight implications. Are these implications accounted for and if so, in what way? To this end, we systematically reviewed ten leading urban planning journals, using as a diagnostic lens the concept of ‘large freight generators’, i.e., facilities that produce and attract a large number of freight trips. Our findings reveal that the spatial and temporal dimensions of freight operations are rarely treated as explicit objects of urban governance. Planning should more explicitly account for the moving, storing, and handling of goods within cities, anticipating rather than merely accommodating freight demand. When freight is overlooked, facilities are displaced to peripheral areas and operations spill excessively into streets and curbs, exacerbating congestion and conflicts, and concentrating environmental externalities. In response, we outline a planner-facing research agenda that calls for systematic consideration of freight operations across space and time and deliberate integration of goods and services, especially in new residential neighborhood developments.

title: Editorial Board
The spatial heterogeneity effects of urban renewal: Evidence from Shenzhen, China
Anticipating China's profound urban shrinkage with a fine-grid perspective in the latter half of the 21st century
Evaluating probe-based data for travel demand analysis: A comparative study with household survey and regional model data in San Antonio
The implications of a land value tax on urban agglomeration dynamics: Efficiency and equity
abstract: Cities have become widely recognised as pivotal hubs for economic growth, with continued evidence of productivity gains from density and proximity of agglomerations. However, the same externalities of dense urban agglomerations exert pressures on the built environments and are partially responsible for a deepening urban crisis (e.g., increasing wealth disparities, housing crisis), harming both equity and efficiency. While Land Value Taxation (LVT) is widely recognised for its potential to improve land use efficiency and affordability, its implications for agglomeration mechanisms remain overlooked. This article synthesises two largely disconnected bodies of literature—agglomeration theory and LVT—to open a debate on how taxing the unimproved value of land could realign incentives within rigid and exclusionary urban environments. Drawing on a systematic literature review and expert interviews, we identify a notable conceptual gap but strong theoretical compatibility. We argue that LVT can enhance the spatial, temporal, and interactive domains of agglomeration by internalising externalities where they arise. Integrating LVT into Agglomeration theory offers a coherent framework for addressing contemporary urban challenges while reinforcing the productivity benefits of urban concentration. By conceptualising LVT as a dynamic, spatially sensitive policy instrument, this article positions it as an underutilised yet powerful tool for enhancing urban efficiency, equity, and long-run agglomeration potential.

title: Research on spatiotemporal evolution and influencing factors of county-level crime: A case of Guizhou province in southwest China
Urban planning, the built environment, and subjective well-being: A review of recent research advances
abstract: Research on how the built environment shapes subjective well-being has expanded rapidly since 2021, providing new insights for urban planning and policy. Yet, no review has synthesized major recent advances in this field. This narrative review synthesizes five categories of advances – (1) disruptions to urban life, (2) mobility and accessibility, (3) social and experiential dimensions, (4) planning paradigms and urban form, and (5) urban artificial intelligence (AI) – based on a pathways framework linking the built environment to subjective well-being. Recent evidence highlights the importance of walkability, proximity, green space, and housing quality in supporting well-being, particularly under conditions of constrained mobility or when time spent at home increases. A composite of meeting places can foster social interaction and urban vitality, promote inclusion, and help combat loneliness. Public transport investments, including new metro systems and high-speed rail, are associated with social interaction, prevention of exclusion, and subjective well-being. Access to a private car may enhance activity participation and opportunities, particularly in car-oriented environments, while producing important equity and sustainability externalities. Architecture and public space design influence emotional well-being, with traditional styles linked to positive emotional responses. The 15-minute city, urban vitality, high-rise living, telework, and urban AI represent urban concepts and digital developments that transform urban planning and subjective well-being. The outcomes of the review strengthen and enrich the pathways between built environment and subjective well-being and raise attention to inequalities between population groups and contexts.

title: Examining dual exposure to traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding among senior and regular cardholders using smart card data
abstract: In urban travel, traffic congestion often results in prolonged travel times, while in-vehicle crowding causes physical discomfort. Bus passengers uniquely face dual exposure to both congestion (from shared road networks) and crowding (from shared vehicle space), which compounds health risks and undermines sustainable transport goals. Despite this, few studies examine these concurrent exposures or the socio-demographic disparities in who bears this burden, particularly critical for vulnerable populations like senior groups who may face disproportionate impacts. Using Beijing bus smart card data, we measure congestion and crowding levels to identify adverse travel patterns and infer passengers' home locations. We then apply statistical and random forest models to examine how socio-demographic characteristics shape exposure to these adverse conditions across different urban areas. The study reveals the spatial-temporal dynamics of congestion and crowding, the daily rhythms of adverse travel flow across urban spaces, and the socio-demographic characteristic disparities that shape differential exposures among senior and regular cardholders. The findings indicate that congestion concentrates in urban centers and suburban hubs during peak hours, while crowding tends to persist throughout the day on suburban-urban corridors. Urban residents experience more congestion but less crowding than suburban and rural residents. Senior cardholders experience shorter durations but higher rates of adverse conditions than regular cardholders. By revealing dual exposure patterns across space, time, and demographics, this study identifies where and when interventions are needed to reduce congestion for urban commuters and crowding for suburban riders.

title: A joint synthetic housing–household inventory
abstract: Accurately understanding the interactions between humans and the built environment requires integrated representations of both the buildings and the populations that occupy them. However, high-fidelity datasets that jointly capture detailed housing structures and demographic characteristics at the household level do not currently exist. This paper presents a framework for constructing a joint housing-household inventory that explicitly links individuals and households to compatible housing units from the National Structure Inventory (NSI), while preserving realistic population densities and demographic distributions. The framework integrates three components: (i) synthetic population generation from American Community Survey (ACS) Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) records that preserve complex intra-household relationships; (ii) a deep contrastive learning model that quantifies housing-household compatibility; and (iii) a hierarchical optimization-based allocation procedure that enforces building-level capacity and block-group-level demographic constraints. The generated synthetic population attains high statistical realism relative to the census microdata, and the contrastive learning model identifies compatible housing-household pairs with high predictive accuracy. Applied to coastal North Carolina, evaluations at building, neighborhood, and regional scales show that the joint inventory matches block-group-level demographic distributions, reproduces observed spatial population patterns without systematic bias, and maintains consistent allocation quality across urban, suburban, and rural contexts. By enabling coupled household- and building-level analyses, the resulting inventory supports a broad range of applications, including disaster resilience planning, housing and affordability analysis, energy-use assessment, and public health research.

title: COVID-19 as a spatial shock: Uneven land market dynamics in metropolitan areas
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reshaped the spatial dynamics of metropolitan land markets in the Czech Republic. Using a large dataset of transactions and a Bayesian VAR framework, we show that the pandemic reinforced differences between urban cores and surrounding suburban areas. The analysis indicates that demand shocks played a substantial role in driving these patterns, while broader macroeconomic factors had only a complementary effect. Moreover, the shift persisted even after the pandemic, suggesting a lasting transformation in the relationship between centers and their suburbs. The study highlights that structural characteristics of cities critically shape market responses to external shocks and stresses the need for coordinated metropolitan planning to safeguard housing affordability and infrastructure capacity.

title: A CityGML extension for 3D modeling of pedestrian mobility space
abstract: This paper presents a conceptual model of pedestrian mobility spaces in 3D city models. While conceptual models can be specified in various ways, we use standard elements of CityGML and an Application Domain Extension (ADE): The Pedestrian ADE extends CityGML 3.0 to incorporate key parameters related to the physical, legal, and regulatory aspects of pedestrian mobility environments. For this, the extension introduces new feature classes for vertical passages such as stairs and elevators, and adds attributes to existing CityGML classes to represent pedestrian-specific characteristics. The conceptual model is also implemented for demonstration and validation: A real-world case study in Melbourne, Australia, demonstrates the practical application of the Pedestrian ADE to model complex urban environments. Through visualizations, we show how the model can be applied to represent spaces where different types of pedestrians can , cannot , may , or must not walk. This work provides a standardized approach for detailed 3D modeling of pedestrian mobility spaces, supporting various applications in urban planning, transportation, and accessibility analysis.

title: Aligning transit provision with urban morphology: A diagnostic assessment of Porto and Cagliari
abstract: Transit accessibility in cities is shaped not only by service provision but also by the extent to which transit networks align with the structural hierarchy of streets. This paper develops a reproducible, data-efficient framework that integrates angular segment analysis from Space Syntax, proximity-based transit catchments, and population-weighted exposure measures to assess how well transit stops correspond to high-integration corridors. Two indicators operationalise this assessment: the Gap Index, which identifies the share of population exposed to high-integration corridors lacking nearby transit service, and the Equity Ratio, which compares exposure levels across demographic groups. The framework is applied to Porto and Cagliari, two Mediterranean port cities that share comparable urban morphologies but exhibit contrasting mobility outcomes. Findings reveal a strong divergence. Porto demonstrates complete proximity coverage of its structurally high-integration corridors, indicating a close alignment between transit routing and the spatial configuration of the street network. However, Cagliari displays a pronounced proximity deficit, with a substantial share of high-integration corridors lying outside 300 m transit stop catchments. These results suggest that differences in accessibility between the two cities arise not from population distribution or morphological potential but from strategic choices in transit routing. The study shows how morphology-aware indicators can help planners detect accessibility gaps that conventional supply-side assessments overlook and highlights the value of integrating spatial configuration analysis into routine diagnostic practices. The proposed framework offers a transferable basis for monitoring alignment between street structure and transit provision, supporting more responsive and equitable mobility strategies in port-city contexts.

title: Impact of depopulated area designation policy on the population and employment in Japanese small and medium-sized cities
abstract: Small and medium-sized cities (SMCs) are vital to sustaining balanced national development. However, many SMCs have experienced significant population decline in recent years. This study examines the effects of Japan's Depopulated-Area-Designation (DAD) policy on population and employment in SMCs. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach across municipalities designated at different times, we estimate the policy's demographic and employment impacts over a 30-year post-designation horizon. The results indicate that the DAD policy was not associated with significant population change during the main analysis period. Specifically, the policy neither increased nor decreased population levels within the first 15 years after designation. However, approximately 20 years after designation, populations began to decline sharply. The trend in employed persons closely mirrored this population decline, while the number of employed residents showed no significant change even 20 years after designation. These findings suggest that analyses limited to employed residents would fail to capture the subsequent decline in both population and employed persons observed after 20 years. In conclusion, the results suggest that although the DAD policy produced no short- or medium-term effects, disadvantages may emerge in the long term. These findings are striking because they contradict the goals of the DAD policy. The results imply that policy designation alone cannot reverse—or even stabilize—the structural trends of population and economic decline in SMCs. Policymakers should therefore reconsider whether—and how—area-designation instruments can effectively address rural depopulation.

title: County-level new-type urbanization policy and city economic resilience: Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment of 2302 counties in China
Measuring lockdown travel rebound: Experimental insights from the Hong Kong COVID-19 omicron outbreak
abstract: While localized lockdowns emerged as pivotal Non-pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) during the mid-to-late phases of the COVID-19 pandemic, the precise impacts on residential mobility remain understudied, including pre-and post-lockdown travel comparisons, ‘bounce-back’, and long and short-term adjustments. Policymakers were particularly concerned about unanticipated viral transmission from undiagnosed asymptomatic carriers. This study investigates Hong Kong’s Restriction-testing Declaration (RTD) policy, a short-term localized lockdown strategy mainly targeting public housing estates (PHEs) during the omicron outbreak. Employing a Propensity Score Matching and Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) framework, we analyzed anonymized mobile positioning data from 117,370 resident’s mobile devices during omicron outbreak, to quantify the lockdown-induced mobility response, defined as the distance to maximum reach position (DMRP).Our findings reveal that RTD events generated substantial increases in the daily average increase of 1.20 km of DMRP over the two-week study duration, and exhibits an inverted-U-shaped rebound pattern in differed epidemic phases. In the rising phase, RTD immediately increased PHE residents’ DMRP by 0.89 km on the implementation day, and this effect persisted for 11 days, with the maximum surge occurring on post-RTD Day 5. In the peak phase, no immediate impact occurred on the implementation day. However, an increase of 1.04 km occurred one day later, and this effect continued for 5 days, reaching its maximum surge on post-RTD Day 2. No significant DMRP increase was observed for the declining phase. This is the first empirical study to investigate how localized lockdowns impact residents’ travel rebound and provides key insights for policymakers to understand unintended mobility responses.

title: Assessing household's vulnerability to urban flood based on AHP and TOPSIS method: A case study of the flood-prone area in Pakistan
The equity impact of bike-sharing on developing X-minute cities: A case study of 36 cities in Zhejiang Province, China
Shaping socio-functional urban identity: When morphometrics meet social media data to reveal neighbourhood structure and cores
abstract: Understanding how urban form and activity interact to shape neighbourhood structure remains a central challenge in urban analysis. While morphological and activity-based approaches have been widely developed, their integration remains methodologically uneven, which can limit their ability to capture the socio-functional organisation of urban space. This paper proposes a reproducible computational workflow that integrates morphometric descriptors with location-based social media data to address two questions: to what extent does combining form and activity signals reveal socio-functional differentiation that morphology-only approaches cannot capture at comparable spatial resolution, and do the resulting units expose identifiable neighbourhood cores structured around concentrated activity? Using MomePy-based tessellations enriched with Foursquare-derived activity indexes within a unified clustering framework, the method is applied to 29 Southern European cities. The results show that this integration reveals consistent and recurrent patterns across cities: socio-functional differentiation within morphologically homogeneous fabrics, functional convergence across morphologically distinct areas, and the emergence of neighbourhood cores as centres of gravity within the resulting units. These patterns remain less visible when relying on morphology alone. The consistency of these findings across diverse urban contexts supports the robustness of the approach and its transferability as a basis for fine-grained urban diagnostics using open data, with direct relevance for neighbourhood-scale analysis and planning.

title: From dematerialization to well-being in digital cities: The Melting–Relief–Vitality model for Montreal, London and Tokyo, 1900–2050
abstract: Digitalization can reduce the material, energy and travel intensity of urban work, but its environmental dividend becomes urban sustainability only when it reaches residents as lived capability. This paper asks how cities can account for that transmission as urban functions shift from land- and building-anchored routines to code-, data- and platform-coordinated routines. We develop the Melting–Relief–Vitality (MRV) model as a source-based, provenance-coded diagnostic accounting framework. MRV links the structurality-to-digitality transition, the dematerialization-relief account generated by that transition, and two vitality gates representing cognitive and physical transmission conditions. We apply MRV to Montreal, London and Tokyo, 1900–2050, using a decadal panel assembled from public and administrative data, land-use and floorspace records, digital adoption series, health and mobility indicators, population series, documented harmonization and modelled reconstruction where direct series are unavailable. Under the reference calibration, all three cities record increasing dematerialization relief within MRV, but transmission diverges: Tokyo's later threshold crossing and lower accumulated exposure preserve the largest share, Montreal remains intermediate, and London records the strongest vitality discount. Per-capita outcomes show that aggregate environmental improvement does not automatically imply per-resident gain. We also test a post-2025 dividend-to-vitality compact directing 25% of incremental relief to vitality interventions. Stability checks across thresholds, exposure attenuation, recovery, compact strength and population denominators confirm the central transmission ordering and identify policy leverage. MRV makes the environmental-to-social transmission assumption explicit, auditable and operational for city-level policy, planning and governance.

title: Enhancing urban climate resilience via polycentric spatial structure in the pursuit of SDG 13 (Climate Action)
Measuring the unmeasurable: An intelligent and interactive evaluation addressing aesthetic performance of urban texture via CLIP and LLMs
Environment-adjusted port efficiency and port-industry-city coupling coordination: Lessons from China's coastal port clusters
Imagining economic development, enabling sprawl: Planning for logistics in suburban regions
abstract: Due to the changing demands of global supply chains, the facilities and related infrastructures that support the movement of goods have shifted away from inner-city locations toward suburban and ex-urban sites with spaces suitable for the construction of large-footprint warehouses and distribution centres. This article explores the relationship between the demands of the global logistics industry and suburban local governments through a case study of a southeastern suburb in British Columbia's Lower Mainland, Canada. It traces municipal efforts to accommodate large-scale industrial users at the rural-suburban fringe. Through a qualitative approach including analysis of city planning documents, newspapers, real estate publications, Census data, and interviews with local planning officials, we analyze how the post-suburban spatial imaginaries of local officials are propelling industrial growth forward, calling into question not only the long-standing emphasis in the literature on residential growth as the driver of expansion of the suburban edge, but also how various types of sprawl may be perceived differently and thus subject to different planning treatments. The article reveals the deep intertwining of these previously rural communities and their economic futures with the global logistics industry and the need to more explicitly consider logistics development in local and regional planning.

title: Urban green credits: Capturing ecosystem service value in housing markets for redistributive urban planning
abstract: Urban green infrastructure generates substantial ecosystem services, yet the economic value of these benefits is often captured privately through housing markets rather than reinvested in public ecological provision. This paper addresses this gap by introducing Urban Green Credits (UGC), a planning-oriented framework that links ecological performance to fiscal instruments. We develop a parcel-level Index of Ecosystem Services (IES) integrating carbon sequestration, thermal regulation, ecological connectivity, and accessibility to green spaces. Using 5230 residential transactions in Porto, Portugal, we estimate the capitalisation of ecological performance into housing prices through hedonic, spatial econometric, instrumental variable, and difference-in-differences models. Results show that ecosystem services are consistently and significantly reflected in property values, with robust effects across specifications and identification strategies. Building on these estimates, we simulate the fiscal potential of UGC, demonstrating that even modest capture rates can generate meaningful revenues and support redistribution towards ecologically underserved areas. The findings contribute to bridging ecosystem service valuation and urban fiscal policy, advancing a framework that integrates environmental performance, land markets, and equity considerations. While conceptual and requiring contextual calibration, UGC provides a novel pathway for financing urban greening while addressing spatial inequalities.

title: Government relocation and urban spatial reconstruction in China: Effects, mechanisms, and governance implications
Context-sensitive Sponge City strategies: A cross-case and multi-scalar analysis
abstract: Sponge Cities are more than technical solutions to urban flooding–they are dynamic spaces where water, land, and society converge in adaptation and resilience. This study bridges theory and practice through a comparative, cross-case framework that analyzes Sponge City strategies across five Dutch lowland landscape types (coastal, riverine, peat, sandy, clay) and selected international contexts. Emphasizing scale as a critical dimension, the study explores how blue, green, and blue-green strategies are shaped by ecological conditions and local practices. Beyond hydrological performance, it highlights the often-overlooked social dimension, including community participation, equity, and social resilience. The research adopts a qualitative, interpretivist methodology, combining within-case and cross-case analysis. It unfolds in two phases: first, a global typology of 38 Sponge City strategies is developed, categorized as green, blue, or green-blue, and analyzed by spatial scale (site, neighborhood, city), sponge basin principles (protect, delay, store, release), and hydrological processes (infiltration, retention, storage, purification, utilization, drainage). The second phase offers an in-depth evaluation of eight Dutch projects across Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Almere, Purmerend, and The Hague, examining ecological, spatial, and social performance through thematic coding and structured comparison. The findings highlight a gap between the coherence of Sponge City theory and its real-world application, particularly regarding social integration. Successful implementation depends on context-sensitive strategies that go beyond water management to include accessibility, inclusivity, and community engagement. This study contributes to a broader understanding of how human-centered, adaptive design can support climate resilience across diverse urban landscapes, grounding its analysis in a landscape-based Sponge City framework that links Sponge Basin principles (protect, delay, store, release) with lowland landscape typologies and cross-scalar design strategies.

title: Urban–rural economic inequality in western China's reform frontier: Nighttime light-based insights from Chengdu–Chongqing
Assessing the economic effects of micromobility sharing using credit card transaction data: Evidence from accessibility, mobility, and connectivity
Exploring the role of politicians and bureaucrats in governance of metropolitan areas. Experiences from Czechia
abstract: Problems of governance are a recurring theme in research on metropolitan areas, yet the role of politicians, bureaucrats, and political-administrative relations remains underexplored. This article addresses this gap by analyzing political-administrative relations in the governance of Czech metropolitan areas. As metropolitan areas in Czechia were established relatively recently, it is possible to observe the dynamics between politicians and civil servants from their inception. Based on semi-structured interviews with politicians and civil servants from two metropolitan areas, the findings suggest that civil servants hold a relatively strong position due not only to their expertise and knowledge of EU funding opportunities and project management, but also to the limited interest of politicians in the metropolitan agenda. Politicians' low engagement appears to result from a focus on immediate economic benefits and difficulties navigating issues beyond electoral district boundaries. This passive political role contributes to the uncertain status of metropolitan areas, which lack strong political advocacy.

title: Classification of medium and small cities for the implementation of Low Emission Zones
abstract: Growing mobility within cities has led to an unacceptable increase in the negative externalities of transport. In order to reduce this negative impact, Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are being implemented; among other actions and objectives, they include some type of circulating restriction for vehicles to improve air quality. Given the differences among cities, and the great variety of measures that a LEZ may include, it is necessary to develop aids for choosing the most appropriate type of LEZ to be implemented. This study identifies groups of cities having similar geophysical and socioeconomic characteristics, as well as other traits related with the generation of negative impacts by transport. Our classification may be used to propose common policy guidelines —in some cases even specific proposals— for planning an adequate LEZ in each city group, or for other municipalities that could identify with a particular group.The study case is Spain. A total of 61 cities were considered, described by means of 11 variables. Cluster analysis was used to define the groups of cities, giving eight clusters; in view of their most relevant characteristics, different policy guidelines and actions could be put forth for the design of a particular LEZ for each group.

title: Governance of overwork among migrant workers: Effective measures or effective beauty?
Your place or mine? Overcoming neoliberal placemaking as commodification of built environments in the inclusive city
abstract: This paper critiques the neoliberal application of placemaking in urban development, highlighting its often exploitative outcomes. While intended to promote community engagement and sustainability, placemaking frequently becomes a tool for commodifying spaces, resulting in gentrification, displacement, and cultural erasure. Using Rotterdam's Urban Leisure and Tourism (ULT) Living Lab as a case study, the research illustrates how top-down regeneration initiatives, masked as inclusive, marginalize vulnerable communities. It emphasizes the need for critical reflection on placemaking as a social practice.The study advocates for bottom-up, community-focused placemaking strategies to foster resilience and equity in disadvantaged neighborhoods. It explores how such communities can mitigate the extractive impacts of tourism and development while amplifying historically excluded voices. By sharing citizen perspectives from urban activation projects, the research underscores the importance of systemic, participatory approaches prioritizing local ownership, inclusivity, and sustainable resource management.Ultimately, the paper challenges the prioritization of short-term economic interests over long-term societal well-being. It calls for authentic, transparent urban planning models where developers and policymakers act on community-driven proposals. These approaches align with the paradigm of New Urban Tourism (NUT) and aim to build more inclusive cities that genuinely reflect and serve all residents' needs.

title: Revealing urban vitality structures in South Korea: A nationwide analysis of 225 cities
When transit stops: Causal evidence on travel times from a transit strike in Quebec city
abstract: Public transport can generate positive economic externalities by reducing transportation cost. Evaluating the economic impact of the presence of public transport is challenging, as no one must identify the travel-time savings attributable specifically to its availability. So far, most of the literature dedicated to allocating a value to public transport has been devoted to measure the willingness-to-pay to be located close from station. The paper proposes a different avenue by exploiting the impact of a strike in 2025 that paralyzed all public transport services to assess whether, and how, the absence of service affects travel times to reach a specific location within a medium-size city. To do so, travel time for trips that reach or leave a summer music festival, organized each year in Québec City (Canada), are compared between 2023 and 2025 before and during the event, when the strike hits. The analysis, based on a difference-in-differences framework uses travel time data obtained through smartphone tracking, suggests that trips to and from the festival site were significantly longer when public transport was not operating, particularly for travelers who typically benefit from the service located within the city center and the inner suburbs. The results indicate that public transport has a meaningful economic impact on individual travel, even in a medium-sized city where its modal share is relatively small.

title: Innovative approaches to sustainable E-waste management: Green finance for metal extraction and reuse
How accessibility perception can improve accessibility measurement
abstract: The concept of perceived accessibility (PA) provides a way of capturing individual disparities in the context of the spatial analysis of travel behaviors. However, the measurement of perceived accessibility raises certain issues. Based on the standard gravity-based accessibility indicator, we propose a theoretical analysis for estimating perceived accessibility. We take account of individual heterogeneity by considering the differences between individuals' perceptions of travel time. We capture this perception through individual travel cost sensitivity and an enhanced impedance parameter. We test our method on urban data from the Household Transport Survey (HTS) conducted in Lyon (France) which permits disaggregated spatial analysis. This survey uses 4-stage model calibration and provides transport data that takes account of the socioeconomic characteristics of more than 11,000 households. A comparison between measurements of standard gravity-based accessibility and perceived accessibility confirms that there is a difference between the two, with lower results for PA than the standard accessibility indicator. Our results also reveal that measured PA is highly dependent on the spatial zone: in the CBD, which has a relatively wealthy population, travel sensitivity is lower than in suburban spatial zones. Therefore, a transport policy change impacting accessibility can have beneficial spatial impacts.

title: “The money is too big to ignore”: The logics of everyday speculations and the transformation of Ghana's peri-urban landscapes
How municipal planning authorities' ways of acting influence plan feasibility: Studies of four city-centre zoning-plan processes in small and medium-sized Norwegian cities
abstract: To promote sustainable urban development and vital city centres, small and medium-sized cities need to ensure that desired city-centre transformation and densification projects are realised. However, zoning-plan processes in complex city-centre environments are often demanding and may result in plans that do not enable feasible projects and therefore are not implemented. Municipal planning authorities play key roles in such processes, yet limited scholarly attention has been given to how their ways of acting influence plan feasibility. This paper addresses this gap through a qualitative multiple case study of four city-centre zoning-plan processes in small and medium-sized Norwegian cities, based on document review and in-depth interviews with key actors. The paper analyses how municipal planning authorities' actions related to goal conflict resolution, goal prioritisation and articulation, use of knowledge and exercise of agenda-setting power influenced process progress and whether the resulting plans were perceived by developers as feasible. The findings show that plan feasibility was shaped by interrelated forms of municipal planning authority action. Authorities increased the likelihood of feasible plans when they engaged actively in handling goal conflicts, clearly prioritised and articulated city-centre development goals, used professional, legal and contextual knowledge to identify workable solutions and exercised agenda-setting power to support collaboration, progress and plan flexibility. The paper contributes empirically grounded insights into how municipal planning authority practices shape plan feasibility in complex city-centre zoning-plan processes and offers practical knowledge for authorities seeking to realise desired city-centre development.

title: Assessing the opportunities for retrofitting Nature-based solutions to streetscape areas: Planning for climate resilience
Exploring the interplay of motivation, civic engagement, and institutional entrepreneurship in fostering participation and innovation: Insights from the Medialab Prado experience
abstract: Civic participation, fostered using digital media, has grown in response to the perceived crisis in traditional channels of political intermediation. Some institutions have responded to these demands by adopting and promoting participatory processes, such as innovation labs. The main aim of this paper is to investigate the extent to which institutional variables (perceived institutional entrepreneurship) and personal variables (civic engagement attitudes and motivation) explain intention to become involved in civic participation and innovation, and subsequent actual innovation behaviour. Our sample consists of participants following a course oriented towards the development of innovation labs—organized by Medialab Prado. Data were obtained through a questionnaire administered online and relationships between variables were modelled and analysed by using a structural equation modelling approach (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that both, institutional factors (perceived institutional entrepreneurship) and personal factors (civic engagement and motivations) significantly influence the formation of intentions to participate. Contrary to what we would expect, neither intrinsic motivation nor extrinsic motivation linked to external rewards (external regulation) emerged as statistically significant predictors of innovation intention in this sample. The most influential motivational factor was identified regulation, reflecting participation based on the perceived personal value and relevance of the activity for professional development. Notably, perceptions of the institution carry too much relevance to be ignored and, therefore, the design and implementation of participative processes cannot rely solely on individual intentions.

title: Official rotation and urban economic growth in China: Political signaling from South-to-North Official Transfers
It's hard to live in a tourist city: Explaining residents' responses to tourism pressure through stress and self-efficacy
authors: Ana Isabel Damião de Serpa Arruda Moniz
abstract: Purpose Research on residents' attitudes toward tourism has relied on cost-benefit frameworks, offering limited insight into how tourism pressure is experienced in everyday life. This study applies Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory to examine how sustained tourism exposure shapes residents' responses. Focusing on Lisbon's historic parish of Santa Maria Maior, the study analyses how perceived negative impacts influence tourism acceptance through psychological processes. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 1496 residents using a combined online and face-to-face survey. The model was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling, enabling the assessment of mediation and moderation effects. Findings Tourism-related impacts are internalised through stress, with effects that vary across domains. Environmental degradation and congestion reduce tourism acceptance through both stress and disruptions to everyday urban life, while economic drawbacks act through stress alone. Self-efficacy attenuates the negative effects of perceived pressures on tourism acceptance. Originality/value The study reframes residents' attitudes as coping processes shaped by resource conditions. It introduces a process-based explanation of how tourism pressure translates into attitudes and links tourism research with environmental psychology. Practical implications Sustaining tourism in urban environments requires attention to environmental quality, spatial access and residents' capacity to cope with pressure. Measures addressing congestion, housing dynamics and resident participation are necessary to maintain tourism acceptance under high intensity.

title: Khulna: A climate-vulnerable post-industrial city in transition—Decline or revival?
Smartwashing mobility: Governing smart mobility through urban imaginaries
abstract: The smart city has become a dominant paradigm in urban governance, projecting futures of environmental sustainability, and an enhanced quality of life through, through technological innovation, digitalisation and data-driven governance. Within this framework, smart mobility has emerged as a powerful domain, promising solutions to congestion, emissions, and accessibility. While critical scholarship has examined the discursive and political dimensions of smart urbanism, less attention has been paid to how such imaginaries are enacted in everyday governance. Building on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, this paper introduces the concept of ‘smartwashing’ to analytically engage with the dynamics between urban mobility governance, and smart city imaginaries Smartwashing captures how mobility initiatives invoke smart city imaginaries to secure legitimacy, visibility, and institutional traction, even when transformative outcomes remain limited. Smartwashing does not imply deliberate deception; rather, it refers to routine and everyday processes of symbolic and institutional alignment with collectively imagined futures. Empirically, we apply this framework to four mobility projects in Stavanger (Norway) and Gothenburg (Sweden). Our findings suggest that collectively stabilised imaginaries of smart futures become politically consequential in the local context through mechanisms of discursive alignment, mobilisation, and attachment to generate project legitimacy, momentum and value. The paper contributes to critical smart city studies by advancing smartwashing as a conceptual tool, and to STS scholarship by showing how imagined futures shape urban governance at the project level.

title: Aesthetic preferences for traditional versus contemporary architecture: Cross-national evidence from real-world buildings
abstract: Aesthetic experiences of the built environment represent an important pathway linking cities and subjective well-being. Despite growing interest in public evaluations of architectural design, existing research is largely based on single-country samples. This study aims to advance understanding of aesthetic preferences for building facades using survey data from two national contexts, Norway and Greece ( N = 2997). It examines whether contemporary or traditional buildings are preferred and how sociodemographic and spatial characteristics relate to building preferences. Respondents in both countries evaluated the same four pairs of buildings, with each pair consisting of a contemporary and a traditional facade, both located in Norway. The results show that traditional architectural designs were preferred over contemporary architectural designs across all comparisons. This pattern was significant in seven out of eight pair tests. Public preferences for traditional architecture were similar across the two countries despite all buildings being located in Norway. Two of the four comparisons involved contemporary buildings that had received architectural awards or nominations, and traditional buildings were preferred over these professionally acclaimed buildings as well. In addition, women and residents of denser urban environments exhibited stronger preferences for traditional designs. Together, these findings raise important questions for architectural education, urban development practices, urban planning regulations, and public participation in shaping the qualities of the built environment.

title: Deprivation and access to discount food supermarkets in England: A cross-sectional analysis
abstract: Food supermarkets play an important role in improving food availability and accessibility. The recent growth in the market share of discount food supermarkets in England raises new questions about their impact on food access, especially in deprived communities. Focusing on physical access, this study examines spatial inequalities in access by exploring the relationship between physical access to discount food supermarkets and socioeconomic conditions. Our analysis controls for population, conventional food supermarkets, urbanisation, regional (north–south) effects, and the availability of public transport. We use Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and quantile regression techniques. Our results suggest that more deprived areas have higher accessibility to discount food supermarkets. We also find that the relationship between access to discount food supermarkets, deprivation and control variables systematically differed in the north and south, and between urban and rural areas. Overall, the results suggest that efforts aimed at reducing food insecurity in England should integrate equity-oriented considerations into supermarket provision strategies.

title: Integrated urban resilience strategies for water management and climate adaptation in Africa: A systematic review aligned with the SDGs
abstract: Urban resilience strategies are crucial for addressing the interlinked challenges of water management and climate adaptation in Africa's rapidly urbanizing regions. This review synthesizes studies from 2015 to 2024, categorizing strategies into four thematic areas: urban water security, climate risks, green infrastructure, and community-based water management. Using the PRISMA methodology and a structured coding framework, the analysis highlights the critical roles of GI and CBWM in mitigating urban flooding, water scarcity, and related climate risks, while advancing Sustainable Development Goals 6, 9, 11, 13, and 16. The review situates African urban resilience research within the global literature, emphasizing how regional governance dynamics and resource constraints influence adaptation choices. A comparative analysis reveals geographic variation: North Africa prioritizes solutions for water scarcity, Sub-Saharan Africa focuses on flood resilience, and Southern Africa demonstrates integrated technical and participatory approaches. Innovative assessment methods—such as hydrodynamic modeling, participatory mapping, and sustainability evaluations—emerge as key tools for tailoring interventions to local conditions. However, challenges including limited data, weak governance, and the exclusion of informal settlements persist. Despite these barriers, hybrid approaches that combine technical innovation with inclusive community-based strategies offer scalable and equitable solutions. The findings underscore the importance of context specific, multi-level planning and institutional coordination. Key recommendations include strengthening governance, enhancing stakeholder collaboration, and leveraging technology to align resilience strategies with the SDGs. By identifying regional trends and implementation gaps, this review offers actionable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers striving to build sustainable and resilient urban systems in African cities facing escalating climate impacts.

title: Bridging digital divides: User-generated data and volunteered urban sensing for inclusive smart city governance
abstract: Urban digital transformation has the potential to improve quality of life by connecting data generated by sensors, mobile phones and networked everyday objects to enhance services, participation and sustainability. However, when such technologies are implemented in a purely technocratic manner, they often deepen existing social and digital divides, this meaning that only well-connected groups benefit from smart-city innovations. This paper advances an Urban Living Lab approach that combines citizen-generated data with the WIN (Wishes, Interests and Needs) methodology of diverse residents to co-design and test solutions in real urban settings, emphasizing inclusion from the outset to the innovation process. By centering local knowledge and everyday experiences, the approach seeks to develop more sustainable, fair and holistic smart-city configurations in which a broad majority of citizens can meaningfully shape and share the benefits of urban digital transformation.

title: Does fare-free public transport reduce social exclusion for older persons? Empirical evidence from Vietnam
Framing artificial intelligence as a policy instrument in urban climate action: Practitioners' perspectives from Paris
abstract: Urban practitioners increasingly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into tasks related to the implementation of climate action. Research identified potential AI applications and traced implementation processes, yet it remains understudied how practitioners introduce AI and how AI systems change workflows and decision hierarchies in urban climate action. Treating AI as a policy instrument, this study examines the city of Paris through semi-structured interviews and documents from grey literature. We show that AI currently produces incremental shifts in tasks related to climate action, for example, in maintenance of infrastructure, urban planning and building regulation. These shifts in practice do not replace, but position urban practitioners as curators of AI systems, responsible for including socio-technical risk assessment and translation to deliberative formats. We also document how practitioners mediate AI’s integration into urban climate action through technocratic, moral, and political logics of action, contrasted with their doubts about the usefulness of AI. Doubts include, for instance, that AI risks depoliticizing urban climate action. By assessing AI as a socio-technical policy instrument rather than a neutral tool, our study unpacks both technical operational utility and its symbolic values, including tensions in between, such as complexity-handling versus oversimplification, and acceleration versus accountability. We argue that urban practitioners must critically reflect on their expectations towards AI systems and engage with fundamental concerns to reduce tension. Based on our findings, we created a checklist for urban practitioners who engage with AI in climate action and aim to operationalize democratic AI governance as a means to reduce adverse consequences.

title: Sex and the city: A spatial analysis of shifting attitudes toward gay rights
Impact of nature connectedness on loneliness among university students living away from home: The mediating roles of meaningfulness, peace of mind, and resilience
abstract: Loneliness is a growing mental health concern globally. Since the advent of smartphone and internet use, urban youth have been disproportionately affected by loneliness. Disconnecting from tech and connecting with nature could be a solution to reducing loneliness. This study explored the relationship between nature connectedness and loneliness in urban youth, examining the novel and potentially mediating variables of meaningfulness, peace of mind, and resilience. A sample of 257 Indian urban youth aged 19–26 were recruited through convenience sampling. Participants completed an online survey measuring nature connectedness, meaningfulness, peace of mind, resilience, and loneliness. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was employed and the results indicated that nature connectedness, meaningfulness, peace of mind, and resilience were negatively associated with loneliness. Mediation analyses revealed that the negative association between nature connectedness and loneliness was significantly mediated by meaningfulness and peace of mind but not by resilience. These findings suggest that enhancing nature connectedness can reduce loneliness by fostering individuals' sense of meaningfulness and peace of mind. This research underscores the importance of integrating green spaces in urban planning, and supporting nature connection programs like forest bathing, community gardening, or group hiking to reduce loneliness among urban youth.

title: 15-Minute City and beyond: Linking local and regional accessibility with urban vitality
abstract: The 15-minute City concept has recently gained prominence, reigniting the debate on the ideal urban form and the importance of local versus regional accessibility in promoting vibrant cities. Our study contributes to this scholarship by exploring the relationship between these two scales of accessibility and urban vitality. Using Hong Kong as our case study and based on longitudinal restaurant registration records, we investigate how urban vitality, proxied by the number of restaurants, relates to both local accessibility, measured by walking time to the neighborhood center, and regional accessibility, measured by public transit time to an urban border. Our findings offer support for the 15-minute City concept by identifying a positive correlation between local accessibility and urban vitality. Additionally, through a quasi-natural experiment approach enabled by the closure and resumption of cross-boundary borders between Hong Kong and Mainland China, we identify a modest (approximately 2%) positive impact of regional accessibility on vitality. The results also suggest a synergistic effect. Areas that excel in both local and regional accessibility witness an increase in restaurant numbers, while high regional access cannot compensate for poor local access. These findings suggest that local accessibility plays a more significant role than regional accessibility in shaping urban vitality, but enhancements in regional access are still beneficial, as they can drive further economic growth where good local accessibility exists. Our findings underscore the necessity for cities globally, irrespective of their population density or existing transit infrastructures, to implement holistic development strategies that enhance accessibility both locally and regionally.

title: Urbanization and housing market dynamics in Türkiye's reclassified cities after the metropolitan reform: Quantile-based insights
Telework and residential location: Evidence from a stated-preference experiment in the Lisbon Metropolitan Area
abstract: The surge in teleworking during the COVID-19 pandemic has intensified debates on whether it reshapes residential preferences in ways that may enable suburbanisation. This paper examines how telework affects residential location preferences in the Lisbon Metropolitan Area using a stated-preference experiment combined with attitudinal constructs estimated through a Hybrid Choice Model (HCM). The analysis relies on a sample of 642 dual-earner households actively considering relocation, allowing stated choices to reflect realistic decision-making contexts. Results indicate no uniform decentralisation tendency. Dual-teleworker households with higher income and a stronger central-living preference favour central apartments, consistent with amenity access remaining valued even as commuting constraints loosen. Suburban apartments show higher utility among younger teleworkers and among those who do not seek to increase telework, consistent with an affordability-oriented apartment option still close to the centre/office hubs. Suburban houses show a higher utility among households with teenagers, conditional on the possibility of high-intensity teleworking (more than 3 days/week or 10 days/month). The utility of village/small-town houses increases with age for households where the respondent teleworks while the partner does not, and aligns closely with a quietness-oriented preference, suggesting that telework can bring forward a residential option that would otherwise be considered only at later life-course stages. Overall, by relaxing workplace proximity constraints, telework may enable households to act upon pre-existing preferences, suggesting planning responses that expand housing supply in accessible locations to reduce incentives for outward relocation.

title: Local practices addressing migrants' housing precarity: Evidence from the Veneto Region, Italy
abstract: Access to adequate housing represents one of the most critical and persistent challenges faced by migrants in contemporary European cities. Drawing on an in-depth qualitative study conducted in the Veneto Region (Italy), this article examines how migrants' housing precarity is produced through the interaction of structural housing shortages, institutional arrangements, and socio-cultural mechanisms of exclusion. The analysis combines policy review, interviews with institutional and civil society actors, and three case studies of locally grounded initiatives addressing migrants' access to housing across different segments of the housing system. The findings show that migrants' exclusion from housing cannot be explained by individual vulnerability alone, but emerges from a dual failure of the housing system, characterised by a constrained and discriminatory private rental market and by an underfunded and institutionally exclusionary public housing sector. At the same time, the article demonstrates that locally embedded practices can partially counteract exclusion by mobilising relational and institutional infrastructures, including intermediation, trust-building, and sustained accompaniment. By conceptualising housing as a socio-spatial process rather than a static asset, the article contributes to broader debates on housing, migration, and urban governance, highlighting both the potential and the limits of local action in addressing structural housing inequalities.

title: Urban park use patterns across gender and age in Seoul: Multivariate and long-term time series analysis based on mobile communication data (2017–2024)
Nonlinear environmental effect thresholds of port activity intensity under structural heterogeneity: Evidence from Chinese port cities
Navigating stakeholder engagement for inclusive urban planning: Introducing the Generative Method Recommender Model
abstract: The integration of a diverse array of stakeholders is essential to ensure sustainable and inclusive development of cities that aligns with community needs while supporting social cohesion and decision-making legitimacy. Although existing literature on urban planning offers valuable insights into the ways of stakeholder engagement, yet a systematic approach to selecting the most suitable method of stakeholder engagement remains absent. This study introduces the Generative Method Recommender Model (GMRM) to satisfy this need. Through a combination of Multi-Criteria Decision-Making and Bayesian Belief Network techniques, GMRM provides a tailored method-selection paradigm that considers contextual specifications for stakeholder engagement. This model transcends traditional boundaries by illuminating the relationships between practical principles of stakeholder engagement and offering conditional recommendations, enabling urban planners and practitioners to make well-informed choices of methods for engagement realization, even in the face of uncertainties. The model's reliability is validated through sensitivity analysis, establishing GMRM as a solution to navigate the intricate landscape of method selection, fostering inclusive urban development and sustainability.

title: “How far is too far to order?”: Distance threshold effects and food-type heterogeneity in residents' willingness to use online food delivery services
A Fuller City: Rekindling the work of Buckminster Fuller in the age of planetary urban crisis
abstract: Crisis increasingly characterises urban life in the twenty-first century, as intersecting ecological, economic, geopolitical and social pressures converge on the city under conditions now described as permacrisis. This paper argues that the imaginaries of the twentieth-century designer Buckminster Fuller, when critically rather than celebratorily scrutinised, offer a productive resource for crisis-facing urban thought. Fuller is a frequent figure within design history but a marginal one within urban studies, and we bring the two fields into closer conversation to consider both the possibilities and the limits of his work. We do so through three of his designs, each read principally through one urban lens: the Geodesic Dome through architecture, the Tetrahedronal City for Tokyo Bay through infrastructure, and Skyrise for Harlem,through utopia. Read together we argue that urban studies is enriched by interrogating Fuller's designs, creating new opportunities to explore the contradictions inherent in his work and the politics they contain. We contend that Fuller's designs can enrich post-crisis urban imaginaries while cautioning against the seductive technological fixes they embody. Fuller, we conclude, is best read not as a blueprint for the post-crisis city but as a provocation to imagine it otherwise.

title: Data-driven urban planning: Real population estimation using water consumption records and tourism data
abstract: Accurately estimating de facto population in dynamic urban environments is essential for predictive planning, service provision, and Smart City resilience, particularly in areas with strong seasonal fluctuations. Census-based approaches lack temporal resolution and overlook transient populations, while alternative methods often rely on restricted data, high computational demands, or indirect proxies. This study presents a scalable computational framework for estimating de facto urban population at monthly resolution by integrating high-resolution smart-meter water consumption records with census data, climatic normalization, and tourism indicators. The approach integrates IoT-based remote-reading records, supply-contract databases, census information, and official accommodation registers within an end-to-end ETL pipeline to infer monthly population variations in Alicante (Spain) between 2022 and 2024. A thermal-correction model isolates temperature-driven changes in water demand, improving estimation accuracy. K-means clustering with Dynamic Time Warping identifies neighborhood-level seasonal patterns, distinguishing stable residential areas, high-tourism zones, and districts with marked summer vacancy. Results reveal a robust methodology for population estimation, rigorously verified through out-of-sample validation for 2024, yielding a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 6.34% and an R 2 = 0.9874. Between January and July 2024, Alicante experienced an estimated 8.78% population increase (+32,749 people). Coastal tourist neighborhoods showed summer rises above 50%, whereas central medium-to-high-income areas exhibited declines up to −22.2% due to seasonal displacement to second residences. Consolidated residential areas remained stable year-round, with deviations below 5%. The methodology offers a low-cost, high-resolution, and privacy-preserving tool for strategic decision-making in Smart Cities and is fully replicable in urban contexts equipped with domestic smart-metering infrastructure to capture resident and floating population dynamics.

title: Why smart mobility alone does not ensure accessibility? Social, spatial, and digital dimensions of mobility as a service in island contexts
abstract: Mobility as a Service (MaaS) is increasingly promoted as a key component of smart and sustainable urban mobility; however, empirical evidence on its capacity to deliver socially accessible and satisfactory travel experiences remains limited, particularly in constrained and insular contexts. Addressing this gap, this study investigates the role of social accessibility in MaaS and its impact on user experience, focusing on airport-to-city mobility in the island context of Sardinia, Italy. The research adopts a quantitative multi-method approach, combining a questionnaire survey ( N = 391) with Space Syntax analysis. The survey examines the association between perceived social accessibility, user experience and satisfaction, and perceived spatial accessibility through Pearson correlation and linear regression analyses. In parallel, syntactic segment analysis evaluates the topological accessibility of airport-to-city corridors in selected island urban systems. The results reveal that accessibility is not merely determined by the availability of services, but by the interaction between social inclusion, spatial configuration, economic affordability, digital integration, and temporal reliability. While public transport affordability and safety were generally perceived positively, fragmented digital platforms, inadequate pedestrian connections, and service unreliability during peak periods undermined overall user experience. These insights underscore that MaaS effectiveness depends as much on physical and institutional coherence as on technological innovation. By foregrounding accessibility as a multidimensional and lived experience, this study provides a grounded and actionable contribution to the development of more inclusive, resilient, and user-centred MaaS systems in island and peripheral contexts.

title: Bridging circularity and inclusion in urban metabolic transitions: Through the lens of waste system evolution in Almere, the Netherlands
abstract: Waste is a key material stock and flow in urban metabolism, and circular economy (CE) strategies are increasingly promoted to enhance resource efficiency and reduce environmental burdens. Yet CE practices do not always evolve in harmony with dynamic social needs, leading to exclusionary outcomes. To examine how circularity and inclusion interact in urban metabolic transitions, this paper analyses the evolution of Almere's waste system from the 1970s to the 2020s as a longitudinal case study.
