Using the Municipal Solid Waste Infrastructure System (MSWIS) model and a combination of qualitative and quantitative indicators, we identify three phases of sociotechnical system change. The findings reveal that while regulatory reforms and infrastructure upgrades advanced material recovery, more transformative outcomes emerged where inclusive governance arrangements and grassroots innovations were integrated into the waste system. Almere's experience demonstrates that when technological efficiency is aligned with social equity, waste systems can become engines of circular and inclusive urban transitions.

title: Corrigendum to “Development and validation of a smart destination perception scale for tourists and residents (SDPS): Evidence from Madrid [Cities 178 (2026) 107327]
Media framing and political discourse of Barcelona's urban transformations (2016–2024)
abstract: Superblocks have become a symbol of climate-oriented urbanism; however, their implementation has generated significant controversy, public protest, and electoral mobilisation. These conflicts reveal the inherently political nature of urban transformations, in which competing visions of the city are negotiated, resisted, and reimagined. As institutions, public discourse, and the media collectively shape public acceptability, this study examines how the press has constructed, amplified, and challenged narratives around superblocks, and how these discourses have influenced political debate and responsive planning. The analysis draws on 896 news articles and headlines concerning Barcelona's superblocks, published between 2016 and 2024. Using a natural language processing (NLP) model, the study traces temporal changes in the press sentiment and emotion. The findings indicate a persistent bias towards a negative tone. Emotions such as anger and fear appear alongside anticipation and joy, reflecting polarisation in public discourse around superblocks. Notably, peaks in negative media coverage coincide with periods of protest, urban lawfare, and electoral cycles. This pattern suggests that the media has both mirrored and reinforced conflictual framings of superblocks. By emphasising risks such as gentrification, participation deficits, and traffic disruption, the media have helped shape the political stakes of superblocks. Yet the analysis also suggests that legitimate criticisms prompted municipal responses to address these concerns. Additionally, the study identifies a dissonance between media framings and other indicators, suggesting a potential gap between journalistic accounts and lived urban realities. These findings highlight the importance of acknowledging the media's political role in shaping public acceptability and urban transformation processes.

title: Analysis of green practices priorities in local government units for sustainable development in Palestine: An analytical hierarchical process approach
Recreation versus conservation: The capitalization of parks and protected areas in the German housing market
abstract: The value of open space is often capitalized into higher residential property prices for homes located nearby. But is closer always better? We examine this question using a hedonic regression applied to pooled cross-sectional housing data from Germany spanning 2007–2023. We distinguish between two types of open space – parks and protected areas (PAs) – which differ in their primary objectives of recreation and conservation. Identification relies on fine-scale regional fixed effects combined with a difference-in-differences framework. We find that proximity to parks significantly increases home prices, with effects that attenuate as distance increases. In contrast, proximity to PAs outside their boundaries has little effect on prices, while properties located within PAs experience substantial price discounts. Using spatially referenced socio-economic data, we conduct a post-estimation analysis to quantify the aggregate value of open space and its distribution across income groups. We estimate the total value of parks at approximately €983 billion – about 4% of the housing stock. In terms of residential proximity, this value is distributed relatively evenly across income groups, though value-weighted analysis reveals that higher-income households capture a disproportionate share of the aggregate benefit, reflecting higher property values in wealthier neighborhoods near parks. The aggregate value of PAs is estimated at -€5.2 billion, though sensitivity analysis reveals this figure is highly uncertain, ranging from -€21 billion to +€16 billion.

title: “Food demons have taken over our cities”: Unpacking foodification and airbnbification of an historical market in a southern Europe city
abstract: This paper explores the interrelations between foodification, touristification, and airbnbification through an in-depth case study of a historical fish market area in Catania, a mid-sized city in southern Europe. Drawing on a mixed-method approach that combines on-site field surveys, GIS-based mapping, and long-term ethnography, the study explores how these processes, although spatio-temporally sequenced, become mutually reinforcing in a middle-sized city of Southern Europe characterized by a fragmented local governance, and without clear or coherent institutional tourism strategies. In so doing, first the paper provides a novel insight on the literature on foodification and its triangulation with tourism-driven transformation in a “peripheral” city of the Global North: food acts first as an urban manifestation of global consumption-driven restructuring, while, in a second stage, as a co-producer of touristification and airbnbification, which are growingly fostered by - and intertwined with - consumption of food. Moving across different scales - from the circumscribed space of the market to the surrounding neighbourhood, and from material transformations of retailscapes to the restructuring of symbolic everyday rhythms, the paper shows how touristification amplifies the symbolic and commercial remaking initiated by foodification, while airbnbification consolidates these dynamics by exacerbating the symbolic displacement of local retailscapes, deeply connected to the shift in urban imaginaries produced by the historical market's transformation.

title: Lived experiences of women in precarious housing conditions under different tenure statuses in selected cities of Ethiopia
abstract: Despite extensive research on urban housing precarity in Sub-Saharan Africa, limited attention has been paid to how women's lived experiences differ across diverse tenure arrangements, particularly beyond the conventional dichotomy of formal versus informal housing. This study addresses this gap by examining how precarious housing is experienced by women across different positions along the tenure continuum, using qualitative evidence from three Ethiopian cities: Addis Ababa, Mekelle, and Bahir Dar. Drawing on 108 in-depth interviews, the study employs the tenure continuum as an analytical lens to move beyond legal classifications and instead capture the varying bundles of rights, levels of perceived security, and infrastructural access associated with different tenure configurations. The findings show that women's experiences of housing precarity cannot be adequately explained by tenure status alone, as both formally rented kebele housing and informal settlements are characterized by significant insecurity and deprivation. By situating these experiences along the continuum, the study reveals how governance gaps, infrastructural deficits, and socio-economic constraints intersect to shape distinct yet overlapping forms of vulnerability. In doing so, the article demonstrates the analytical value of the tenure continuum for understanding housing precarity as a relational and context-dependent phenomenon, grounded in everyday lived experiences rather than formal legal categories.

title: Transit-associated land use patterns in selected station areas along Dar es Salaam's Bus rapid transit phase one corridor: A longitudinal assessment from 2005 to 2025
Beyond brain drain: Spatial and non-spatial determinants of highly skilled Turkish professionals' mobility to Dutch city-regions
Local governments, gender balance and service delivery performance
abstract: Previous research has examined how gender within local governments affects the relationship between municipal services and costs, using role congruence theory as a framework for understanding leadership competence. Drawing on arguments from social self-categorization theory, our study complements previous research by analyzing whether gender balance within these governments affects this relationship. From a binary categorization, considering the potential heterogeneity arising from the mayor's gender and the political ideology, our research analyzes whether greater gender balance within local government improves municipal performance. The results of this study, which were derived from regressions on corrected efficiencies obtained from a data envelopment analysis of 102 large Spanish municipalities with populations exceeding 50,000 inhabitants in the 2022 fiscal year, indicate that greater gender balance within the municipal government team leads to higher performance in service delivery when a female mayor is in office. The services' performance is also improved by the interaction between right-wing female mayors and gender diversity within government.

title: From nature to urbanization: Evolutionary models of green space in landscape cities over the past 60 years — A case of Hangzhou
Child-friendly streets: Inferring street environments through vision-based child movement behaviors for child-friendly cities
A tale of many cities: The role of inter-municipal food networks in changing the dominant food regime
abstract: Inter-municipal food networks (IFNs) have become an increasingly prominent vehicle for local governments to develop more social and ecologically sustainable urban food strategies. IFNs are highly diverse, operating at different scales and specializing on different practices, from mutual exchange to policy advocacy, thereby offering a wide range of possibilities for local governments to develop transformative capacities. Yet, surprisingly little research has examined the inter-municipal dynamics and impact of IFNs, as most studies remain focused on individual city case studies. This raises questions about how IFNs operate and to what extent they contribute to sustainable transformations within their member cities. This article explores these questions through a systematic review of academic literature on IFNs. It seeks to identify the scale, governance modes, political activities, as well as drivers and barriers to impact of IFNs studied in the literature. Drawing on the multilevel perspective, the article discusses what we know about IFN's potential for food regime transformation, and which questions remain unanswered. While it finds some indications that IFNs can inspire new urban food strategies and respond to diverse political economic contexts, significant knowledge gaps remain concerning their scale, organizational governance, ambitions and impact, which inhibits a comprehensive assessment of their transformative potential.

title: Unpacking the impact of China's low-carbon city pilot policy on physiological health among middle-aged and older adults and its heterogeneous effects: Evidence from integrated macro-micro national data
Associations of school neighbourhood built environment profiles with active commuting behaviour in Spanish adolescents
abstract: Objective To investigate whether school neighbourhood built environment (SNBE) profiles are associated with adolescents' active commuting to/from school (ACS) and related outcomes (i.e., basic psychosocial needs, motivation, and barriers). Methods A total of 311 adolescents (14.36 ± 0.63 years; 54.34% girls) self-reported ACS-related outcomes. The SNBE was assessed at both the macro- and micro-scale . Principal component analysis followed by hierarchical clustering was applied to classify schools into different macro-scale and micro-scale profiles. Multilevel linear mixed-effects models and multilevel logistic regression models were conducted to examine the associations between ACS and related outcomes and macro- and micro-scale environment profiles. Results At the macro-scale level, no significant associations were observed between SNBE profiles and ACS-related behavioural or psychosocial outcomes. Similarly, no significant independent associations were observed for micro-scale environments. However, a non-significant tendency towards higher odds of active commuting from school was observed in high-support micro-scale environments (OR = 2.60; p = 0.069). On the other hand, when both environmental scales were considered jointly, adolescents attending schools in green and walkable macro-scale and high-support micro-scale environments reported lower planning/psychosocial barriers (β = −0.50; p = 0.004), as well as higher intrinsic (β = 0.75; p = 0.038) and integrated motivation (β = 1.10; p = 0.002). In addition, these combined environments were associated with greater odds of actively commuting to school (OR = 7.31; p = 0.012), while a non-significant tendency was observed for commuting from school (OR = 4.75; p = 0.098). Conclusion This study suggests that independent associations of macro- and micro-scale school neighbourhood environments with adolescents' ACS and related outcomes were limited. However, the combined presence of favourable macro- and micro-scale environments was associated with lower planning/psychosocial barriers, higher autonomous motivation, and greater odds of ACS.

title: Cross-scale collaborative planning approach for sustainable water management: A blue-green infrastructure vision for the Huangyan–Taizhou Region, China
abstract: Accelerating urbanization and growing water demand make cross-scale approaches to sustainable water management imperative across hydrologically connected urban regions. Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) has long emphasized coordinated, multi-scale governance linking upstream–downstream allocation, basin-scale management, stakeholder participation, and institutional coordination. Yet translating these principles into spatially explicit, community-supported planning actions remains challenging. Blue–green infrastructure (BGI) can serve as a practical, place-based instrument for this translation, but existing BGI research remains fragmented by scale, limiting coordination between regional strategies and local implementation, especially in rapidly urbanizing and institutionally complex contexts. In response, this study develops a cross-scale collaborative planning approach integrating multi-level mapping and stakeholder engagement for BGI planning. Conducted within the six-year Sino–German Urban–Rural Assembly project (2019–2024), it is applied in the rapidly urbanizing Huangyan–Taizhou Region, China, where inequitable water allocation, pollution, ecosystem degradation, and shifting sociocultural water dynamics pose major challenges. We investigate: (1) How can cross-scale mapping translate regional water concerns into localized BGI actions? (2) What governance mechanisms enable map-based analysis to support coordinated multi-stakeholder planning? (3) How can cross-scale collaborative BGI planning be embedded in top-down local governance while enabling bottom-up participation and cross-departmental coordination? The approach integrates regional visioning through expert workshops, transect-scale co-mapping of agricultural and industrial transition zones, and site-level co-design refined via workshops and interviews. Findings show that cross-scale mapping strengthens regional-to-site linkages, while collaborative planning translates analysis into stakeholder-supported interventions across scales and institutions. The study delivers actionable BGI strategies for Huangyan–Taizhou and a transferable framework for similar regions.

title: Measuring gentrification through commercial amenities: The case of Paris
Global analysis of functional patterns of individual cities in scientific collaboration networks
Moving to nowhere: The impact of informal employment on the social integration of rural-urban migrants in Chinese cities
From participation to relational infrastructuring: Rethinking inclusion in contemporary placemaking
abstract: This article advances a relational understanding of placemaking, examining how inclusive urban development emerges through the interplay of institutional structures, civic agency, and participatory design. Moving beyond the binary of top-down versus bottom-up planning, the study proposes the Relational Placemaking for Inclusion (RPI) framework, which comprises three interdependent dimensions: temporality, institutional resonance, and design agency. Drawing on three European case studies the article explores how inclusion is enacted, negotiated, and sometimes constrained across diverse urban contexts. The analysis shows that participation alone does not yield inclusive outcomes; rather, inclusion emerges when civic relationships extend beyond project cycles, institutions absorb and legitimate emergent practices, and mediators curate participation in ways that recognize plural knowledge and attend to power. By reframing placemaking as relational infrastructuring, the article advances a socio-technical understanding of how public space is co-produced and how placemaking can provoke institutional and societal transformation. It concludes with propositions for shifting placemaking analysis from events to relationships and from outputs to capabilities, offering guidance for scaling inclusive placemaking in diverse governance settings.

title: Affordable yet constrained: Is shared housing a long-term strategy for migrants' settlement in high-cost cities?
Causal impacts of multimodal network expansions on urban mobility: Evidence from a fast-growing megacity
Smarter and healthier cities in the era of AI: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: The smart city agenda has focused on technological solutions to urban problems. However, rapid social, environmental, and technological change, especially the rise of AI, have revealed significant transformations, highlighting the need for a state-of-the-art academic concept. This study demonstrates the concept of the Smarter and Healthier city, grounded in a systematic review of smart and healthy city research using the PRISMA protocol. We analyse the literature across three domains (governance, environment, and modelling) with particular emphasis on the AI. Our review identifies a substantial rise in research on smart cities and healthier cities, with IoT, healthcare, and air quality emerging as dominant keywords. Thematic analysis demonstrates that the AI is driving conceptual transformations within the governance domain toward (1) integrative framework, (2) participatory, and (3) anticipatory governance, and within the environmental domain toward (1) dense IoT and crowdsensing infrastructures, (2) multimodal and transferable learning approaches, and (3) edge intelligence architectures. We further propose core principles to address the challenges in the smarter and healthier city development, emphasising (1) ethical safeguards, (2) environmental justice, and (3) trustworthy AI systems. Overall, this study contributes to the evolving smarter and healthier cities framework by offering a robust conceptual foundation for future research.

title: City-level green space coverage as protective urban infrastructure for healthy ageing
Density-based incentives in private residential projects to promote social integration? Evidence on its difficulties
Integrating AI into urban vitality promotion: The impact of building morphology on daily consumption quality in Hong Kong
Perceiving “city of proximity” beyond spatial closeness: Explaining travel and consumption behavior through perceptions and preferences
abstract: Proximity-based planning has gained traction as a powerful concept for neighborhood planning and design in response to the mobility restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic—evidenced by the global enthusiasm for the 15-Minute City. However, deterministic strategies and objective measurements of physical proximity have left little room for understanding how people perceive a city of proximity, as well as their desires and needs. The present study seeks to uncover the perceptual dimensions of the concept by examining how these perceptions influence travel and consumption behavior, moving beyond mere consideration of objective proximity. To do so, this research employs structural equation modeling, based on data from an online survey conducted in the Brussels-Capital Region (Belgium), to analyze how public perceptions and individual preferences impact perceived proximity and, subsequently, self-reported travel and consumption behaviors in a complex relationship. The results show that preferences toward urban facilities and mobility are stronger contributors to behaviors than perceptions of facilities and built environments. Another key finding confirms that the perception of proximity is a central mediating factor in understanding what influences behavior. This is especially relevant when objective factors like physical environments and availability of opportunities provide an insufficient explanation. The research also cautions against overemphasizing specific thresholds, soft mobility, and neighborhood self-sufficiency, as this may negatively impact travel behavior and reduce the concept's inclusiveness. These results add to the rapidly expanding field of proximity-based planning by enhancing our understanding of how perceptual determinants are associated with the concept of the city of proximity and behaviors.

title: A spatiotemporal comparison of urban shrinkage in Chinese and American urban agglomerations: Evidence from nighttime light data (2012−2020)
How can land development intensity and land use benefit be coordinated in high-speed railway station areas? Evidence from 1570 station areas in China
Social perception of cadastral tax implementation in Poland in the context of global cadastre modernization trends: A pilot study on social readiness and implementation barriers
abstract: The transformation of the real estate taxation system from an area-based model to a cadastral (ad valorem) model represents one of the key challenges for Central and Eastern European countries. Despite international recommendations, Poland maintains an area-based system, which is widely considered socially unjust and economically inefficient. This article analyzes the Polish legal and social reality in the light of tax economic theory and global trends in cadastre modernization, highlighting the diversity of cadastral reform models worldwide and the drive toward their unification. The article presents the results of a pilot study conducted in May 2025 among a group of experts: researchers, land surveyors, spatial planners, property valuers, and local government officials. The study revealed that only 10.9% of the respondents support the introduction of a cadastral tax, while over half (50.9%) oppose it, and 38.2% remain undecided. The primary barrier consists not only of technological issues (the quality of cadastral data), but also of strong concerns regarding a drastic increase in the fiscal burden (average threat rating of 4.43/5) and the risk of economic impoverishment of low-income groups (the 'asset rich, income poor' phenomenon). The article suggests that Poland primarily requires a profound reform of its cadastre, and the lack of acceptance within the expert community serves as a crucial warning signal for policymakers. This indicates the necessity of considering the implementation of hybrid models and protective educational campaigns in the perspective of changing the taxation system

title: Beyond static census: Hourly mobile phone data reveals 2.6-fold underestimation of urban flood exposure
abstract: Accurate population exposure assessment is critical for urban flood disaster management, yet traditional approaches rely on static census data that fail to capture dynamic activity patterns. Using hourly mobile phone signaling data from four rainstorm events in Suqian, China, in 2023, we develop an analysis framework integrating baseline estimation, anomaly pattern recognition, and severity-graded dynamic exposure assessment. Hourly analysis reveals a W-shaped population response pattern during a prolonged daytime rainfall, with dual troughs aligned with morning and evening commutes. This demonstrates that disaster impacts couple with urban activity rhythms rather than depending solely on rainfall intensity. Population behavioral responses reveal resilience inequalities across functional zones. Industrial areas show high disturbance sensitivity, with 69–97.5% of grids exhibiting declining population responses, while residential zones demonstrate sheltering capacity, with up to 28.6% of grids showing ascending responses during disaster events. Critically, dynamic exposure assessment reveals that static census-based methods are estimated to underestimate exposure by 2.6-fold on average, with underestimation occurring in over 84% of industrial zones during daytime events. Our differentiated risk zoning framework identifies “High-High,” “Population-Driven,” and “Hazard-Driven” priority zones, enabling targeted resource allocation aligned with specific risk drivers. These findings suggest that hourly-resolution dynamic assessment can play a critical role in accurate flood exposure characterization and evidence-based emergency planning in rapidly urbanizing contexts.

title: Spatial-economic networks in global cities: Multinational firms and urban affiliations from 2010 to 2019
abstract: Global cities function as pivotal nodes in the spatial organization of the world economy, where multinational firms, capital flows, and regional dependencies shape interconnected urban networks. While prior research has focused on hierarchical dominance and spatial clustering patterns, this study investigates how these networks evolve over time through longitudinal analysis (2010–2019) of owner-subsidiary linkages among urban centers. To do so, we develop a novel network-analytic framework that identifies global cities, maps their evolving affiliation networks, and traces the changing structure of these affiliation networks. Our empirical analysis reveals where the global cities of New York, London, Paris, and Tokyo exert particularly strong influence, highlighting the world subregions most closely tied to these urban hubs. We interpret these patterns by situating them within historical path dependencies, institutional contexts, and geopolitical dynamics that shape the uneven evolution of global urban networks. European cities exhibit fluid and shifting affiliations, whereas North American cities display more stable and persistent ties, underscoring regional variation in global city formation. We extend Taylor’s interlocking network theory by integrating complementary perspectives from urban political economy, global production networks, innovation and knowledge cities, migration and cultural capital, and urban governance and state power. Together, these frameworks deepen the theoretical foundations underlying our empirical findings and position global cities as differentially embedded actors within multinational capitalism, with implications for understanding spatial inequality and regional resilience.

title: Delivering development and governance through local institutions: Slum dwellers associations in the smart cities of an eastern Indian state
Pioneer Regionalism in China's city-regions
Urban crime trends in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic: Evidence from Krakow, Poland
Rental compound housing: A culturally beneficial need sustaining livelihoods in urban spaces in Ghana
Stories of control: Digitalization narratives in smart city strategy papers of German municipalities
abstract: Most definitions of smart cities refer to improving citizens' quality of life through the use of digital technology in urban areas. This article aims to provide a better understanding of the intentions that guide cities with different structural characteristics (city size, centrality, or socioeconomic growth) in the planning and implementation of digitalization measures with regard to the digitalization's impact on quality of life of citizens. Using a mixed-methods approach, digitalization narratives in the smart city strategy documents of 12 German cities are examined using the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) and the analytical lens of the capability approach. Six distinct digitalization narratives in three public problem areas are identified in the Smart City Strategies, with particular attention being paid to the characterization of citizens and the narrated influence of digitalization on their capabilities. Evaluating the frequency and distribution of narrative-use allows the identification of narrative profiles that are examined for differences and similarities using cluster analysis. To explore the influence of the local context on the composition of narrative profiles and clusters, the relationship with urban structural characteristics is examined, and other potential influences are discussed.

title: Taking refuge: Prioritising park climate adaptation strategies based on urban design and planning professionals' insights
abstract: This novel paper assesses the perceived effectiveness of strategies to improve thermal comfort in local parks under hot daytime conditions across the Hot semi-arid (BSh), Hot desert (BWh), and Mediterranean (Csa) Köppen climate regions in Western Australia. This assessment is conducted through a survey of urban design and planning professionals ( n = 87) from Local Government, State Government, and private practice, and, as such, delivers a case study of locally initiated and adapted planning for climate change. The survey results indicate a consistent preference for nature-based solutions to improve thermal comfort on hot days. This preference raises questions about water availability for irrigation, given reduced rainfall and diminished evapotranspiration-related cooling as humidity increases. Despite such challenges, the survey findings provide an evidence base for urban design and planning professionals and urban policymakers to reimagine existing local parks, in part, as climate refuges with improved thermal comfort in summer conditions.

title: What rights and whose rights count? Housing activism in urban redevelopment in Shenzhen
abstract: The politics of spatial inclusion in Chinese urban redevelopment is largely dominated by the state, developers and owners. Tenants lacking property rights are typically considered passive victims with little agency. Linking the discourse of “right to the city” to China's urban redevelopment processes, this paper argues that urban villages are spatial products of broader deficits in the rights to appropriate and participate. Our empirical data focus on both the housing activism of property owners and the concurrent practices of non-owners, comprising migrant tenants, NGOs and intellectuals. The findings illustrate how “privileged recognition” functions as a governmental rationality that prioritises the ordering of aesthetic space and property owners. This rationally is operationalised through a specific suite of instruments, including redevelopment initiatives, regulatory frameworks, market-determined compensation, consent rules, mobilisation of police forces and digital platform censorship, that collectively recompose resident subjectivities and exacerbate the marginalisation of migrants. The results suggest that the right to the city in urban China needs to be extended to protect and involve non-owners in building people's cities.

title: Nonlinear and spatial spillover effects of manufacturing agglomeration on urban ecological resilience
The invisible hand of God: faith-based organizations and the governance of food poverty in Rome
abstract: Despite increasing attention in urban studies to the role of third-sector actors in food aid provision, limited research has examined how faith-based organizations, as key actors within urban food systems, shape strategies and practices for addressing food poverty in advanced economies. Adopting a governance lens, this article investigates the conditions that have enabled faith-based organizations to become dominant food aid providers in Rome and the implications of this role for policy coordination and institutional change. The study applies a qualitative research design based on documentary analysis, non-participant observation, and semi-structured interviews. Findings show that welfare retrenchment and weak public steering, combined with the historically accumulated material and immaterial resources and organizational capacity of major faith-based organizations, have entrenched these actors at the centre of Rome's food aid system. Over recent decades, this configuration has sustained service continuity and emergency responsiveness, but it has also reproduced a fragmented and predominantly charitable model characterised by power asymmetries and scarce policy integration. Recent governance and policy developments have broadened participation and advanced a more rights-based and multidimensional understanding of food poverty. However, they have yet to produce a substantial redistribution of resources, institutional authority, and responsibilities. The article concludes that Rome is undergoing an incipient and uncertain transition towards more coordinated food poverty governance and comprehensive policy arrangements. Consolidating this shift will require enduring public commitment, stable funding, equitable access to resources, effective collaboration among actors, and reliable systems for data collection and accountability.

title: Process justice in transit-oriented development in Hong Kong: The case of Kai Tak station development
abstract: Original conceived to create equitable and sustainable communities, Transit-oriented Development (TOD) has received increasing scholarly attention on its adverse social equity and justice implications. However, existing research largely focuses on outcomes and less on justice in the planning processes. In this paper, we aim to analyse process justice in the planning of Kai Tak station TOD as a case to gain insights into the planning of TOD in Hong Kong. Guided by an analytical framework we developed for analysing justice in TOD, we examined stakeholders’ interaction and dynamics in its planning process mainly through the lens of Rules-in-Use under the Institution Assessment and Development (IAD) model. Through this, we found four key issues in the planning process of Kai Tak station development: (i) dominance and unilateral nature of government actors, (ii) imbalances between ‘transit’ and ‘housing development’ stakeholders, (iii) different (and often opposing) sets of Rules-in-Use observed by the formal project team and external stakeholders, and (iv) inconsistency and ambiguity in many of the Rules-in-Use. On this basis, we put forth some recommendations with a view to providing policymakers with insights to implement TOD more justly in Hong Kong’s future.

title: Sensing the city: Experiences of loneliness among students in Amsterdam
abstract: There is ample evidence that loneliness is shaped by the environments in which people live, work and spend their leisure time. While quantitative studies have demonstrated links between characteristics of the built environment and loneliness, emerging qualitative research highlights how this relationship is mediated through embodied experiences. This article advances this line of research by focusing on how the affective and multi-sensory qualities of urban environments – such as sound, light, smell and atmospheres – influence individuals' feelings of loneliness in their daily lives. Using a photo-elicitation method, 35 undergraduate students (aged 19–25) reflected on places in and around the city of Amsterdam (the Netherlands) that positively or negatively affect their experiences of loneliness. The thematic analysis of the reflections identifies four binary place dimensions that shape loneliness in diverse ways: 1) places for lingering versus movement, 2) calm versus stimulating settings, 3) sheltered versus exposed spaces, and 4) personalised versus anonymous places. In view of this complex place-loneliness dialectic, this study concludes that policy and planning approaches should move beyond a singular focus on place interventions that stimulate social interaction. Instead, it should prioritise equitable access to a diverse spatial spectrum that acknowledges the varied ways individuals engage with places when feeling lonely. This range includes both communal, sensory-stimulating places that allow for distraction, and sheltered, calm settings that afford solitude and self-reflection. • Feelings of loneliness emerge and transform through engagements with multiple places on a daily basis. • This is contingent on the affective and multi-sensory qualities of places. • Both sensory-rich places and calm settings can help reduce feelings of loneliness. • Policy and planning practices should prioritise equitable access to this diversity of places.

title: Between city and countryside: The (un)sustainable development of peri-urban areas (PUA) of large cities in Poland – The case of Warsaw
abstract: The paper investigates the dynamics of spatial development in the peri-urban area of Warsaw, Poland. It focuses on the processes of suburbanization and urban sprawl occurring within the city's administrative boundaries and its neighbouring rural municipalities. Drawing on spatial data from 2014 to 2024, the study identifies the most intensive zones of border residential development and analyzes the morphological characteristics of emerging housing patterns. The research reveals a fragmented and functionally monotonous urban fabric, heavily reliant on individual transportation and lacking in public infrastructure and services. These patterns contradict the principles of sustainable urban planning. Adopting the concept of the “urban fringe zone” from the existing literature, the study examines this transitional space where urban and rural features intersect and proposes a typology of development forms based on density, continuity, diversity, and multifunctionality. The findings underscore the need for integrated spatial planning across administrative boundaries and advocate for the formal recognition of peri-urban zones as distinct planning entities to better manage urban expansion and mitigate its negative environmental and social impacts.

title: Inequality in bridging the digital divide among older adults across 115 Chinese cities during the public health emergencies
Is the accessible truly walkable? Does proximity to services translate into walking?
The role of living labs for cities sustainable transition: evidence from the Turin living lab
abstract: The transition to sustainability has become imperative in mitigating the ecological impact of human activities. Living labs, as experimental environments within cities, offer a dynamic platform for testing and refining sustainable solutions. Local governments are increasingly turning to Living Labs as a means to confront sustainability issues. The study aims to comprehend how cities can promote sustainability. Accordingly, we analyzed the case study of the Turin City Lab. This research shows the importance of Living Labs in fostering interactions among stakeholders, accelerating innovation, and facilitating sustainable transition. The direct approach facilitated by Living Labs emerges as a powerful tool, capable of refining innovative ideas and meeting citizens' needs, acting as a catalyst, and laying the foundation for the transformation of cities into vibrant innovation hubs.

title: Spatial exclusion on public land: Fragmented governance and Vancouver's golf courses
abstract: Cities face growing pressure to justify how scarce urban land is allocated and whose needs it serves. This article analyzes spatial exclusion in Vancouver, British Columbia, a Canadian city under housing and land-use pressure. The analysis centers on municipal golf courses as an understudied site of urban governance: they occupy extensive public land while limiting everyday use through pricing, design, and activity-specific requirements. I use a mixed-methods design that combines distributional spatial analysis of golf courses across Vancouver, including inequality metrics and tract-level models, with qualitative analysis of governance processes. The spatial component examines the concentration and socio-demographic patterning of proximity to golf-course land. I examine Langara Golf Course as a focal, revelatory governance case through which actors contest yet ultimately stabilize these broader land-allocation patterns. The qualitative analysis draws on interviews with former mayors, councillors, and Park Board commissioners, alongside planning documents and deliberations. The analysis identifies three governance pathways associated with the persistence of access-limiting public land use: fragmented authority across governing bodies; legacy zoning and long-term recreational designations that constrain reconsideration; and arm's-length administrative arrangements that diffuse accountability while preserving exclusive uses of public land. The article closes by advancing three policy takeaways to enhance spatial inclusion: the need to clarify authority and accountability across overlapping municipal institutions; the importance of revisiting legacy zoning and long-term recreational designations on public land; and the value of redesigning participatory processes to ensure redistributive and access-oriented claims are incorporated into land-use decision-making. • Vancouver golf courses occupy vast public land while restricting everyday access. • Golf courses are ~1% of park sites but ~13–19% of total park area in Vancouver today. • Mixed-methods design links spatial exclusion patterns to urban governance structure. • Exclusion persists via fragmented authority and legacy land-use designations rules. • Policy reforms clarify authority and redesign participation toward access outcomes.

title: Geographies in flux - how time and location influence shrinking medium-sized cities
abstract: Urban shrinkage has emerged as a significant challenge across Europe, particularly for medium-sized cities (MSCs) with populations between 20,000 and 100,000. While previous research has largely focused on demographic decline in large cities, the spatial and institutional dynamics of shrinkage in MSCs remain underexplored. This study offers a comparative, longitudinal analysis of MSCs in Germany and Poland, two countries with different urban systems and planning traditions. Drawing on a harmonised shrinkage score composed of six demographic and socioeconomic indicators, the paper investigates spatial patterns over 15 years (2003–2018 for Germany; 2006–2021 for Poland). Spatial tools, including Moran's I, k-means clustering, and multivariate regression, are used to explore how proximity to large and metropolitan cities, as well as regional context, influences city trajectories. Results show that in Poland, shrinkage has intensified over time, particularly in the southern and eastern regions, while growth is concentrated around a few large urban centres. In Germany, spatial patterns are more stable: growth is concentrated in the southwest and around metropolitan areas, while shrinkage remains moderate but geographically selective. Multivariate models reveal that proximity to large cities (in Poland) and metropolitan centres (in Germany) negatively correlates with shrinkage scores, but regional structures and governance contexts explain more variation. The study identifies six MSC typologies and highlights the need for spatially and institutionally differentiated planning approaches. By integrating spatial and statistical methods across national contexts, this paper contributes to a more nuanced understanding of urban shrinkage as a territorially embedded and governance-dependent process.

title: Editorial Board
Toward precision urban resilience: Integrating multimodal large language models with spatial analytics for fire risk governance
Decomposition of anthropogenic and climate forces of carbon sequestration in the urban agglomeration
abstract: Past human activities and climate change have jointly affected ecosystem carbon sequestration in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) during 2001–2020. This study estimated the net primary productivity using the Carnegie–Ames–Stanford Approach model, integrating meteorological data, NDVI and land cover. Temporal trends were quantified via the Mann–Kendall (MK) test and Theil-Sen's slope estimator. Driving forces of carbon sequestration dynamics were assessed through partial correlations analysis between climate variables and carbon sequestration changes. The contribution of climatic versus anthropogenic factors were decomposed using a spatially constrained residual trend method, enabling identification of dominant drivers of ecosystem restoration and degradation. Results reveal that the average carbon sequestration was 987.7 (± 68.5) gC/m 2 /year, with a total annual carbon sequestration of 52.80 (± 3.75) TgC/year. Spatially, distribution of carbon sequestration displayed a pattern of high value peripherally and low values centrally. Carbon sequestration in human-dominated ecosystems showed a relatively low but increasing trend, while natural ecosystems maintained relatively high and stable sequestration rates. Interannual variation in the carbon sequestration flux remained within 7%, with a slight increasing trend of 6 (±12.5) gC/m 2 /year. The ecological quality improvement offset the negative effects of carbon sequestration area shrinkage. Climate factors alone affected 36.2% of the GBA, while 63.8% were affected by both climate and anthropogenic factors. Solar radiation and precipitation imposed positive contributions on carbon sequestration, whereas temperature exerted a negative effect. Human activities contributed a substantial positive trend (6.68 gC/m 2 /year) to carbon sequestration, contrasting with minor negative contribution from climate change (−0.46 gC/m 2 /year). For ecosystem degradation, human activities contributed 10.8% and climate change for 9.55%. Conversely, for ecosystem restoration, human activities contributed 55.4%, compared to 18.4% for climate change. The five clusters based on the trajectory and contributors, as well as natural and socioeconomic factors showed strong spatial stratified heterogeneity of carbon sequestration.

title: Public value mapping in the smart city: Assessing emerging urban technologies
abstract: City governments must increasingly grapple with how to assess and deploy new and often disruptive technologies to advance public policy goals and community needs. While technology companies assert the transformative change smart technologies offer, significant tensions exist between the market values sought by industry and the public values that city governments are responsible for supporting. In this paper, we analyze two smart city technology cases – facial recognition in Portland, Oregon and autonomous vehicles in Tempe, Arizona – using public value mapping, a concept from public administration and science policy. This process allows for an evaluation of the mismatch between public values and market values. The two case studies show two different approaches to governing emerging technologies and different trajectories based on previous policy efforts. Our analysis suggests that increased cooperation between government, the public, and industry can benefit both public and private interests in relation to public value goals. Through our analysis of these case studies, we also demonstrate how public value mapping can be applied in practice by urban planners and other policy makers tasked with implementing smart city technologies. Public value mapping adds to an increasingly diverse toolkit available to policy makers to ensure that the development of policies and plans that more closely align technology deployment with public value outcomes.

title: Geographies and changes in homeownership in the United States, 1970–2020
Does urbanization formalize the economy? The role of local governance in Vietnam
Ideal migrants in an ideal city: Discursive constructions of talent in Hong Kong's relocation branding campaign
Spatial governance under polycrisis: Reconfiguring agglomeration policy
abstract: Agglomeration policy has long been a dominant paradigm in spatial development, premised on the assumption that large, integrated city-regions drive national economic growth through productivity, innovation, and global integration. This paper examines how this paradigm is reworked under conditions of polycrisis, a durable state in which economic, geopolitical, and institutional shocks interact and reinforce one another. We argue that, while a crisis is often addressed through recalibrating policy tools and objectives, polycrisis reshapes the underlying rationalities of spatial planning. Focusing on Russia, the study analyses how national spatial priorities shift from growth and competitiveness toward territorial stabilisation, population retention, and the management of systemic vulnerability. It compares the 2019 and 2024 Spatial Development Strategies, drawing on policy documents, implementation materials, and expert discussions, and applies a process-tracing approach to reconstruct changes across two planning cycles. The findings show that agglomeration policy is not a universally stable development model but a contingent framework dependent on growth, openness, and functional integration. As these conditions erode under polycrisis, agglomeration policy is reworked from a governance technology of growth into a mechanism of territorial anchoring and control, signalling a broader shift from development to stabilisation in spatial planning.

title: Revisiting the 15-min city through accessibility assessment: A critical systematic review of FMC-based studies
abstract: Proximity-centered planning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. In particular, the 15-minute city (FMC) and other X-minute notions are widely promoted as approaches to support sustainable and equitable urban living. Despite this growing interest, there is a lack of systematic reviews that assess how these proximity-based frameworks, especially the FMC, have been operationalized in transport accessibility studies. This study conducts a systematic and critical review of 149 publications that applied the FMC to evaluate accessibility. The analysis examines five domains that repeatedly appear in the literature: operational and methodological design, social equity and inclusion, implementation feasibility, governance and participation, and the quality and scale of services. The findings indicate that most studies rely on a 15-minute threshold, prioritize quantitative spatial methods, and focus on residential and leisure amenities, while essential services such as work and education are significantly underexamined. Also, limited engagement with socio-demographic diversity, low stakeholder participation, and minimal inclusion of public transport further limit the applicability of current assessments. The scale and quality of services are rarely assessed, leading to an emphasis on potential accessibility rather than actual accessibility. According to the findings, existing practices do not fully align with the conceptual intentions of proximity-based planning and may limit the FMC's adaptability across diverse contexts. Future research should pay more attention to standardized service definitions, context-sensitive thresholds, multimodal mobility approaches, and participatory strategies. The results of this research are essential for enhancing robustness, inclusivity, and policy relevance of the FMC as a tool for accessibility planning.

title: Marrakech at the intersection: Hybrid identity and the politics of urban inclusion
abstract: In Marrakech, urban space is increasingly governed through the instrumentalization of local identity as a tool of economic development. This paper examines how the medina, historically a lived, adaptive, and socially-dense urban fabric, has become a primary site through which hybrid local identity is fixed and mobilized in service of tourism-led, neoliberal urbanism. Building on the distinction between plural identities, as multiple and competing identity claims, and hybrid identity, where one synthesis is stabilized as the legitimate representation of place, the paper argues that exclusion emerges not only through heritage commodification but through the institutionalization of a single, governable narrative. Drawing on diachronic morphological analysis, cartographic mapping, and an audit of planning instruments, the study traces how this process extends colonial logics of aesthetic fixing and epistemic control. Framed through spatial justice and the “right-to-the-city”, this study shows how selective preservation and visibility regimes recast the medina as an open-air museum, producing a dual-spatial order: a selectively-regulated historic core preserved for global consumption, and a retrospectively-regulated periphery absorbing displaced populations. These dynamics reshape access to housing, public space, and mobility, displacing vulnerable populations toward peripheral areas while consolidating symbolic and economic value in the historic core. By situating Marrakech within broader debates on neoliberal urbanism and postcolonial governance, this paper contributes an empirically-grounded account of how identity-based urban strategies function as spatial tools of inclusion and exclusion. It concludes by outlining actionable pathways that re-centre resident agency, lived experiences, and bottom-up approaches in planning supporting inclusive forms of urban inhabitation.

title: Motorcycle safety outcomes on light-segregated corridors: An observational assessment of São Paulo's Blue Lane
abstract: Light-segregated motorcycle facilities are expanding in motorcycle-intensive cities, yet their safety effects remain uncertain when corridors are selected because of prior traffic volume and conflict. This study evaluates São Paulo's Blue Lane using a balanced monthly panel of 12,820 normalized named-road identifiers from January 2019 to October 2025, totaling 1,051,240 road-months and 37 treated identifiers. The analysis prioritizes within-treated-road estimates with small-cluster corrections and complements them with citywide two-way fixed-effects benchmarks, event-time and pseudo‑lead diagnostics, Callaway–Sant'Anna and Sun–Abraham estimators, count models, sensitivity analyses, and a System Dynamics model. Within treated roads, the CR2 estimate was imprecise (β = 0.595; SE = 0.494; 95% CI = −0.450 to 1.640; p = 0.246), with an 80% minimum detectable effect of 1.384 motorcycles per road-month, approximately 33% of the treated-road pre-treatment mean; CR3 inference was similarly inconclusive (p = 0.265). Although the citywide TWFE estimate was positive (β = 0.902; p = 0.008), a three-month pseudo‑lead reproduced nearly the entire association (β = 0.889; p = 0.002), a twelve-month pseudo-treatment was also positive (β = 0.513; p = 0.003), and pre-treatment trends were nonparallel (p < 0.001). Heterogeneity-robust estimates were inconclusive, while severity results were specification-sensitive and underpowered. The System Dynamics model shows that lower crash risk per unit of exposure could coexist with unchanged or higher aggregate crashes if motorcycle exposure increased, but it does not establish that this occurred. Overall, the evidence does not identify a post-implementation change attributable to the Blue Lane or demonstrate reduced motorcycle crash outcomes.

title: Uncovering hidden inequities in access to urban public spaces: A multimodal and configurational accessibility in island cities
abstract: Ensuring spatial equity and equitable access to public spaces remains a critical challenge in contemporary urban planning, particularly in geographically constrained island cities. This study develops an integrated analytical framework to assess multimodal accessibility and spatial equity in urban public squares by combining configurational accessibility, derived from space syntax analysis, with operational accessibility, evaluated through multimodal isochrone mapping and public transport accessibility. Focusing on three representative Sardinian cities, the research examines how urban spatial configuration and transport infrastructure jointly influence accessibility across walking, cycling, and wheelchair modes, with particular attention to people with reduced mobility (PRM). Space syntax is first employed to identify spatially integrated public squares, which subsequently serve as the basis for multimodal accessibility assessment. By integrating these complementary analyses within a sequential analytical workflow, the framework enables accessibility to be interpreted from both structural and functional perspectives, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of accessibility conditions in urban public spaces. The findings demonstrate that spatial centrality alone does not guarantee inclusive accessibility, as highly integrated locations may still present substantial barriers for wheelchair users owing to infrastructural limitations. By focusing on urban public squares—an important yet comparatively understudied category of public space—the study demonstrates how the complementary interpretation of urban morphology and multimodal accessibility can reveal spatial inequalities that remain overlooked when either approach is applied independently. These findings provide evidence-based insights for promoting more inclusive planning strategies and improving accessibility to public spaces in island and regional urban contexts.

title: The gender dimension of homeownership: Evidence from China
abstract: This paper presents findings on the relationship between gender and three key housing asset indicators in China: homeownership, second homeownership, and housing asset value. The analysis also considers whether having a son modifies the relationship between gender of the household head and the housing asset indicators. The empirical analysis found that male household heads are more likely to have homeownership, female household heads are more likely to own a second home, and female homeowners tend to own more expensive homes than male homeowners. These findings are robust across alternative functional forms and variable definitions. The results highlight the importance of exploring the differential likelihood of homeownership and second homeownership as well as disparities in housing asset values from a gender perspective.

title: Materialism and subjective well-being among rural migrant women in China: The mediating role of residential conditions
Housing developers' resilience in a crisis-prone region: An analysis for Turkey-Istanbul
Smart-city wellness interventions: An AI-driven ideal future self approach
State entrepreneurialism and the growth-equity trade-off: Dipiao and public rental housing in Chongqing, China
Promoting inclusive transit-oriented development in urban regeneration: A network-based spatial multi-objective optimization framework
Freight in the 15-min city: An exploration of key concepts
abstract: The 15-Minute City (15mC) concept, developed by Carlos Moreno, aims to address urbanisation challenges by ensuring that essential services and amenities are accessible within a 15-minute walk or cycle from residents’ homes. By promoting proximity-based living, the model aims to reduce dependence on motorised transport and foster more sustainable, human-centred urban environments. While the 15mC concept focuses on passenger mobility to reach activities, it overlooks the increasingly significant role of consumer-related urban freight movements. Ignoring the logistics dimension, however, risks undermining the core goals of the concept: sustainable accessibility for citizens. There is a need to operationalise the 15mC framework to recognise the influence of city logistics. Thus, the paper evaluates and extends the 15mC framework by embedding urban logistics and "freight thinking" into its foundations. It addresses a critical gap in both academic literature and policy practice by highlighting the role of freight transport in shaping the success of 15mC models. The extended framework proposed in this paper emphasises that freight transport introduces new design objectives, variables, and constraints for the development of the 15mC. Home delivery may reduce the demand for access to shopping areas. Accessibility of shops for people can be traded off against accessibility to pick-up points and competes with accessibility for freight carriers. Urban sprawl of logistics activities improves access for freight carriers but may reduce the performance of the 15mC for people. These complex relations between freight and passenger transport systems imply that 15mC designs cannot be developed in isolation for either user group.

title: Determinants of the spatial relationship between morphological and functional centers across different stages of economic development: Evidence from 338 ASEAN cities
Nonlinear relationships between public space recreational services and mental well-being: Mediating roles of passive and active exposure
The spatiality of informal settlement displacement: Insights from Mumbai, Ho Chi Minh City and Manila
The knowledge complementary potential of cities: Opportunities for technological diversification in multilocational firms
Negotiating city futures: Foundation-driven urban development in the governance gap
Do local politicians share their constituents' attitudes on housing policy?
abstract: In this paper, we combine a nationally representative survey of Canadians with a survey of more than 700 mayors and councillors in municipalities across Canada to explore (a) the extent to which politicians align with their constituents in their housing policy attitudes and (b) the extent to which politicians' views are more representative of more privileged local residents, such as homeowners. We find strong evidence of macrolevel attitudinal congruence: when local communities are more supportive of a housing policy proposals, local politicians tend to be more supportive as well. We also find that politicians' attitudes on housing are not more aligned with privileged local residents; instead, elite-mass alignment is primarily shaped by ideological congruence.

title: Street characteristics and obesity: Evidence from Toronto and Greater Manchester using a scalable GeoAI framework
abstract: Obesity is increasingly recognised as being shaped by the built environment, yet evidence remains incomplete regarding how eye-level street characteristics relate to obesity across different urban contexts. This study examines how street-level environmental characteristics are associated with obesity prevalence and whether these relationships differ across urban contexts. Using Greater Manchester (UK) and Toronto (Canada) as comparative case studies, we develop a scalable geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) framework that integrates Google Street View imagery, deep learning–based feature extraction, and machine-learning models. Objective street features and subjective perceptual attributes are analysed alongside neighbourhood-level environmental, socio-economic, and behavioural variables using Random Forest models with spatial block cross-validation and SHAP-based explainable AI. The results show that street-level characteristics contribute meaningfully to explaining spatial variation in obesity and exhibit pronounced non-linear and context-dependent associations. These findings highlight the importance of micro-scale street environments in urban health research and support more context-sensitive street-level planning interventions.

title: Exploring the role of built environment and regional context in promoting bicycle commuting: A neighborhood-level analysis in the United States
Assessing urban heatwave vulnerability through a multiscale and multicriteria GIS-based approach: Evidence from three Spanish cities
abstract: As climate change intensifies, heatwaves are becoming more frequent and severe, increasing risks for urban populations. This study presents a multiscale and multicriteria GIS-based methodology for assessing urban heatwave vulnerability, grounded in the IPCC framework and applied to three Spanish cities: Bilbao, Madrid, and Caceres. A key innovation lies in evaluating vulnerability at two spatial scales—buildings and open public spaces—which captures the existing interaction between them. The assessment integrates expert-defined indicators, AHP-based weighting and value function normalization, addressing constructive, socioeconomic, cultural and environmental factors. The methodology produces vulnerability maps that reveal spatial patterns and inform climate adaptation priorities for decision support. The results show that heatwave vulnerability is highly uneven within cities and strongly shaped by both the socioeconomic profile of the population and the characteristic of the urban fabric. The approach is transparent, scalable and adaptable, providing a valuable tool for urban heat waves adaptation and resilience planning.

title: The legitimacy of city networks in international multi-stakeholder governance
abstract: City networks have become consequential infrastructures of transnational urban governance, yet their institutional legitimacy remains under-theorised and under-measured. This article asks how they institutionalise legitimacy when public authority is redelegated by municipal and subnational governments rather than by sovereign states. We develop a framework centred on legality, accountability, legitimate membership and effectiveness, and examine it through two original datasets covering 102 city networks and board-level profiles in 36 networks. The analysis shows that heterogeneity is structured rather than random. Since the Rio/Agenda 21 period, city networks have diversified beyond older municipal-associational forms, while converging around assemblies, boards and secretariats. Procedural safeguards cluster together as a legitimacy package, especially in older, larger and more formalised networks. City networks are therefore neither miniature international organisations nor ordinary NGOs, but public-subnational authority arrangements whose legitimacy rests on legal anchoring, delegated organs, transparency, representation and performance-oriented coordination.

title: Evaluating the differential impacts of formal and informal environmental regulation on urban wellbeing
How culture shapes cities' economic resilience: Global evidence on individualism-collectivism
From the ground(water) up: How households are reshaping post-drought urban resilience in Cape Town
abstract: Urban water stress is a growing problem across the world. How city authorities and urban residents respond profoundly shapes the resilience of cities. This paper examines households' perspectives on groundwater as a resource for resilience to water stress, the ways in which this shapes collective post-drought resilience in Cape Town, and the evolving governance challenges this invokes. Based on interviews with 32 residents we show that groundwater use is more complex than urban elites exploiting a shared resource. More recent users tend to dig deeper for their water, are more concerned about water supply, and live on smaller properties in less affluent neighbourhoods. These changes are part of a newly emergent relationship between residents, the state, and water resources, partly in response to a loss of trust in the city government's ability to ensure water supply. Newer users of groundwater value it not just as a way to lower their cost for municipal bill; it is also something that can strengthen their own resilience, but that requires consideration about the fairness and sustainability of relying on a common resource in a highly unequal city. This is an important complement to critical analyses of the injustices that self-interested urban elites can cause by over-exploiting common resources. As groundwater use becomes more prevalent among residents, their informal influence on Cape Town's water future will grow. This study shows why nuancing our understanding of what drives such development is critical for cities that want to mobilise residents' potential to foster urban resilience.

title: SAFE-CITY-AI: Responsible governance of AI-enabled surveillance for mega sporting events
abstract: AI-enabled surveillance technologies are increasingly deployed at mega sporting events to support crowd management, security screening, access control, and real-time operational decision-making, often as part of broader smart city strategies aimed at enhancing urban efficiency and public safety. Despite their rapid uptake, existing research remains fragmented across technical, organisational, and ethical domains, offering limited guidance on how AI surveillance reshapes urban surveillance ecosystems or how governance should respond in high-risk, time-bounded event contexts. This study examines the adoption and governance of AI-driven surveillance in mega sporting events and develops a framework to support their responsible and ethical implementation. Based on a systematic review of 70 peer-reviewed studies, the paper synthesises key technologies, institutional actors, governance mechanisms, and recurring challenges shaping contemporary practice. The findings show that while AI surveillance adoption is accelerating, governance approaches remain uneven and reactive, with persistent concerns surrounding transparency, accountability, proportionality, data governance, vendor influence, and post-event surveillance legacies. In response, the study proposes SAFE-CITY-AI, a responsible governance framework that provides principles and practical guidance for AI surveillance across pre-event planning, live operations, and post-event legacy management. By integrating smart city governance with responsible AI principles, this study offers a timely foundation for policymakers, event organisers, and researchers seeking to balance innovation, security, and public trust in the use of AI-enabled surveillance at global mega sporting events.

title: Urban vertical equity under the Matthew Effect: A case study of spatial differentiation of housing prices in Nanjing
Managing curb space in smart cities: Opportunities and challenges for emerging urban mobility
abstract: Curb space is a scarce, multifunctional urban resource that supports parking, PUDO, commercial loading/unloading, public transit stops, and outdoor seating for certain businesses. The rise of on-demand mobility services, shared micromobility fleets, autonomous sidewalk delivery robots, and electric vehicle infrastructure has intensified competition for curb space, creating complex management challenges in smart cities. This study presents a systematic literature review of curb space management, synthesizing existing research on influential factors, management strategies, demand modeling approaches, and data collection techniques. The findings highlight key determinants of curb space utilization and the reported effectiveness of various strategies across different contexts. Key factors influencing curb space utilization, including user types, traveler behavior, land use, and temporal dynamics, are identified. Management strategies such as flex zones, dynamic pricing, automated enforcement, designated PUDO zones, and real-time digital platforms are evaluated for their potential to optimize curb allocation. Building on these insights, we propose an integrated framework that combines digital curb platforms, predictive demand models, and Pareto-efficient allocation mechanisms to enable real-time, equitable, and adaptive curb space management for both traditional and emerging users. The framework leverages heterogeneous data streams, from vehicle telematics to micromobility and delivery robot operations, to inform dynamic allocation and minimize conflicts. This study highlights gaps in current research, including limited evaluation of multi-user interactions, multifunctional curb usage, and challenges related to technical integration and privacy. The findings provide a foundation for future research on scalable, adaptive, and empirically validated curb management solutions that support efficient, sustainable, and inclusive smart cities.

title: Toward inclusive city-regions: How inter-city cooperation shapes cultural-symbolic mobility
Optimizing 2D/3D urban form for cooling and jogging support across local climate zones in Shanghai: A machine learning and multi-objective approach
What influences the social acceptance of floating urban developments? Insights from a floating neighborhood in Amsterdam
abstract: There is increasing interest in floating urban developments as an innovative approach to urbanization pressures and climate change. Although smaller-scale floating housing projects already exist in the Netherlands and globally, developing and upscaling floating neighborhoods involves various complex governance challenges. Particularly the social and political acceptance of living on water remains a central, yet underexplored issue. Existing floating urban developments in the Western world are often engineered and largely focused on relatively wealthy home-owners, raising questions about inclusiveness, accessibility, and affordability that may influence broader social acceptance and long-term viability. Therefore, this article examines which aspects influence the social acceptance of floating urban developments and what can be learned from an existing floating neighborhood - IJburg's Steigereiland in Amsterdam - to support potential future upscaling. Drawing on renewable energy literature, we conceptualize social acceptance as comprising socio-political, market, and community dimensions. Using in-depth interviews, short street interviews, policy document analysis, and site visits, we analyze how these dimensions interact in practice. The findings show that floating developments face challenges of fragmented policy support, regulatory uncertainty, limited affordability and financing options. Community perceptions are ambivalent: there is a strong sense of community among floating residents, but limited integration with surrounding neighborhoods. Together, these dynamics form a reinforcing cycle in which socio-political ambiguity constrains market confidence; limited affordability, transparency, and socio-spatial integration restrain community support; and insufficiently demonstrated feasibility or local support hamper political commitment. Breaking this cycle requires clearer regulatory frameworks, improved affordability, and stronger socio-spatial integration to support future upscaling.

title: From stress to strategy – Conceptualizing urban infrastructure transformation under climate pressure
abstract: More than two-thirds of the global population will live in urban areas by 2050, emphasizing the need for climate mitigation and adaptation strategies. Despite their importance in public services, urban infrastructures – social, technical, and green-blue – often lack an integrated, interdisciplinary governance approach. This research explores the characteristics of urban infrastructures concerning municipal governance across their transformation towards climate mitigation and adaptation. Initially, a literature review and a workshop with scientific experts were carried out to identify topic areas as limiting and enabling factors towards the transformation of urban infrastructures under climate pressures. These climate pressures, e.g. heat or flooding, force municipalities to mitigate their infrastructures' emissions and to adapt to the impacts of climate change. This can be accomplished by either reconstructing, retrofitting, adding, substituting or establishing a stand-alone solution. The identified topic areas are the availability of resources, evolving requirements, changing expectations, a multiplicity of responsibilities, path dependencies, conflicting objectives, the ensuring of justice as well as care and maintenance. Since no single theory fully addresses these challenges, this study assesses three theoretical approaches, i.e. the Long-term Governance Framework, Multi-level Perspective, and Change Management, for their contributions to municipal governance in climate mitigation and adaptation of urban infrastructures. The key results of this research (i) conceptualize urban infrastructure and climate pressure, (ii) identify enabling and limiting topic areas and specify their reference points to the three identified conceptual approaches and (iii) assign transformation topic areas along an infrastructure transformation model for further application in municipal governance.

title: Measuring overlapping suburbanization and peri-urbanization processes in Warsaw Metropolitan Area
The perforated metropolis: Enclavisation and the morphological transformation of Istanbul (2000–2026)
abstract: This article examines the transformation of Istanbul's urban character between 2000 and 2026 through three interrelated processes: the rise of new suburban gated enclaves on previously undeveloped land; the demolition-led renewal of inner-city districts, encompassing both former informal settlements and established middle-class neighbourhoods; and the conversion of inner-city public land into private residential compounds. Although these processes originate in distinct institutional, legal, and economic contexts, they produce similar morphological outcomes. Using a comparative urban morphological framework, the study analyses changes in street networks, public–private interfaces, scale and grain, and land-use composition across six case studies. The findings reveal that enclaves of all three types erode street life, reduce permeability, privatise public space, and remove spontaneity from the environment. Inner-city enclaves in particular demonstrate how enclavisation now penetrates the core of the urban fabric, replacing established neighbourhoods of street-facing buildings with introverted compounds and importing the morphology of gated communities once limited to the periphery into the heart of the city.,The article argues that these processes are progressively perforating the continuous urban fabric of Istanbul, inserting controlled, inward-facing compounds into a tissue that elsewhere remains permeable, mixed-use, and morphologically rich. Enclavisation in Istanbul is an ongoing process, not a completed condition, and the trajectory is the central concern.
