The article further argues that this transformation is not simply market-produced but state-engineered, enabled by a specific political architecture in which centralised planning authority and the legislative override of local resistance have been deployed to legitimise enclavisation through earthquake-risk discourse.

title: Investigating data center site planning of major ICT companies in the U.S.: A spatial and methodological framework
A spatial point pattern analysis of public and private urban social facilities in Barcelona. A balanced and equitable model?
abstract: The expansion of privately provided social facilities has significantly transformed urban service landscapes, rising concerns regarding equity and territorial cohesion. This study investigates whether public and private secondary schools, libraries, and sports facilities in Barcelona exhibit distinct spatial logics, and how these patterns correspond to neighbourhood socioeconomic conditions. Moving beyond conventional area-based approaches, we employ a spatial point process framework combining inhomogeneous Ripley's K-functions and Gibbs (Geyer) interaction models to jointly estimate spatial intensity, clustering dynamics, and covariate effects at the point level. The findings reveal systematic differences in the spatial distribution of facilities. Public facilities exhibit pronounced yet highly localized clustering patterns aligning with objectives of regulated planning and territorial coverage. Conversely, private facilities display weaker yet more spatially extensive agglomeration, closely linked to population density and affluent neighbourhoods. Methodologically, the study underscores the utility of spatial point process modelling in disentangling contextual socioeconomic influences from endogenous spatial interactions, thereby mitigating aggregation bias. Substantively, the research seeks to contribute to urban planning and policy debates on privatisation, accessibility, and social cohesion by providing spatially explicit empirical evidence.

title: Data-driven bike-sharing rebalancing for smart cities: Reinforcement learning, operational constraints, and service-cost trade-offs
abstract: Dynamic bike-sharing rebalancing can improve bicycle availability, but its practical value depends on whether the service gains justify vehicle use and whether scarcity is merely transferred between locations. This study compares nine non-learned policies (no-op plus eight active comparators) with Maskable Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in a full-network replay of the 2023 Warsaw station-based system. The analysis uses 2,994,604 recorded trips, 18,427,085 station-inventory observations, weather and spatial attributes for 310 physical stations, and a single modeled relocation vehicle with explicit travel, handling, depot, load, shift, route, and daily-resource constraints. Returns are always feasible; installed rack count is treated as infrastructure rather than as a hard inventory limit. Policies are evaluated over independent daily replays initialized from observed midnight states. The scientific configuration and five PPO checkpoint hashes were frozen before a 28-day November retrospective evaluation. No additional modeled rebalancing achieved a recorded-trip fulfilment rate (RTFR) of 99.036% with 1374 unfulfilled departures. Maskable PPO achieved 99.137% ± 0.011% and 1230.2 ± 16.0 failures, avoiding 143.8 failures (10.5%) relative to no-op; the paired moving-block interval for the failure difference was [−245.2, −56.6]. The myopic exhaustive analytical optimizer attained the highest RTFR (99.179%; 1171 failures) but used 1137.8 vehicle-km and 99.7 vehicle-hours, compared with 802.2 km and 60.0 h for PPO. PPO remained Pareto-efficient, but no active policy produced a positive modeled net benefit under three economic scenarios; the base-case PPO break-even value was 31.82 PLN per avoided failure. PPO improved 64 stations, worsened 33, and left 213 unchanged. These findings support selective, value-justified rebalancing rather than universal intervention or universal RL superiority.

title: Unravelling the dual displacement risks of urban renewal: A causal inference framework integrating double machine learning and XAI
State-led flexibility through temporary land use: Governing time-bounded land rights in urban China
Behaviorally calibrated metrics for comparing alcohol outlet configurations along after-work walking commutes in Mannheim, Germany
abstract: Moderate alcohol use is increasingly viewed as a potential health concern. Existing spatial exposure metrics, however, remain largely behavior-agnostic: they map the presence of outlets but do not account for how people's routine movements enable same-day alcohol purchases. We introduce behaviorally calibrated, detour-based indices tailored to after-work alcohol acquisitions on walking commutes. Using a revealed- and stated-preference survey of 230 eligible adults who reported a recent on-foot after-work alcohol purchase in Mannheim and Heidelberg, Germany, we calibrate three detour thresholds for after-work alcohol runs and embed them in two path-based metrics on Mannheim's pedestrian network: a home-level index capturing the share of transit–home walking paths that include at least one feasible purchase opportunity, and a store-level leverage index capturing how many such paths each outlet can intercept. At the 250 m detour threshold, half of stop–home walking segments contain a purchase opportunity, and 29% of homes have such opportunities on all stop–home paths. Kiosks, while only about 28% of outlets, account for roughly 38% of this after-work leverage. We then use the indices in a comparison of three outlet rules. When exposure is recalculated from the remaining outlets, a specialist-only rule produces about 75% lower mean route-based opportunity than the current outlet set, while excluding the 25% highest-leverage outlets produces a mean reduction close to a convenience-channel restriction that excludes more alcohol-sale locations. We conclude by outlining extensions toward a broader class of purchase-chain-specific exposure metrics.

title: 15-min education circle: Multi-stage accessibility assessment and inequality-reduction capacity—A case study of Beijing, China
On the other side of the river, where housing security shivers: Nepali men’s caring masculinities in rescue, reconstruction, and cremation toward disaster recovery
Diagnosing cross-city transferability of cycling speed models using interpretable machine learning: Evidence from four Nordic cities
Are low-income neighborhoods greener and safer in Amazonian cities? Exploring for the first time the relationships among green cover, crime rates, and socioeconomic aspects in Belém, Brazil
The threshold effect of green space-urban expansion allometric growth on healthy cities: A multi-city panel analysis
A graph-based geospatial framework for delineating neighborhood planning units with barrier-aware isochrones
abstract: Graph-based GIS workflow is a relevant tool to urban planning and governance, yet most operational accessibility tools still rely on flat or Euclidean representations which can overestimate local dynamics in cities shaped by complex topography and fragmented urban forms. This limitation is especially critical at the neighborhood scale, where short walking trip structure everyday access to opportunities and services. This paper presents an original algorithm to delineate neighborhood scale planning units through the integration of slope-sensitive, territorial barriers, and urban morphology into isochrone modeling. The method structures a barrier-aware pedestrian graph on the block fabric, assigns edge costs from topography, and produces dual time–distance isochrones through an iterative seeding procedure to identify shortest walkable paths. A subsequent classification stage generates a typology of accessibility polygons based on area, population, radii, elevation, and administrative overlap. Applied to the municipality of São Paulo, Brazil, the framework generated 639 neighborhood scale isochrones and demonstrates that a 10-min or 800-m walking threshold does not correspond to a uniform spatial scale once topography and territorial discontinuities are explicitly incorporated. By analytically associating isochrones with transitional areas, the model reconceptualizes neighborhoods as flexible spatial perimeters rather than fixed administrative units, allowing their limits to be refined through public governance or participatory planning processes. In doing so, the study shifts isochrones from isolated accessibility outputs to a citywide system of planning-oriented units and offers a transferable geospatial computational framework for capturing local urban dynamics and supporting evidence-based active mobility and neighborhood planning in complex urban environments.

title: Multidimensional injustice and systemic urban crisis: Youth perspectives from African cities
From representation to foresight? How 3D urban simulations and deep learning are reshaping theoretical and quantitative geography
abstract: The advent of high-resolution 3D urban simulations and transformative deep learning (DL) architectures is precipitating a paradigm shift in theoretical and quantitative geography (TQG). The field lacks a comprehensive synthesis examining how these tools are reconfiguring spatial reasoning, predictive modeling, and the theory–practice interface of geography. This paper addresses this gap by articulating a conceptual and empirical investigation into the transformative interplay between 3D simulation and machine learning. Using a structured analytical framework grounded in material screening, we identify three major findings: (1) the shift from visual representation to experimental spatial laboratories, where simulations become operational epistemic instruments; (2) the emergence of a new predictive geography driven by deep learning’s capacity to learn high-dimensional spatial dependencies; and (3) an ongoing epistemological reconfiguration in which traditional geographical theory is challenged, and sometimes displaced, by data-driven inference, opaque models, and algorithmic urban foresight. We further discuss critical issues related to model interpretability, reproducibility, ethical risks, and epistemic justice in the governance of AI-based spatial knowledge. By situating 3D urban simulation and deep learning within the broader trajectory of TQG, this paper offers a synthesized perspective on the future of the field. It argues that geography now stands at a turning point: either integrate these computational paradigms into a renewed theoretical framework or risk a widening gap between technological innovation and disciplinary meaning-making.

title: Why some cities feel inclusive: The city ethos model of institutions and population-rootedness in European cities
abstract: How do cities sustain inclusive coexistence under conditions of diversity and demographic mobility? This article shifts the analytical focus to city-level inclusiveness , understood as a property of the city's institutional-normative order rather than of interpersonal relations. Building on a thin conception of city ethos, the article develops a City Ethos Model that conceptualizes perceived urban inclusiveness as an interpretive outcome shaped by the interaction between institutional perception and population-rootedness. The model treats population-rootedness as a temporal infrastructure that shapes how institutional performance is interpreted: where more residents have accumulated exposure to local institutions, institutional signals are more likely to settle into durable city-level expectations. Empirically, the analysis draws on approximately 108,000 respondents across 70 cities in 28 EU member states ( European Commission, 2019 , European Commission, 2023 ). Multilevel models show that positive institutional perceptions are associated with higher perceived inclusiveness. However, population-rootedness does not operate as an independent source of inclusion. Instead, it significantly moderates the institutional effect: in cities with greater population-rootedness, institutional perception is associated with higher perceived inclusiveness, whereas in contexts where institutions are viewed skeptically, rootedness may reinforce exclusionary interpretations. These findings suggest that population-rootedness functions as a conditional amplifier of institutional signals rather than as a direct driver of inclusion.

title: Institutions, inclusive innovation, and the post-industrial city: Why equitable development will fail without attention to local politics
abstract: Aspirational demands to improve equity have gained some traction alongside the growth imperative on post-industrial urban policy agendas, but the pressing question of how to expand economic opportunity to people and places ‘left out’ of technology-driven growth remains a pressing puzzle. Adding granularity about the actors involved, the power dynamics that ensue, and the consequences for urban policymaking, comparative institutional research over the past decade suggests that equitable post-industrial development will fail without attention to local politics. The institutional capacity required to implement these types of agendas requires cross sector coalitions that are difficult to build and even more difficult to sustain. Illustrative cases of unsuccessful inclusive innovation in two mid-sized restructuring cities, one in the United States and one in France, indicate that these initiatives failed due to weak engagement from local politicians and the business community, suggesting the need for meaningful participatory incentives. Regardless of differences in national policy context, size and specialization matter: these types of cities must work especially hard for economic reinvention while juggling equity imperatives that vie for attention on local policy agendas.

title: Introduction to the SI: Conceptualizing the effects of COVID-19 on urban conditions and urban governance in a polycrisis environment
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic constituted a profound disruption to urban life worldwide, sharply altering social practices, economic activity and demographic dynamics. While many studies have examined specific short-term consequences of the pandemic, comparatively little attention has been paid to how its effects interacted with other simultaneously unfolding crises and how disruptions might translate into permanent effects, embedded into a larger systemic conceptualization. This Special Issue addresses this gap by situating the pandemic within a broader polycrisis context, in which long-term structural stresses and fast-moving triggers intersect across economic, social, demographic and political systems. Drawing on systems thinking and the emerging polycrisis framework, we conceptualize how pandemic-induced changes in three urban domains—economic restructuring, demographic and migration shifts, and housing market transformations—have produced complex and uneven community-level effects. We further highlight how modes of policy and governance response have shaped outcomes, noting that actions taken to mitigate immediate impacts have often reinforced underlying systemic stresses or generated new risks. The contributions to this Special Issue present empirical evidence from cities across the Global North, illustrating both shared dynamics and diverse local trajectories. Together, these studies provide a foundation for understanding how crises may act as catalysts, accelerators or turning points in urban development. They underscore the need for analytical and policy approaches capable of addressing interconnected risks and supporting socially cohesive, resilient and sustainable urban futures in an era where polycrisis is becoming the new normal.

title: Urban stillbirth: Urban autopsy and the structural failure of state-led transformation
Placemaking as affective practice: Navigating pathways of connection and fragmentation
abstract: This study investigates how affect takes shape in placemaking, and which underlying drivers influence the creation or consolidation of a connective sense of place. Drawing on 30 interviews with placemakers, residents, and municipal actors in Rotterdam, Zoetermeer, and Vlaardingen, the research uses narrative walks to explore affective experiences in three urban placemaking projects. Walking interviews proved particularly effective in revealing how affective dynamics unfold in situ, offering insight into the relational undercurrents of spatial transformation. The analysis shows that affect in placemaking is not inherently connective. Instead, it manifests in multiple, sometimes conflicting forms. Based on empirical patterns, the study introduces a typology of affect (disruptive, dissociative, transmissive, and coalescent). To conceptualize these findings, an axis model was developed that maps affect along two dimensions: connecting vs. fragmenting, and near vs. distant. This model offers a more operational lens than the often abstract notion of sense of place, highlighting affect's reflexive and diagnostic potential. The study identifies three key drivers that shape affective outcomes: governance structures, spatial context, and relational dynamics. When space is co-produced, when actors are locally embedded, and when institutional support is sustained, placemaking tends to foster stronger affective bonds. Ultimately, the study argues that affect should not be seen merely as an outcome of placemaking, but as a guiding principle, one that can help steer urban transformation towards more inclusive and grounded futures.

title: Spatialising degrowth in affluent urban areas: Limits and contradictions of sustainability policy in Zurich
abstract:
Although affluent cities in the Global North are often celebrated as urban sustainability frontrunners, their strategies are increasingly criticised for perpetuating externalisation, social inequalities, and growth-dependent development pathways. We explore these tensions by critically analysing Zurich, a hyper-affluent and highly ranked “sustainable” city. Drawing on an analysis of 22 public policy documents produced between 2016 and 2025, complemented by situated qualitative insights, we examine the policy rationalities, instruments, omissions, and contradictions that shape Zurich's urban development and sustainability agenda from a degrowth perspective.
Building on recent advances in degrowth spatial politics, we propose a new, multiscalar analytical framework for evaluating urban policies across four dimensions: planetary-scale thinking, structural economic dependencies, social and ecological well-being, and democratic governance. Applying this framework to Zurich reveals deep contradictions between its green growth agenda and its stated environmental and social objectives. Despite demonstrating strong institutional capacity and policy innovation, Zurich's strategies largely remain confined to territorial emissions, voluntary measures, and incentive-based instruments, leaving consumption-based impacts, growth dependencies and displacement dynamics insufficiently addressed.
We show how inward densification, net-zero strategies, and circular economy initiatives can simultaneously reduce local environmental pressures while intensifying social inequalities and shifting socio-ecological costs to hinterlands. These outcomes are further shaped by multilevel governance constraints and limited municipal competences. Unless structural growth dependencies and extraterritorial impacts are addressed, urban sustainability strategies in affluent cities risk perpetuating the very dynamics they seek to overcome. Our framework offers a diagnostic tool for critically assessing sustainability policies in other affluent urban contexts.

title: The gap between inclusionary urban visions and exclusionary housing practices: Converting progressive support and electoral wins into practical authority
Bridging the implementation gap: A framework for sustainable neighborhood facilities in transitional China
Unraveling post-socialist urban expansion: Long-term built-up dynamics in Polish and Romanian urban regions
abstract: Post-socialist urbanisation in Central and Eastern Europe is often described through common processes of decentralisation, land-market formation and suburban expansion, yet the spatial outcomes of transition have diverged substantially across countries. This study examines how contrasting land-ownership reforms and planning instruments shaped long-term built-up dynamics in six second-tier Polish and Romanian urban regions. Using fine-grained Global Human Settlement Layer data from 1975 to 2020, the study applies time-series clustering to identify recurrent trajectories of built-up expansion and compares their spatial distribution, built-up intensity and population-adjusted land consumption. The results show that both countries experienced dispersed peri-urban growth, but in different forms. Romanian urban regions display faster, more fragmented and more land-intensive post-2000 expansion, especially in the newest and lowest-density classes. Polish urban regions also show dispersed development and weak coordination, but their observed spatial signatures are relatively less atomised and more frequently associated with existing settlement structures. These differences are interpreted as the cumulative outcome of ownership reform, parcel structure and development-right allocation within a broader post-2000 context of housing demand, credit expansion, mobility and infrastructure constraints. The paper contributes to comparative post-socialist urban studies by showing that shared socialist legacies did not produce a single urban-regional trajectory and by linking institutional divergence to micro-spatial, multi-decadal evidence beyond capital-city cases.

title: Social infrastructures for the marginalized: The case of subdivided-unit tenants in Hong Kong
Policy coherence and climate adaptation: Insights from multilevel governance and urban vulnerability in South Korea
Hybridizing shared mobility: Collaborative approaches between users, public institutions, and markets
Temperature-Conscious Building Resource Planning by Destination-Earth: Proof of Value
Unveiling inequalities in forgotten enclaves: A geospatial–streetscape integrated framework for assessing urban village livability
Local government climate change strategies: A systematic literature review
abstract: Local governments are at the forefront of contemporary responses and localised community impacts of climate change through a range of strategies. Given their proximity to the community, local governments possess a nuanced understanding of the consequences of climate change on local communities and implement strategies to mitigate these challenges. However, the effective implementation of climate change strategies and the enhancement of capacity building remain pressing issues in many countries, necessitating immediate attention to achieve established targets. This study adopts a systematic literature review method to evaluate the extent to which contemporary literature explains how local government strategies respond effectively to climate change. In this context, 117 papers published between 2005 and 2024 were examined using online Covidence software to screen and focus on seven key themes related to climate change strategies: renewable energy integration, climate action plans, multi-stakeholder collaboration, policy integration, innovative technologies, resilient infrastructure development, and climate risk assessment. We found that there are ten prevailing theories used to understand local government climate change responses including legitimacy and stakeholder theories. Our review revealed that financial constraints are a critical issue in the fight against climate change at the local level, and the inadequacy of community participation in local policy creation limits the efficacy of implementation. This study suggests that fostering partnerships across governmental bodies could help address these challenges. It emphasises the importance of local governments actively seeking opportunities for cross-governmental collaboration to facilitate the exchange innovative and emerging best practice, establish governance frameworks, and scale up successful initiatives.

title: Exploring the links amongst place attachment, urban environment qualities, and psychological restoration: A case study of Hong Kong
Equity, inclusivity, neighbourhood public services and the 15-minute city: An assessment of the strategic initiatives of C40 cities
abstract: This paper explores the potential of the so-called 15/20-minute city (15-MC) – in which the localisation, diversification and digitisation of public services at the neighbourhood level is argued for – to address socio-spatial inequalities within cities and promote social inclusivity via urban planning processes. It explores this potential via an assessment of a sample of ten 15-MC plans from the C40 global group of cities which share a commitment to progressive social and environment policy change. The paper contributes to a developed, nuanced understanding of how notions of equity and inclusion are operationalised in 15-MC plans. This is in order to assess the contribution that 15-MC ideas may have in developing initiatives capable of tackling key challenges identified in urban policy debate including socio-spatial injustices, limited citizen engagement and policy interventions that lead to displacement. It finds inconsistent engagement within plans in relation to operationalising core tenets of the15-MC, suggesting that the 15-MC is not a settled concept in global urban planning. It also finds variation with regard to the extent to which the plans engage with the 15-MC in order to address historic injustices. By categorising the plans into three tiers according to this form of engagement, the analysis demonstrates that more developed ‘first-tier’ and, to an extent, ‘second-tier’ plans can potentially use the sharp focus on neighbourhood services afforded by 15-MC ideas to gain traction on long-standing urban challenges with respect to equity and inclusivity.

title: Spatial disparities in third-place accessibility: Evidence from older adults' mobility patterns in the Seoul metropolitan area
From choreographed tourism to everyday urban life: A grounded theory of visitor experience in city markets
Beyond fixed scales: Decoding the heterogeneous spatial structure of urban mobility via adaptive hotspot detection
Organizing against organized crime: The entanglement of drug trafficking, housing financialization, and urban renewal in Barcelona
abstract: Current analysis of organized crime in the urban space focuses either on its social or spatial embeddedness. As an alternative, this article develops a socio-spatial perspective that recognizes and situates the lived experience of organized crime within urban transformation processes. I developed this perspective by building on ethnographic data about drug trafficking in Barcelona's El Raval, which I examine through the lens of the residents. I focus specifically on the interpretative framework of the “narco-especulació” which links the expansion of the narcopisos phenomenon to rampant speculative practices of real-estate-investors and city-led urban regeneration processes. I argue that this framework articulates a critique of urban governance, underscoring the dispossession of residents' social control, a weakened sense of place, and the fragmentation of community relationships. I also show how this framework can foster collective resistance strategies that express community agency against organized crime while disrupting the ongoing process of urban transformation and public management.

title: Why smart city megaprojects failed: Learning from the past and planning for the future
abstract: Smart city megaprojects routinely fall short of the utopian visions promoted by their creators, yet the failure of these projects has not been systematically compared across cases or grounded in a shared analytical framework. This paper addresses that gap by examining ten smart city new-town projects from around the world, including Songdo, NEOM, Sidewalk Toronto, Masdar City, and others, at various stages of development, construction, suspension, and abandonment. Drawing on literatures in high modernist planning, megaproject failure, splintering urbanism, and smart city critique, we develop a seven-dimensional evaluation framework organized into three reinforcing categories: conception and design (feasible, technological), governance and process (engageable, equitable), and viability and impact (financial, ecological, livable). Each case is scored on a four-point ordinal scale based on documentary evidence, enabling structured comparison across political systems, economic contexts, and geographic regions. Three findings stand out. First, engagement failures were the most universal dimension, present in all ten cases, regardless of regime type or project leadership. Second, technological failure was the least common, challenging the assumption that smart cities fail primarily because the technology does not work. Third, financial failure was present at the highest severity in every abandoned project, extending megaproject optimism bias theory to the smart city domain. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for incremental planning, early-stage participatory governance, equity-centered design, and independent regulatory oversight.

title: Ambivalent attachments: Place, precarity and survival in Lesotho's rough neighbourhoods
abstract: This paper critically rethinks the concept of place attachment through an ethnographic study of Sea Point, a longstanding informal settlement in Maseru, Lesotho. While dominant theories of place attachment often frame it as an emotional or voluntary bond with place, the experiences of Sea Point residents challenge this assumption. In contexts marked by tenure insecurity, infrastructural neglect, and spatial illegibility, attachment emerges less from affection and more from survival. We conceptualise Sea Point as a rough neighbourhood; a space of durable hardship produced through infrastructural deficit and socio-legal uncertainty, showing how place attachment is forged through endurance and constraint rather than voluntary belonging. Drawing on ethnographic participant observations, in-depth interviews and life histories, the study reveals how residents remain tethered to place not through choice, but through constraint, embedded social networks, and the absence of alternatives. Building on the work of Tuan, Roy, Simone, and Bayat, the paper proposes “ambivalent attachment” as a key conceptual contribution, capturing the simultaneous endurance and aspiration, fatigue and care, that define urban life under informality. It argues that informality is not a planning failure but a structuring condition of urban governance in the Global South, producing attachments that are negotiated, contingent, and deeply political. The paper moves the field from emotional bonding toward a critical understanding of how attachment is shaped by exclusion, survival strategies, and everyday forms of resilience.

title: Bridging planning gaps: Multi-dimensional analysis and differential assessment of urban imagery from government and public perspectives
How urban forms shape the cooling efficiency of urban green spaces: Evidence from 1318 global cities
The lightweight proximity: Convenience stores as affective infrastructure for urban youth in Chinese megacities
Buffering structural decline with place-based fiscal transfers in South Korea
Who shapes the streets? A stakeholder analysis of street redesign processes in European cities
Private partners in public spaces: Discourses of philanthropic participation in urban park making
abstract: The growing participation of philanthropic donors in developing, designing, and managing urban public parks raises important questions regarding the equity implications of private sector power in public spaces. Critical analyses of urban greening have explored the uneven sociospatial impacts of philanthropic participation in park making; there remains a need to interrogate the symbolic and discursive processes that make “commonsense” of these governance approaches. This article investigates everyday discourses regarding philanthropy-led park production and evaluates implications for park justice. Using critical discourse analysis, I analyze the content and influence of newspaper coverage of three high-profile, park projects supported by philanthropic donations in Toronto, Canada. I consider how narratives advanced in news articles construct parks as an urban environmental policy challenge and philanthropic partnerships as a policy solution. Articles often circulate discourses produced by donors and supportive coalitions that frame the public sector as inefficient and ineffective, donors as innovative and benevolent, and donor-led parks as delivering broad social, environmental, and economic benefits. By advancing an uncritical view of philanthropy's role in park production, newspapers naturalize the value of philanthropy in parks. Articles rarely include critical perspectives, minimizing concerns related to democratic decision-making, park equity, and responsiveness to community needs, and neutralizing dissent. Together, this constrains the potential of donor-led park projects to advance procedural, recognitional, and distributional justice.

title: The dual fabric of smart cities - Theorizing the integration of informal and formal urban elements
abstract: The dichotomy between formality and informality in modern cities reveals a complex and underexplored interplay in the context of smart cities. While smart cities emphasize data-driven technologies and governance, informality – often associated with exclusion and urban improvisation – has been neglected as a central element. This paper adopts a systematic and multi-method approach to investigate how literature addresses the informal dimension. Agency theory was used to map the dynamics between key actors (citizens) and agents (public sector), revealing how informality reduces information asymmetries, encourages transparency, and generates urban innovation. The results show that informal initiatives create crucial capacities, such as participatory monitoring and interest alignment, enabling marginalized communities to influence urban policies. This paper argues for the integration of informality as an essential feature of a more inclusive, sustainable, and adaptive smart urbanism.

title: Income-specific mobility networks reveal persistent socioeconomic representations of metropolitan functional structure
abstract: Metropolitan functional structure is commonly inferred from population-wide mobility flows, but the extent to which this representation is shared by different socioeconomic groups remains unclear. We address this question using harmonized Origin-Destination household travel surveys for the São Paulo Metropolitan Region in 2007, 2017 and 2023. Weighted directed networks were constructed for five income quintiles and the aggregate population and evaluated using complementary network indicators, permutation tests, bootstrap intervals and equal-person rarefaction. Lower-income networks were consistently sparser, more compartmentalized and characterized by lower duration-based reachability, whereas higher-income networks contained more direct interzonal connections and weaker community separation. The functional-center sets of the poorest and richest quintiles overlapped by less than 10%, and none of their ten highest-PageRank zones coincided in 2023. These differences were persistent but not static: community compartmentalization was the most durable socioeconomic distinction, while connectivity gaps narrowed and centrality concentration changed more substantially. Aggregate networks also represented income groups unevenly, exhibiting consistently lower center-set similarity with the poorest quintile than with upper-income groups. The findings reveal a socially differentiated polycentricity in which multiple centers exist but do not constitute the same functional metropolitan system for all populations. Income-disaggregated networks therefore complement aggregate representations and provide a planning-relevant basis for evaluating metropolitan integration beyond population-wide averages.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution of ecological resilience, catch-up dynamics, and carbon-carrying constraints in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration (2000–2023)
Space-sharing and kerbside conflicts in urban deliveries: A framework for understanding space allocation challenges
abstract: Increasing demand for scarce urban streetside creates space-sharing conflicts, compromising cities’ liveability. Conflict assessments predominantly adopt traffic-centric perspectives, neglecting place-making functions of streets and the role of freight. This paper investigates space-sharing conflicts between freight and other streetside users during delivery operations, aiming to understand challenges in creating liveable streets. Based on empirical evidence from the West End of Central London, a framework is proposed to systematically identify these conflicts, and explore implications on the health, social, economic, and environmental value dimensions of streets, from the freight operators’ perspective. The framework proposes four types of freight-related space-sharing conflicts: collision risk, traffic obstruction, space overuse, and sidewalk pavement damages. Findings highlighted the pressures the identified conflicts create on freight operators, exposing them to high-stress levels and endangering both their own and other street users’ health and safety. Additionally, the framework informs right-of-way decisions by considering freight aspects across three distributive justice principles, i.e., sufficientarian, utilitarian, and egalitarian. Analysing last-mile freight operations and their interactions with other users introduces a novel approach to city logistics that traditionally studies freight in isolation. Furthermore, the paper contributes to urban planning, providing insights for right-of-way decisions that include the freight perspective—often overlooked in urban studies.

title: A race without rules: Industrial transfer, competition, and the coordination dilemmas in the Shanxi-Shaanxi-Henan Region
The impact of New York City's Open Streets Program on local traffic
Urban analytics: Definitions, disciplines, diversity and data - A systematic literature review
abstract: Urban analytics has developed as an interdisciplinary field to understand and address urban complexity. Despite rapid growth, the field remains fragmented, lacking conceptual clarity and interdisciplinary dialogue. This paper presents a comprehensive systematic review of 427 publications across relevant disciplines. Information about publication details, publication type, research objectives, research fields, methods, main data and data source, data accessibility, data representativeness, geographical and temporal scopes, ethical concerns and policy implications of each study are extracted and categorised. The following analysis traces the evolution of urban analytics, identifies methodological or thematic paucity in current research, and evaluates whether existing studies have approached urban issues in methodologically sound, ethical, and appropriate ways. The findings reveal persistent challenges in definitional contestation, data “firehose” and flood of bias, interdisciplinarity, fragmentation and uneven integration, as well as institutional and practical limits. This review further identifies emerging directions that integrate theory and practice, support responsible innovation, and promote more actionable insights for urban analytics. It also contributes a conceptual framework and research roadmap for developing responsible, context-aware and practical urban analytics that support equitable and sustainable urban futures.

title: Planning for public charging: Contrasting choices by electric-vehicle and non-electric vehicle users
abstract: Accessible and well-designed public charging points are key elements towards the wider adoption of electric vehicles (EVs), highlighting the need to understand user preferences. This study examines public charging choices of 300 EV users and 288 non-EV users in Great Britain through a stated choice experiment and latent class modelling. Results revealed two distinct segments within each user group. Among EV users, a larger segment prioritised charging price, while a smaller one valued waiting time, charging speed, convenience, available amenities, and high station ratings. By contrast, both non-EV segments remained sensitive to charging price and waiting time, including the larger service-oriented segment. These patterns align with Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation Theory, highlighting behavioural and socio-demographic variations in readiness to engage with public charging infrastructure. The findings provide practical guidance for developing more inclusive and targeted public charging infrastructure that improves user experiences, lowers adoption barriers, and supports the broader shift towards electric mobility.

title: Not in my backyard, but in my City: Experimental evidence on what motivates citizens to co-design
State-coordinated metropolitan expansion and land-use change in Tashkent, 1990–2025
Mobility-system compatibility and bus underuse in Ho Chi Minh City: Explaining elastic mobility mismatch
Ashaiman revisited: Unpacking Ashaiman as a slum of hope or slum of despair
abstract: Debates on informal settlements often portray slums as spaces of uniform deprivation, obscuring internal variations in socio-economic trajectories, housing investment, and residents' aspirations. Drawing on the conceptual distinction between slums of hope and slums of despair, this study re-examines household survey data collected in Ashaiman, Ghana to assess the settlement's position along a continuum of hope, despair, and transition. Using a multidimensional set of indicators capturing livelihood dynamics, housing consolidation, tenure security and social capital, the analysis provides an integrated assessment of informal settlement trajectories. The findings indicate that while Ashaiman continues to face significant infrastructural and environmental constraints, most households exhibit characteristics consistent with a transitional settlement, combining elements of economic agency and social resilience with persistent vulnerabilities, particularly in relation to tenure security. By moving beyond binary classifications, the study highlights the value of incorporating both objective conditions and lived experiences into slum analysis and contributes to broader debates on urban informality and socially sustainable urban development in the Global South.

title: Who supports urban climate adaptation? Climate literacy, age and urban context in Polish cities
Accountability to God, We the People and local government activism in rural Shasta County, California
abstract: Political polarization is increasing globally through the rise of national actors further to the political right who often invoke faith-based values. In the United States, they argue for defending God-given unalienable rights and stewarding God's Kingdom on Earth. Local government increasingly is the locus of so-framed debates on policies from school curriculum to immigration and vaccination requirements. Efforts to reflect religious/faith-based beliefs in policies challenge the role of governance and are antithetical to decision making where separation between church/faith-based institutions and the state is long-standing. However, scant scholarly attention alongside rising conservatism at the local level has stymied our understanding in planning scholarship. In response, a novel conceptual framework is developed to guide research and analysis of faith fueled local activism and may align with broader political right efforts. It integrates religious studies, populism, social movement and planning scholarship. I present the case of conservative actors in rural Northern California's Shasta County, which is emblematic of broader trends in political right politics, polarization and faith-based motivations and influence, drawing upon in-depth interviews with respondents who largely identify as Christian and further to the political right and field observations. I find that local activism is interconnected with broader political right and faith-related U.S. efforts. Residents prefigure desired futures through policymaking engagement by creating civic opportunities and ecosystems of alternative news sources, education and governing. Interviewees recounted having direct callings from God and argued rights come from God, not government. This is in stark contrast to secularized society's norms. • Political right polarization infused with faith-based values is rising globally. • Local government increasingly is the locus of so-framed staunch contention. • Scant scholarship of religion and conservativism in planning stymies theorization. • A rural local California case emblematic of such polarization is analyzed. • Faith-based actors had significant impact anathema to secularized local governing.

title: Car ownership in Chinese metropolitans: Valuation, age-related differences, and policy implications for sustainable transport
The role of social capital in immigrant travel mode choice: A multilevel analysis
Happy to stay? Residential environment satisfaction, happiness, and settlement intention among foreign residents in Seoul
Sci-tech finance and urban industrial chain resilience: Empirical evidence from Chinese prefecture-level cities
Racialised rider experiences in Uber: Evidence from an audit-based field study
abstract: This paper examines how race and ethnicity shape service outcomes and rider experiences in Uber in Melbourne, Australia. It reports one of the first Australian field studies of rider experiences in a ride sharing platform, using trained field testers from Anglo Australian, East Asian Australian and African Australian backgrounds. Between January and February 2023, testers undertook 447 Uber rides and recorded wait times, cancellations, route directness, driver tone and race related comments. The study combines audit-based field testing with naturalistic observation of real-world ride share interactions. The findings show little evidence of ethnicity-based difference in access outcomes. Wait times were similar across groups, cancellation rates were not higher for African or East Asian riders, and route deviations were infrequent. Differences were more evident in interpersonal experience. African riders reported less favourable driver tone, while African and East Asian riders were more likely than Anglo riders to report race related comments. These findings suggest that racialisation in this setting was less visible in-service refusal than in conversation, tone, assumption and comfort during the ride. The paper argues that platform mediated mobility should be assessed not only through access measures, but also through the quality of interaction once access is provided. The study also highlights important methodological trade-offs in conducting field research within commercial ride sharing platforms. Its real-world design strengthens ecological validity, but limits causal inference because rides were not matched across identical geographies, routes and operating conditions. Future research should incorporate stronger geographic controls, driver side analysis and more granular platform data.

title: Built environment determinants of e-scooter route deviations: A macro- and micro-scale analysis
Urban form and densification as drivers of intra-urban inequalities: A 30-year LCZ-based analysis of Casablanca and Rabat
abstract: Rapid urbanization is reshaping cities and increasing thermal inequalities in the Global South. The combined influence of urban structure and densification on Land Surface Temperature (LST) and thermal stress remains poorly understood in North African cities. This research looks at these relationships in Casablanca and Rabat from 1994 to 2024 using the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework. Landsat images taken in 1994, 2004, 2014 and 2024 were joined with the Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) and vegetation proportion (PV). Correlation analysis, two-way fixed-effects panel models the Mann–Kendall test and GeoDetector were used to separate differences among LCZs from changes linked to densification inside each zone. Compact and industrial LCZs consistently recorded the LST and UTFVI values in both Casablanca and Rabat. LST and UTFVI were strongly linked (R = 0.88 in Casablanca and R = 0.84 in Rabat) while NDBI emerged as the explanatory factor. GeoDetector q-values for NDBI ranged from 0.52 to 0.56 in Casablanca and from 0.44 to 0.49 in Rabat. Panel models also showed that higher NDBI was significantly connected to LST and UTFVI whereas vegetation offered a weaker mitigating effect. LST captured the warming trend while UTFVI highlighted relative thermal differences within each city. Casablanca displayed thermal persistence matching more intensive urban compaction. These results suggest that urban heat mitigation must go beyond simply adding space and instead include urban form, density and spatial layout, in planning decisions.

title: Transportation integration dynamics in a transportation-first regionalization strategy: A case of the Yangtze River Delta, China
Uncovering the residential relocation during urban renewal with time-series big data and spatial interpretable machine learning
From the Medellín Miracle to the Postponed City: Social Urbanism as a shifting planning paradigm
Understanding commercial gentrification of Seoul through multi-task learning and explainable artificial intelligence
Book Review
Mission-oriented urban transformation: Value regimes and variegated firm agency in Shenzhen's electric mobility transition
abstract: Mission-oriented policies are increasingly deployed to address grand societal challenges, yet such missions are often only partially specified and open to multiple interpretations at the regional levels, giving rise to divergent imaginaries of industrial futures and development pathways. Against this backdrop, this paper examines Shenzhen (China) as a leading urban policy laboratory for promoting New Energy Vehicles (NEVs), to show how a regional industrial mission is interpreted and enacted by firms with different degrees of territorial embeddedness in the process of regional industrial path development.Drawing on the notion of value regimes from the political economy literature, this paper analyses how firms engage with the NEV mission through distinct and sometimes competing understandings of value creation - ranging from sustainability-oriented to profit-oriented regimes. It further demonstrates how these cognitive frameworks are differentially integrated into firms’ strategies and practices depending on their embeddedness within local economic structures, institutions, and networks. Based on this analysis, we identify four types of firm agency - path architects, path scalers, path followers, and path expanders - that collectively enabled Shenzhen to emerge as a global exemplar of green mobility. By revealing how open-ended missions are translated into heterogeneous firm strategies, the paper contributes to urban policy debates on governing sustainable urban transitions.

title: Analyzing redevelopment-induced displacement in Ulaanbaatar's Ger Areas, Mongolia
abstract: Mongolia's land administration system entitles each citizen to 300–700 m 2 of residential land in the capital city. Accordingly, this entitlement applies equally to residents of Ger areas, indicating that what is often described as urban sprawl in Ulaanbaatar consists primarily of legally owned residential plots rather than informal or irregular occupation. Despite their legal recognition through land privatization, these areas continue to lack adequate infrastructure and face significant environmental and social challenges. Focusing on a Ger area neighborhood in the Bayankhoshuu sub-center, this study draws on document analysis and semi-structured interviews to examine how redevelopment policies reshape residents' housing, livelihoods, and everyday lives. Using Cernea's Impoverishment Risks and Livelihood Reconstruction, the findings reveal that redevelopment generates interconnected forms of loss, including tenure-based exclusion, housing insecurity, disrupted access to infrastructure, and social disarticulation, particularly among renters and multi-household residents without formal land rights. Although redevelopment is promoted as a strategy to improve living conditions and environmental quality, its implementation often creates new vulnerabilities and reinforces existing inequalities. The study argues that Ger area redevelopment in Ulaanbaatar produces forms of state-led informality by formalizing land while overlooking the social, cultural, and relational infrastructures that sustain everyday life, highlighting the need for more inclusive and participatory planning approaches.

title: Associations between ecosystem services perceptions and human activities differ across social groups in peri-urban areas: Policy implications from participatory mapping
Coupling effects assessment and multi-scenario simulation of ecosystem services and rural residents' well-being: A case study of ecologically fragile regions
How urban amenity factors shape the geography of innovative enterprises: A geographical random forest approach in Beijing
Urban expansion reshapes spatial justice: A multi-temporal assessment of vulnerability trajectories in a rapidly urbanizing secondary city
Nature as relation, not place: Two registers of urban nature experience in a biophilic city
From town to learning city: Developing a distributed urban learning ecosystem through community-embedded heritage nodes
Graffiti as a socio-environmental device: Rethinking SDG 11.7 through environmental perception in São Paulo and Curitiba
abstract: Sustainable Development Goal 11.7 calls for inclusive, safe, and accessible public spaces, yet its operationalization in urban policy has remained anchored in material and managerial indicators that overlook the symbolic and perceptual dimensions of urban experience. This study investigates how graffiti influences the qualification of public spaces and the socio-spatial interactions produced within them, drawing on a qualitative cross-case analysis of two emblematic Brazilian sites: the Minhocão Municipal Linear Park in São Paulo and the pedestrian stretch of XV de Novembro Street in Curitiba. Adopting an inductive design grounded in data triangulation — semi-structured interviews with artists, observers, and managers; systematic field observation; and the mobilization of urban landscape attributes — the research mobilizes the concept of dispositif to interpret graffiti as a relational practice. Findings reveal that inclusion, symbolic safety, and cultural accessibility emerge as situated effects produced in the encounter between landscape, use, memory, visibility, and experience, rather than as attributes objectively present in space. The cross-case synthesis exposes structural tensions between authorized muralism and unauthorized inscription, recognition and erasure, and aesthetic domestication. The study proposes a paradigmatic shift in urban policy and planning — from the management of physical resources to the mediation of socio-spatial interactions — and conceptualizes graffiti as a socio-environmental device whose contribution to urban sustainability is ambivalent, situated, and politically contested.

title: Not too far from the madding crowd. Tourism-led growth and urban dynamics in the Kansai region before and after the coronavirus pandemics
Integrating urban resilience, transformation and sustainability: A framework and empirical evidence from China's urban agglomerations
“Why do they think we're different?” The making of an inhabited ruin and residents' perceptions of tourism
abstract: This paper dialogues with scholarship on both ruin tourism and the production of stigmatized, inhabited urban ruins by examining the Vele of Scampia, an iconic public housing complex on the northern periphery of Naples (Southern Italy). It explores how such spaces function as lived homes while emerging as sites of touristic interest. Specifically, the study pursues two aims: first, it conceptualizes the Vele as inhabited ruins, analyzing how political dynamics, material decay, and processes of symbolic degradation have jointly shaped the built environment and inhabitants' everyday lives. Second, it investigates how inhabitants perceive and navigate the presence of tourists, a dimension largely overlooked within ruin tourism literature. Findings reveal a central paradox: while tourism can bring visibility and a sense of inclusion to a marginalized community, it simultaneously risks reproducing social stigma and reinforcing feelings of otherness. The paper calls for closer attention to how inhabitants experience and negotiate tourism within lived spaces of ruination.

title: How does regulation impact housing rental prices? Evidence from Spain using fractional integration techniques
abstract: This paper examines the impact of housing regulations on rental prices in Spain from 1962 to 2024, focusing on fiscal policies and contract duration regulations. Employing fractional integration techniques, we assess the effectiveness of supply- and demand-side measures in stabilizing rental prices. The findings reveal that regulatory interventions have not achieved consistent long-term price stabilization, with shocks to rental prices displaying persistent effects. Notably, the 1999 fiscal policy changes temporarily influenced demand, but no significant lasting impact was observed across other regulatory measures. These results highlight the structural deficiencies in Spain's housing policies, characterized by a lack of effective supply-side incentives and protection and inadequate demand-side measures. To address affordability challenges and meet constitutional housing mandates, the study recommends adopting comprehensive policies, including fiscal incentives for landlords, expanded social housing programs, and stronger tenant protections. This research contributes to understanding the interplay between regulation and housing market dynamics in Spain.

title: A meta-synthesis of the big data in urban transportation planning processes
abstract: This study conducts a qualitative meta-synthesis to examine how big data has transformed urban transportation planning processes. Drawing upon the pre-analysis, technical analysis, and post-analysis phases, the review classifies data sources into four overarching groups (i.e., Mobility Sensing, Infrastructure and Environment, Social and Behavioral, and Synthesized/Simulated) and identifies five analytical mechanisms through which big data generates planning value. The findings reveal that Mobility Sensing and Infrastructure and Environment datasets dominate the pre- and technical stages, while Social and Behavioral and Synthesized/Simulated data are most prevalent in post-analysis, reflecting a shift from data collection toward integration and feedback. Mechanistically, big data enhances planning through data processing and extraction, analytical and modeling approaches, real-time monitoring and adaptive control, decision-support and knowledge translation, and institutional and governance enablers. Across all stages, hybrid methodologies that combine traditional surveys with large-scale digital traces prove most effective, balancing behavioral interpretability with temporal precision. Nonetheless, challenges persist, including representativeness bias, the decline of traditional survey data, and institutional fragmentation in data governance. The study concludes that big data's value lies not in replacing conventional methods but in complementing them through multi-level fusion across data, feature, and decision layers. Future urban transportation planning will therefore depend on integrative, multi-source frameworks that combine technical innovation with ethical, equitable, and transparent governance, enabling continuous learning and adaptive policymaking in data-driven cities.

title: From generic to salutogenic urbanism: Evidence of the landmark paradox and the role of biodiversity and walkability in mental health
abstract: Public open-space walkability is central to health-oriented landscape and urban planning. Faced with a global polycrisis (interwoven climate, mental health, physical activity, and biodiversity challenges) research focused on salutogenic environments is crucial for forming cross-sector recommendations. Yet, evidence that integrates psychological and urban planning perspectives remains limited. The aim of the study was to determine how urban design influences psychological integration in public open spaces, which dispositional versus environmental variables most strongly predict psychological outcomes, and what human-centred recommendations may inform the prototyping of salutogenic urban environments. We employed a novel experimental approach to operationalise environmental variables, which were biodiversity proportion, landmark salience, and walkable surface. We assessed nature connectedness, sense of coherence, and generalised anxiety as dispositional variables, and well-being, sense of coherence-meaningfulness, inclusion of nature in self, and place meaning as psychological outcome variables. Hierarchical regression analyses showed that walkable surface and high-quality biodiverse proportion (rather than quantity of the greenery) significantly predicted sense of coherence-meaningfulness, with walkable surface emerging as the strongest predictor of well-being. Landmark salience proved to be the most consistent negative predictor across all outcomes, including place meaning-essentialism. These results highlight the salutogenic potential of walkable, biophilic cityscapes and reveal the detrimental effects of excessive landmark dominance, suggesting that integrative, pedestrian-oriented urban planning should be prioritised over hierarchy-enforcing or car-oriented affordances. Our findings have transdisciplinary implications, forming human-centred, evidence-based recommendations for resilience and mental health enhancement in public open space users.

title: “We are beautiful.” Creating political and societal traction through multi-stakeholder participation. Insights from 12 European cities' processes of establishing Food Policy Councils.
abstract: Food Policy Councils (FPCs) are increasingly used to coordinate Values-based Territorial Food Networks (VTFNs) in European cities. Their contribution, however, extends beyond formal policy outputs to the processes that enable deliberation, collaboration and stakeholder engagement. Drawing on four years of empirical work with 12 cities participating in the FUSILLI Project, we examine how FPCs are initiated, established, organised and embedded within local governance settings. The analysis revisits the distinction between “bottom-up” and “government-mandated” FPCs and shows that cases frequently combine characteristics of both. Rather than two distinct models, they form a spectrum of co-created arrangements in which civil society, municipal administrations, businesses and researchers negotiate roles and responsibilities. The urban scale emerges as a critical locus for this work, offering institutional proximity, opportunities for coordination across sectors and the capacity to link community initiatives with formal policy processes. Using a comparative framework, the study assesses FPCs along three dimensions: food system sustainability, food democracy and good governance. It considers stated objectives, governance practices, activities and outputs, and the outcomes that follow from them. The findings indicate that even early-stage or partial initiatives can strengthen participation, improve cross-sector coordination and generate conditions supportive of incremental or even transformative system change. Overall, the paper clarifies the organisational configurations through which FPCs contribute to food system transformation. It identifies core features that underpin their durability and policy relevance, alongside optional elements that can enhance their performance. The results offer practical insights for policymakers and practitioners seeking to design or refine FPCs capable of supporting resilient and values-driven urban food systems.

title: Housing price, digital finance, and entrepreneurship in urban China
When tourists move next door: Airbnb and rent dynamics in Milan
abstract: This paper studies whether the relationship between Airbnb density and long-term rental prices persisted in the post-pandemic urban context. It analyses the case of Milan (Italy), a city characterized by strong economic and tourist attractiveness, rising housing affordability pressures and comparatively weak regulation of short-term rentals. Using geo-referenced data on long-term rental advertisements and Airbnb listings for the period 2019–2023, this study estimates the association between the change in local Airbnb density and monthly asking rents per square metre, controlling for dwelling characteristics, neighbourhood attributes, accessibility and time effects. The results show that, after the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the renewed growth of short-term rentals was significantly associated with higher long-term rents in Milan. These findings suggest that the Airbnb rent-gap mechanism persisted or re-emerged in the post-pandemic period, contributing to housing affordability pressures and raising important questions for urban housing policy and the regulation of platform-mediated accommodation.

title: Making green rent gaps: Housing price impacts of the 606/Bloomingdale Trail in Chicago
abstract: Urban greening initiatives present a paradox: they often improve environmental quality and public amenities intensifying real estate speculation and displacement pressures. This study examines these dynamics through Chicago's 606 Trail (Bloomingdale Trail), a 2.7-mile elevated park opened in 2015. We conceptualize and empirically measure a policy–market temporal mismatch: the gap between rapid housing market responses to infrastructure investment signals and the timing of municipal housing preservation measures. Using residential property transactions from 2009 to 2024, we estimate hedonic price models with spatial econometric specifications across eight project phases and five distance buffers extending 1.5 miles from the trail. Results show that a statistically significant proximity premium emerged during the 2011–2013 recommitment-to-construction period, when the project returned to active development and full funding was secured, well before construction or opening, and persisted long after completion. In the immediate post-opening period, properties within 0.25 miles sold for 29% more than comparable properties 1–1.5 miles away. Although Chicago aldermen attempted a demolition-fee ordinance in 2017, the first enacted housing preservation measure — a demolition moratorium covering the trail area — was not adopted until 2020, nine years after the initial market response. We argue that such temporal mismatches reflect structural constraints on the speed of municipal protective action under prevailing urban governance arrangements, including informational asymmetries that allow markets to capitalize anticipated amenities immediately, institutional configurations in which constructing new protective arrangements takes longer than executing development transactions, and political economy dynamics in which pro-growth coalitions mobilize more rapidly than housing preservation coalitions.

title: An affordable yet expensive city: Explaining Vietnam's housing paradox through informality and upgrading
Exploring drivers and impacts of construction halt measures in Guangzhou: A systems thinking approach
abstract: The construction sector is a major contributor to the climate crisis. In China, rapid urbanisation has intensified these effects, prompting cities like Guangzhou to implement construction halt measures targeting high-emission and resource-intensive projects. While these measures aim to reduce pollution and carbon emissions, their systemic consequences remain poorly understood. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the environmental, social, and economic impacts of construction halts in Guangzhou through a systems thinking approach. We integrated desk-based analysis of halted construction projects, expert interviews, and a public survey in a causal loop diagram, displaying hypotheses of the causal chains underpinning construction halt measures. Findings show that construction halts can mitigate soil, water, air, and noise pollution, and reduce direct and indirect carbon emissions. However, they also generate unintended effects, including unemployment, debt risks, and public opposition, particularly when applied through a “one-size-fits-all” governance model. As moratoria on new construction gain traction globally, our results highlight the limitations of authoritarian environmentalism, and underscore the need for context-sensitive, deliberative, and participatory governance to implement a new post-growth planning paradigm to achieve ecological justice and urban well-being.

title: Multi-dimensional intercity linkages, industrial structure, and their cross-level interactive effects on impervious surface expansion: Evidence from Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, China
abstract: Regional integration is reshaping urban spatial patterns by strengthening intercity linkages and fostering cross-level interactions among influencing factors. Yet the interactive effects of these multilevel factors under regional integration remain poorly understood. To address this gap, this study used geospatial big data to quantify intercity linkage intensities across five dimensions—population mobility, information flow, transportation connectivity, capital linkage, and regional cooperation—in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei urban agglomeration. A hierarchical generalized linear model (HGLM) was then constructed across the pixel, county, and city levels to examine the associations of multilevel factors and their cross-level interactions with impervious surface expansion from 2012 to 2022. The results showed that the interaction between information flow and secondary industry share, and that between transportation connectivity and tertiary industry share, were negatively associated with impervious surface expansion, whereas the interaction between capital linkage and secondary industry share showed a positive association. Furthermore, interactions between industrial development and population mobility, transportation connectivity, and regional cooperation were associated with a higher probability of peri-urban expansion, while stronger capital linkage combined with industrial development was associated with impervious surface expansion near urban cores. These findings advance the understanding of impervious surface expansion under regional integration and offer policy insights for optimizing spatial structure and balancing core-periphery dynamics.

title: Impact of green spaces on the Viennese housing market
abstract: Urban greening is becoming a popular policy response in preparing cities for global environmental challenges linked to climate change and biodiversity loss. Concurrently, concerns about the trade-offs of using urban areas for urban greening have risen. A growing number of studies link urban greening initiatives to rising housing costs and displacement in surrounding neighbourhoods. So far, only a small part of the literature discusses how to prevent unwanted consequences of urban greening (such as green gentrification), focusing on utilising housing policy. In our study, we examine the impact of urban green spaces on rents in Vienna, Austria and the potential of housing policies in the development of rent prices. We show that in Vienna, urban greening only has a small influence on rents, in comparison to flat characteristics and rent control. In our case study with a predominantly rental market, private rents are mainly influenced by the location of the accommodations, their state of renewal and the applicability of rent control. Further, the impact of green spaces is concentrated in the green belt in neighbourhoods with a low share of rent control. All this indicates that in Vienna, urban green has only limited potential to increase rents to the extent that it leads to displacement. The mitigating effect of rent control on the rents of the affected apartments in Vienna far exceeds the rent-increasing effect of urban greenery, raising questions about the possibility of utilising rent control as a mechanism in policy making.

title: Polycentricity as a process: An evolutionary morphological analysis of the Tehran Metropolitan Region (1975–2025)
Conceptualizing the interplay between remoteness and modes of governing solid waste in Arctic small and medium-sized cities
abstract: Municipal solid waste management (MSWM) remains a significant yet often overlooked challenge in cities located in the Arctic, particularly with respect to societal, environmental, and governance considerations. These cities, often located far from decision-making centers and recycling infrastructure, face the need to develop innovative, context-specific waste strategies, challenging the idea that they are peripheral to national and international environmental (waste) governance. Instead, they act as actors and sites where unique waste-related policies are created. In this conceptual paper, we draw on the modes of governing municipal waste framework developed by Bulkeley and colleagues, and further developed by Pollans, to examine how remoteness impacts the advancement of MSWM in the Arctic. In this vein, we demonstrate that the impacts of remoteness are reflected in Arctic cities and their national governments' capacity to manage solid waste at a distance. These impacts affect national governance's ability to enforce waste regulation locally, and cities' capacity to develop, acquire, and fund waste treatment innovations and infrastructure. The impacts of remoteness are also evident in residents' engagement in environmental initiatives and their development of a sense of place attachment. Future research on the relationship between remoteness and MSWM in the Arctic should include comparative studies of metropolitan and remote urban areas to gain a broader understanding of their unique features and shared characteristics.

title: Migrant trust in public services: Institutional encounters and urban inclusion in Finland
abstract: Trust in public services is important for migrants to navigate institutions and participate in the societies where they live, yet less is known about how trust develops through repeated institutional encounters across different levels of public service provision. This qualitative study examines how Iranian migrant women in Finland develop, revise, and sustain trust through encounters with national and municipal public services. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 13 Iranian women living in Helsinki and Tampere, the study uses reflexive thematic analysis to trace trust trajectories across different migration pathways and institutional contexts. The findings show that trust is not a fixed attitude toward public institutions, but an evolving process shaped by institutional performance, perceived fairness, transparency, responsiveness, consistency, and the quality of everyday encounters. Participants described administrative delays and competence-related difficulties, while accounts of unfairness, opacity, and discriminatory treatment were particularly associated with erosion of trust. Frontline professionals played an important intermediary role by translating institutional rules into lived service experiences, while family, community networks, and other intermediaries helped participants interpret procedures and navigate difficulties. These relational resources could buffer negative institutional experiences and support continued engagement with public services. The findings further show that institutional encounters have implications beyond trust: respectful and responsive interactions can strengthen migrants' sense of recognition and inclusion, whereas repeated experiences of disregard or exclusion may reinforce perceptions of marginalisation. The study highlights migrant trust as relational and evolving, and public services in urban settings as important sites where trust and inclusion are experienced and negotiated.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and drivers of rural multifunctional transformation in metropolitan areas: A case study of Beijing
Governing through incompletion: Diaspora-funded infrastructure and urban governance in South Lebanon
Corrigendum/Erratum to “City profile: Yiwu and the making of a new platform-corridor city. Logistics, digital capitalism, and bottom-up silk road urbanization” [Cities volume 174 (2026) 107029]
How do public planners perceive their scope of action?
abstract: Agency and structure are frequently identified as crucial determinants in shaping planning policies, although in-depth insights into the agency of individuals remain scarce. This article studies how public sector employees working in the field of planning perceive their own scope of action, understood as their ability to affect plans and policies. The study builds on empirical data collected through an online survey featuring a Q methodology sorting exercise to which 104 civil servants from Finland responded. The data reveals four clusters of respondents with similar sorting patterns: “collaborative administrators”, “frustrated workers”, “active experts” and “individualist innovators”. These clusters are characterized by differences regarding the perceived importance of individual initiative, collaboration and structure. When contrasting these groups against planner archetypes defined in the literature, it seems that some characteristics of doers, bureaucrats and entrepreneurs can be found among Finnish planners. However, the results also highlight a rarely addressed dimension related to satisfaction with work. While most respondents are content with their own scope of action and confident about their own contribution, a group of “frustrated workers” is evident: planners who are dissatisfied with their work and impact. Within this group are a significant number of women who are relatively new to the planning profession. The findings suggest that the dimension of satisfaction/frustration among planners, and public servants in general, warrants further investigation, as it might provide new insights into the complex processes of policy development and decision making in planning.

title: Green gentrification beyond residence: Diverging residential change and park-user restructuring in Shanghai
