Neoliberal policies as catalysts of inequality after disasters: Mapping (Im)mobilities and the effects of floods in Porto Alegre, Brazil
Internal migration policy and migrants' mental health: Evidence from China's hukou reform
Built environment and Indigenous mental health service use: Evidence from Medicare microdata in South-East Queensland, Australia
abstract: This study provides a systematic exploration of whether neighbourhood-level built environment factors are associated with mental health service (MHS) utilisation by Indigenous peoples in South-East Queensland, Australia, while controlling for individual socio-demographic factors. Using population-based Medicare microdata linked with administrative records, we quantify individual-level MHS utilisation and employ multi-level negative binomial regression models to assess associations between MHS utilisation and environmental characteristics. Results indicate that built environment factors and their interactions with socio-demographic characteristics are statistically associated with Indigenous individuals' MHS utilisation. Specifically, greater MHS utilisation is associated with living in neighbourhoods with greater green space among younger individuals, and with living in inner regional areas (i.e., outskirts of major cities) among individuals with lower family incomes. Lower MHS utilisation is associated with living in neighbourhoods with greater green space among older individuals; with living in inner regional areas among those with higher incomes or two-family households; and with living in neighbourhoods with higher housing diversity among individuals with higher family incomes or three-or-more-family households. Furthermore, while overall lower MHS utilisation is associated with living in neighbourhoods with poorer public transit accessibility and residing in areas with better street network connectivity, these built environment conditions are associated with higher MHS utilisation among individuals needing assistance with daily living activities. These findings highlight a set of environmental attributes that merit deeper, community-led inquiry. As a cross-sectional observational analysis, this study identifies associations only—not causal evidence—offering an empirical starting point for future quasi-experimental and participatory research in partnership with Indigenous communities.

title: Short-term rentals, urban sustainability and governance policy: An analytical regulatory framework proposal
abstract: Short-term rentals (STRs) have become a major source of urban tension, intensifying housing pressure, neighbourhood conflict, and governance complexity. Despite growing academic attention, existing regulatory approaches still remain fragmented, focusing on single instruments rather than integrated governance strategies. This article aims to develop a more general and updated analytical framework for short-term rental regulation helping policy makers to confront main challenges. With this objective, in a first stage, we conduct a systematic review of 90 studies (2009–2025), identifying the key regulatory instruments, together with the institutional and contextual conditions where they develop. The synthesis informs the integration of regulatory choices, governance arrangements, and urban sustainability objectives within a common analytical structure. In a second stage, we propose a wider, more general and updated framework for STR regulation comprising six main components: host differentiation, adaptive regulation, multilevel governance and platform cooperation, enforcement and transparency, taxation schemes, and regulatory innovation. The framework contains all pieces identified in the current regulatory debate taking place at major worldwide cities, providing a playground for policy makers seeking to make cities a sustainable place for the future. Practical and policy implications emerge from the research.

title: Environmentally sustainable transportation, micromobility, and large sport events: Bikeshare usage in Austin, Texas
abstract: Human activity and mobility in cities are shaped by environmental conditions and by spatial and temporal patterns of economic and social activity. Large sport events intensify these dynamics, generating substantial short-haul travel that remains underexamined in sport ecology and micromobility research (Bae & McCullough, 2026). This study explores how college football game days at the University of Texas are associated with changes in the spatial and temporal demand for Austin's Metrobike system. Guided by time-geography and gravity-based perspectives, and drawing on sport ecology, we analyze 966,027 Metrobike trips recorded between 2021 and mid-2024. Trip data were aggregated into daily observations and spatially categorized across 89 kiosks, then examined using GIS, Negative Binomial Regression, and a probit model to assess how home-game Saturdays relate to bikeshare usage near campus and the stadium. Results show statistically significant increases in ridership and in the probability that rides begin and end near the venue on game days, even after controlling for weather, seasonality, holidays, and weekday–weekend differences. However, the absolute scale of this increase appears constrained by limited capacity and accessibility. These findings advance sport ecology by incorporating large-scale behavioral data, extend micromobility research by identifying large sport events as distinct, capacity-constrained demand peaks, and demonstrate how geography-informed frameworks can support data-driven planning for sustainable event-related mobility.

title: Multi-scale functional restructuring of urban green spaces across 329 Chinese cities from 1990 to 2020
But who is watching?": Imaginary audience effect and adult play inhibition in urban public space
abstract: Urban spaces offer various spontaneous and design-led opportunities for ludic-also referred as playful engagements. Yet, adult participation often remains constrained, and reasons are insufficiently theorized in urban design scholarship. This article reintroduces imaginary audience theory- the heightened perception of being observed and judged as an analytical lens for examining barriers to adult ludic engagement in public space. Drawing on qualitative research with nine south Asian migrant women participants from, the small town of Oamaru, New Zealand, the study analyses how internalized surveillance, cultural norms of respectability, and uncertainty about appropriate public behaviour inhibit playful action. Data were gathered through two phenomenology-based workshops and photovoice methods running through a year. The findings show that while the imaginary audience effect operates across all participants, it intensifies at the intersections of gender, migration status, and cultural difference, producing heightened constraints on ludic engagement. The article argues that urban designs having collaborative, convivial shared spaces and inclusive design elements can mitigate these psychological barriers by diffusing perceived scrutiny and normalising adult play. By synthesising insights from developmental psychology and ludic urbanism, the study advances a socio-psychological understanding of migrant women’s play in Oamaru and offers practical implications for designing more inclusive and equitable ludic urban environments.

title: Textual symbol of urban spatial differentiation: An empirical analysis on nomenclature of tea restaurants in Hong Kong
How does the provision of urban subsidized housing impact the migrant workers' rural homestead withdrawal: Evidence from the Chengdu-Chongqing region, China

Identifying intersectional inequalities in spatial healthcare accessibility using self-organizing maps
abstract: Background Spatial accessibility studies often examine sociodemographic characteristics separately, limiting understanding of how access varies across intersecting forms of social advantage and disadvantage. This study develops a novel analytical framework using unsupervised machine learning to assess intersectional inequalities in spatial healthcare accessibility across a fast-growing, diverse metropolitan region. Methods We analyzed 4250 healthcare facilities across nine service types in Metro Vancouver, Canada, a metropolitan region with roughly 2.6 million residents as of 2021. Census sociodemographic data were downscaled to a 1-km grid, and self-organizing maps were used to identify intersectional population clusters based on age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and income. Spatial accessibility by driving was estimated within 15-, 30-, and 45-minute thresholds using a network-based routing engine. Inequality was quantified using population-weighted Gini coefficients. Results The overall Gini coefficient was 0.18, with notable variation across geographic areas, population clusters, and facility types. Accessibility was highest in urban areas and lowest in suburban and peripheral areas. The greatest inequality was observed among older, affluent White populations in peripheral areas (Gini = 0.34), followed by racially and ethnically diverse populations with low educational attainment in outer suburbs (Gini = 0.28). Across facility types, inequality was highest for hospitals (Gini = 0.27) and lowest for walk-in clinics and pharmacies (Gini = 0.17). Conclusions This reproducible framework demonstrates how access to healthcare services varies across intersecting sociodemographic characteristics at high spatial resolution. The findings provide evidence to inform more equitable planning, resource allocation, and policy to support healthy, inclusive, and sustainable cities.

title: Not all debt is equal: Debt type, burden, and life satisfaction among urban young adults in Seoul
AI-oriented policy and urban ecological quality: Evidence from China's national AI innovation and development pilot zones
Proposal and validation of a transferable high-resolution monitoring framework with hotspot analysis for adaptive urban spatial planning in the Global South.
abstract: Adaptive spatial planning requires robust spatiotemporal monitoring of urban land use and land cover change, yet no consensus exists on appropriate spatial, temporal, and spectral resolutions for cities in the Global South. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a high-resolution monitoring framework for urban expansion to support local spatial planning. Using Quito as a case study, impervious surfaces were mapped for 2013, 2017, and 2023, enabling analysis of two five-year intervals. A random forest classifier was implemented using an integrated set of predictors combining vegetation-sensitive spectral indices (NDVI and SAVI), the Perpendicular Impervious Surface Index (PISI), and topographic and textural variables derived from high-resolution multispectral imagery. Classification outputs were integrated with the Getis–Ord G statistic to identify significant spatial clusters of urban expansion. Results show strong classification performance, with consistency values exceeding 91% against independently interpreted reference samples. NDVI and SAVI exhibited the greatest explanatory contribution, while PISI and topographic variables improved discrimination in heterogeneous urban landscapes. The findings support five-year monitoring intervals as an effective balance between change detection and relevance for local spatial planning. Based on these findings, we propose a transferable 5 × 5 × 5 monitoring framework, integrating five-year temporal resolution, multispectral imagery, and 5 m spatial resolution as a baseline for urban expansion monitoring in the Global South, while recognizing that its applicability should be validated across different urban contexts. Hotspot analysis revealed heterogeneous expansion dynamics, providing actionable insights for urban growth management, land-use planning, and sustainable spatial development.

title: The nationalization of elite private middle schools and urban housing market restructuring in Hangzhou, China
Unveiling energy poverty vulnerability in a megacity: A spatial regression approach
abstract: Energy poverty is driven by rising global energy prices and climate-related disruptions. This study examines the spatial dimensions of energy poverty vulnerability in Seoul, a megacity marked by demographic aging, fragmented housing, and infrastructural inequality. Using spatial regression models, we analyse 424 administrative districts to identify both spatially homogeneous and heterogeneous determinants of energy poverty. Citywide drivers include the low-income household ratio, average floor area, and the single-person household ratio. Districts with higher shares of low-income households and larger dwelling sizes exhibit greater vulnerability, whereas districts with higher concentrations of single-person households tend to show lower vulnerability. Thermal-safety infrastructure variables, including cooling centres and warm banks, display positive citywide associations, reflecting their targeted placement in already vulnerable areas. Spatially heterogeneous influences include the elderly ratio, apartment share, population density, and park area. Vulnerability increases in districts where aging populations coincide with structurally inefficient housing, while apartment-dominated neighbourhoods consistently exhibit lower vulnerability. Density and green space exert mitigating effects in selected districts, highlighting locally specific built-environment advantages. We derive three policy implications: (1) spatially targeted adjustment of thermal-safety infrastructure based on neighbourhood vulnerability clusters; (2) place-based housing retrofit strategies focused on structurally energy-intensive districts; and (3) adoption of spatial diagnostics to guide differentiated urban energy policies. By integrating spatial regression with district-level metered utility data, this study offers a transferable framework for diagnosing and addressing intra- urban energy poverty vulnerability in megacities facing similar structural conditions.

Two decades of research on climate change impacts and UNESCO World Cultural Heritage: A comprehensive scoping review
abstract: Climate change constitutes an escalating, systemic, and transboundary threat to cultural heritage, undermining both its material integrity and associated socio-cultural values while exposing persistent limitations in translating international climate-policy commitments into effective heritage-management practice. This study conducts a scoping review of reviews to synthesize two decades of scholarship on climate change and tangible immovable cultural heritage and examine its relevance to UNESCO's climate action agenda. Following the PRISMA-ScR protocol, a Scopus search identified 244 records, of which 23 review-based studies met the eligibility criteria, complemented by one official UNESCO report. Beyond a conventional state-of-the-art assessment, the study develops an integrative analytical structure that organises fragmented scholarship into one foundational heritage–climate domain and four emerging adjacent domains, examined in relation to UNESCO's World Heritage Climate Action Goals for 2030. Its main contribution lies in synthesizing dispersed knowledge into a thematic–conceptual structure that identifies research gaps, clarifies relationships between scientific evidence and climate-action priorities, and guides future research. The review positions climate–heritage research as a strategic knowledge domain requiring integration across risk assessment, adaptation planning, knowledge generation, and governance processes. The findings reveal significant conceptual, methodological, geographical, and operational asymmetries. Research remains largely focused on the physical impacts of climate change on tangible immovable cultural heritage, whereas non-material and socio-cultural dimensions associated with such heritage, community and Indigenous/local knowledge systems, mitigation strategies, and implementation-oriented approaches remain comparatively underdeveloped. Additional challenges include weak methodological standardisation, inconsistent risk frameworks, limited long-term monitoring data, and insufficient incorporation of future climate scenarios. While advances have been achieved in climate-risk assessment, adaptation planning, and capacity building, climate mitigation remains underrepresented. These findings highlight the need for integrated, transferable, and governance-oriented frameworks capable of informing resilience-oriented heritage management, climate policy, and future research agendas.

title: Agglomeration and centralization: The multidimensional impact of the Internet on the spatial structure of urban employment in China

A taxonomy of localized sustainable development goal indicators: Mapping progress, gaps, fragmented monitoring, and priorities in urban SDG localization
abstract: Cities worldwide are endeavoring to adapt the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to their local contexts to ensure their effective implementation. The diversity among cities highlights their varied experiences, resulting in a wide array of localized indicators documented in the literature. These variations in indicators have led to complexities and fragmentation in monitoring and assessment across different cities, thereby complicating global comparisons. To address this issue, we propose a taxonomy that systematically organizes localized SDG indicators. This taxonomy enables the identification of strengths, gaps, and limitations in current indicator frameworks, supporting the enhancement of localized SDG monitoring and implementation. Using systematic review and deductive content analysis, 431 localized indicators were identified from 57 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2023. The findings indicated that approximately 49.7% of the SDG targets were directly aligned with various localized indicators, whereas 50.3% of the targets lacked corresponding indicators, revealing significant implementation gaps. Furthermore, 36.1% of the targets were associated with multiple indicators, underscoring the need to prioritize targets and to address the issue of overlapping indicators, which can complicate effective monitoring and resource allocation. The distribution of indicators was also uneven across sectors and sustainability dimensions, with a pronounced focus on environmental and social dimensions, highlighting imbalances in indicator types. This taxonomy offers a structured tool for policymakers, urban planners, local governments, and researchers to identify gaps in their SDG implementation, enhance comparability, prioritize underrepresented targets, and fortify localized SDG implementation.

title: Urban commons reconfigured: Reclassification and infrastructural transformation in Old Pokhara, Nepal
Regeneration paradox in coal communities: Trade-offs between perceived green space quality, collective memory, and older residents' subjective well-being
Assessing disparities in open space provision for primary and secondary schools: A case study of high-density Hong Kong
abstract: Regular access to open spaces has been found to significantly improve the physical and mental well-being of primary and secondary school students. However, land scarcity in dense urban settings restricts the scale of on-campus open spaces. In response to this constraint, this study posits that urban open spaces adjacent to schools can supplement and compensate for inadequate on-campus open spaces. Taking high-density Hong Kong as a case, this study aims to evaluate the service provision of two types of open spaces: internal on-campus open spaces and external urban open spaces. An integrated framework is constructed to quantify provision disparities; cluster analysis is adopted to generalize typical patterns. The results reveal an undersupply of internal open spaces across most samples, validating the need for supplementary external open spaces. Significant provision disparities exist across districts and school types. Schools in old urban cores and industrial satellite towns provide poorer internal–external open space services than those in garden suburbs and new towns; this pattern is driven by regional development trajectories and planning doctrines. Meanwhile, school funding and site selection rules induce provision disparities among different school types. Schools in Hong Kong present five typical patterns of open space service provision: Balanced Intermediates, Internally Oriented, Internally Sufficient with Polarized Externalities, Comprehensive High Achievers, and Externally Oriented. In summary, this study establishes an evaluation framework for school internal and external open space provision and delivers actionable insights to integrate school and urban open space system planning for more equitable, healthy student environments in high-density cities.

title: Adapting large language models for urban trip purpose inference: A domain-informed textual representation and fine-tuning framework
A comprehensive vision-based framework for understanding nation-wide urban socio-demographics
Voices from the city: Sentiment across public open space types in Hong Kong before and during COVID-19
HPWO model: A housing-price weighted opportunities model for heterogeneous human mobility
What people see, describe, and feel in 97,990 London photographs
Analyzing perceptions of urban agriculture's contributions to sustainable city development
From plan to plate: Assessing food systems and equity considerations in historical and contemporary comprehensive plans from four U.S. cities
abstract: Urban planning is a structural driver of health, shaping environments that influence everyday activities and resources that can enable or inhibit health, including food systems. Yet, the extent to which comprehensive plans support equity and how this has evolved remains underexplored. This study analyzes historical and contemporary comprehensive plans from four U.S. cities—Chicago, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and New York City—to assess how equity orientation and food equity considerations have changed over time. Using a structured evaluation instrument comprising 57 indicators, we assess changes in plan strength, comprehensiveness, and content. Results show that while equity orientation has generally improved—most notably through stronger vision statements—food equity considerations remain uneven and fragmented. Nutritional adequacy, spatial equity, and food affordability are increasingly addressed, whereas culturally preferred foods, social equity, and agency remain underrepresented. Notably, improvements in general equity orientation did not always correspond with enhanced food equity measures. Further, comprehensive planning continues to lack public participation processes and often falls short in specifying how proposed actions will be operationalized and monitored. Findings underscore the need for more comprehensive, accountable, and community-informed planning approaches that center marginalized voices and address the structural determinants of food insecurity. We recommend strategies for embedding equity more deeply into both the content and processes of comprehensive and food systems planning, including participatory governance, equity-focused evaluation, and systems thinking.

title: Reshaping urban residents' daily behavior patterns in the digital age: Multi-source evidence from 2018 and 2024 time-use surveys and GPS trajectories
Uncovering stakeholder preferences for urban blue-green infrastructure siting: Insights from online swing weights elicitation
abstract: Blue-green infrastructure (BGI) location choice requires addressing objectives across environmental, ecological, urban, governance, economic and social domains, necessitating stakeholder engagement. However, preference elicitation in BGI planning often relies on single-disciplinary or expert-driven approaches that may overlook differences in priorities across stakeholder groups. The primary aim of this study was to understand stakeholder priorities for BGI planning objectives across three BGI groups: small systems (bioretention, infiltration systems, and swales), large systems (constructed wetlands and ponds/lakes) and urban trees, while the secondary aim was to test and advance a preference elicitation procedure using an innovative online swing-weighting software within a GIS-MCDA framework. Across two case studies in Quebec, Canada, 12 stakeholders in Trois-Rivières and 20 in Montréal representing government agencies, non-profit organizations, and research services, participated in five online workshops. They provided weights on an objectives-based BGI suitability framework. Results showed broad agreement on needs-related objectives (i.e. addressing site-specific needs that can be fulfilled through BGI placement), particularly water management, climate adaptation, and heat island mitigation, across BGI groups. Greater divergence emerged for opportunity-related objectives (i.e. leveraging site-specific opportunities), such as optimal soil type and planned works, reflecting differences in stakeholder priorities across BGI types and the potential of sites. By revealing shared and divergent planning priorities, this research highlights the value of stakeholder-driven preference elicitation and demonstrates the utility of swing weighting within GIS-MCDA for fostering transparent and participatory decision-making. Integrating stakeholder preferences into suitability mapping provides an approach for making differences in planning perspectives explicit and supporting context-sensitive BGI planning.

title: Global regularities and regional patterns in social media discourse: Topic variety, language diversity, and user behavior across 29 cities
abstract: In our increasingly interconnected world, digital communication operates with variable geographic reach. Distinguishing between regionally and globally discussed issues allows us to better understand the geographical relevance of topics in digital urban discourses. This study compared the diversity of topics, languages, and user behaviors across 29 cities around the world using Twitter (now X) data posted around New Year's Eve 2021–2022. Applying topic modeling, we identified 145 topics and classified them into relative types of geographic diffusion (i.e., ‘low’, ‘intermediate’, or ‘global’) according to the number of cities and world regions where they were discussed. Topics discussed across the globe included “Food”, “Music”, “Family”, “Religion”, and “Politics”, while conversations with a low relative diffusion reflected on region-specific issues such as “Brexit” in the UK or the “Year of the Tiger” in East Asia. Intermediate topics such as “Healthcare/Medicine”, “Feminism”, and “Booster Vaccination” were common across most regions but displayed distinct emphases. Topic diversity tended to increase with language diversity, and the number of languages used increased as topics shifted from low to global diffusion. Twitter user behavior exhibited consistent Zipf-like patterns across all cities, with a small fraction of highly active users producing most tweets and discussing the highest number of topics. Regional differences emerged, with East and South-East Asian cities showing more balanced user participation and European and North American ones being the most unequal. Viewed through the lens of social media, these patterns reveal both the commonalities that connect human societies and the persistent differences that define them, reflecting a world that is increasingly interconnected but far from being homogeneous.

title: Does urban blue-green space rejuvenate residents' mental well-being in megacity? An empirical analysis of Dhaka, Bangladesh
Urban transit preparedness under blackout and aerial-threat conditions: A planning-support city framework for stop-linked shelter provision
Urban regeneration as a mobility intervention: Evidence on travel behavior shifts
Spatial patterns of urban population growth-shrinkage differentiation in China and their associations with multidimensional flow networks
Revisiting Gehl through perceived safety: A computational method
abstract: This study examines how ground-floor urban form relates to perceived safety in Stockholm, Sweden, using approximately one million street view images collected between 2010 and 2021 together with multi-source built-environment data. Jan Gehl’s writings discuss perceived safety as part of a human-centered design framework that integrates both traffic- and crime-related safety through street-level environmental design, drawing together ideas also established in broader planning and safety scholarship. Building on Gehl’s integrative framework, we operationalize a set of design attributes emphasized in his work and evaluate their associations with perceived safety scores derived from locally collected image-comparison surveys and extended citywide using deep learning models. Across multiple modeling approaches and two spatial scales, ground-floor features related to transparency and public–private transitions show the strongest and most consistent positive associations with perceived safety, often exceeding the explanatory strength of neighborhood demographic and land-use controls. Other features such as pedestrian and cycling infrastructure also demonstrate meaningful relationships, particularly at a finer spatial scale. These findings suggest that perceived safety is closely associated with the human-scale, street-level design features integrated within Gehl’s framework and demonstrate how computational urban analytics can operationalize qualitative design principles and evaluate their relevance to urban livability at scale.

title: The internal and external benefits of intentional communities: Cohousing, energy communities, and religion-based communities beyond idealisation
abstract: Interest in intentional communities is growing in both public debate and the academic literature. However, their benefits are often considered from an uncritical or idealised perspective. This paper examines three distinct types of intentional communities – cohousing communities, energy communities, and religion-based communities – and conducts a critical analysis of their respective benefits. It shows that, while internal benefits for their members (i.e. psychological, functional, and economic benefits) are generally well supported, external benefits for society at large (i.e. distributive, environmental, and civic benefits) are often unclear, limited, or contingent on additional conditions.

title: Examining the association between shelter status and homelessness duration: A case study of Halifax, Canada
abstract: Several studies have investigated factors associated with urban homelessness and its duration. Most focus on social and health factors and overlook shelter status, potentially due to reliance on datasets from sheltered homeless individuals. Shelter status, defined as whether an individual was staying in formal temporary accommodation or in an unsheltered location not intended for habitation, represents a critical distinction in subsequent housing pathways. Using a near-complete count and survey of homeless individuals in Halifax, Canada, this study examines the association between shelter status and homelessness duration. The study also examines whether shelter status moderates the association between social and health-related factors and the likelihood of exiting homelessness. The analysis consists of three steps. First, factors related to homelessness duration are identified using Cohen's d and the t -test. Second, a baseline proportional hazards model is estimated, with homelessness duration as the dependent variable, shelter status as the explanatory variable, and social and health factors as control variables. Third, a model including interaction terms between shelter status and social and health factors is developed. The results show that unsheltered status is associated with prolonged homelessness, along with significant interactions with immigrant status, first homelessness after age 50, victimization, and substance use history. These patterns are examined using survival curves to understand differences in exit probabilities over time. Findings indicate that shelter status is associated with homelessness duration and moderates the association between individual vulnerabilities and duration.

title: Spatiotemporal pattern and system coupling coordination evaluation of green low-carbon circular development: A case study of nine cities in Guizhou province, China
Towards healthy homes: Exploring the effects of housing typologies on mental health in Australian capital cities
abstract: Recent growth in apartment living in Australian cities has raised concerns about mental health disparities between apartment and house residents, often attributed to poor construction quality and amenity levels. Notably, apartment residents in Australian capital cities are predominantly renters in the private market, with evidence that tenure instability and inability to control home quality can adversely affect mental health. While there is established literature on the mental health effects of either tenure type or dwelling type, few studies have examined their combined effects and spatial distribution on long-term mental health. To address this gap, this study examined: (a) the effect of dwelling type on mental health; (b) effect modification by tenure type; and (c) variations across Australian capital cities. Fixed-effects regression models were constructed to analyse panel data from the Household, Income, and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey from 2001 to 2019. Results indicated that there was no significant difference in mental health outcomes based on dwelling or tenure type at the national level – a finding that advances understanding by ruling out strong direct effects of dwelling type on mental health. There was no significant variation in dwelling type effects across cities as a whole, but city-stratified analysis revealed that living in an apartment was associated with better mental health compared to living in a house in Greater Sydney. This suggests that the mental health effects of dwelling type may be context-sensitive, highlighting the need for future research to investigate within-city factors affecting mental health in residential settings.

title: Impacts of high-speed railway on carbon emission: A comparative study between China and Japan during 21st century
Beyond proximity: Green space visitation patterns and physical health outcomes
abstract: Urban green spaces (GS) are increasingly recognized for mitigating health risks linked to urbanization, yet most research emphasizes proximity rather than actual use in Mediterranean cities. This study examines how GS visitation patterns, demographic characteristics, and physical health outcomes interact in Chania, Crete, addressing gaps in GS exposure and chronic disease prevention. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 718 adult residents between June and August 2024. Data included demographics, GS use, physical activity, and self-reported health indicators, including BMI, coronary artery disease (CAD), hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. Chi-square tests and logistic regression models were applied. Demographics were significantly associated with GS engagement and health. Men more often visited forests and had higher odds of chronic conditions (e.g., OR = 3.194 for CAD, p = 0.004), while older adults visited GS more frequently. Limited GS accessibility (>20-minute walk) was associated with higher odds of hypertension (OR = 1.603, p = 0.024). Garden visits were associated with more frequent GS use (OR = 3.133, p = 0.017), and longer visits (>1 h) were associated with lower odds of CAD, hypercholesterolemia, hypertension and longer physical activity duration. These findings highlight the importance of actual GS engagement alongside availability and support equitable, quality-focused GS planning.

title: Smart city performance in suburbanizing contexts: A configurational and exploratory analysis of Chinese cities
Welfare or divide? The impact of smart city construction on life satisfaction among middle-aged and older adults: A quasi-natural experiment from China
Governing the margins: Refugee-led informal governance in Peshawar urban marketplaces
Sequential spatial decoupling for street-level crime: An explainable GeoAI framework
Evolving landscapes of division: Industrial bias and the core–periphery employment dynamics in China’s urban agglomerations
From Thirdspace-making to networked Thirdspace: Micro spatial negotiations among Chinese female marriage migrants in Japan
Pricing urban flood risk: Evidence from the housing market in Beijing
Pandemic shifts in urban place use and subjective wellbeing: Evidence from Stockholm
Urban–rural gradient effects on greenspace exposure equality based on an area–structure assessment framework: A case study of the Yangtze River Delta
Toward evidence-based zoning: A machine learning framework for land use compatibility assessment
abstract: Abstract Despite over a century of zoning practice, land use compatibility — the degree to which adjacent land uses coexist without generating negative externalities — remains assessed through expert judgment and inherited assumptions rather than empirical evidence of urban outcomes. Given that compatibility standards underpin billions of dollars in annual zoning decisions, their empirical validity carries direct consequences for urban livability. This study presents a machine learning framework that shifts compatibility assessment from subjective prescription to data-driven discovery. Applying gradient boosting regression to 134,863 census blocks across New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Houston, the model predicts composite compatibility scores derived from six dimensions — functional diversity, activity complementarity, conflict minimization, accessibility synergy, socioeconomic integration, and infrastructure efficiency — using 32 features capturing land use composition, built environment morphology, transportation infrastructure, and socioeconomic context. The model achieves strong predictive performance (R² = 0.895, RMSE = 0.087), establishing that compatibility follows systematic, learnable patterns. Land use entropy dominates prediction (63.7% feature importance), providing robust evidence that functional mixing enhances neighborhood quality — directly challenging Euclidean use-separation zoning. Context-specific compatibility matrices reveal that 45 of 55 land use pairings are empirically estimable in transit-oriented contexts versus only one in auto-dependent suburbs, demonstrating that compatibility is locally conditioned rather than universally fixed. Most pairings fall within a moderate range, with mixed-use designations consistently scoring highest. The study identifies empirically derived attribute thresholds for high-compatibility neighborhoods, offering planners measurable benchmarks — including optimal entropy ranges, building height and coverage parameters, and land use composition targets — to replace arbitrary development standards.

title: Affordable housing vs. unaffordable location: A national investigation on the impacts of urban sprawl on housing, transportation and energy affordability in the United States
‘Don't wait to buy, buy and wait.’ – behavioural and institutional factors affecting delays in land development. The GZM Metropolis in Poland
abstract: Empty or underutilised land has a negative impact on cities’ structure. The literature on timing of land development has already examined market and general institutional factors affecting deferrals in building up land, yet the behavioural reasons have not been fully uncovered. In the institutional framework of post-transition country, with the peculiar remnants of formal and informal institutions from the previous system, this topic gains additional interest. Building on the quantitative results of our previous research, which showed that investors typically delay land development by an average of 3.4 years, we use a mixed methods approach. This research employs a grounded theory methodology to explore the values, attitudes and behaviours of investors and city officials that influence their decisions regarding the timing of land development.The analysis shows that the institutional background of polycentric, post-industrial metropolis - The Upper Silesia MA in Poland influences the behaviour of market participants, and remnants of institutions from the previous system add uncertainty to the land development process. Fierce competition between cities affects pro-investor attitude of city officials. Poorly written procedures and bureaucracy effects in discretionary decisions and less predictability. As a consequence, there is a tacit acceptance of delays in land development, with investors exploiting the legal loopholes. This creates a feedback loop with an established system (lock-in).As many of the reasons for land development postponements stem from 'fuzzy' institutions, the results of this research should be applicable in the other post-transition countries.

title: Benefits of everyday encounters while being out and about: The neighborhood familiarity scale
abstract: Fleeting social and local encounters in the neighborhood might counteract the social uncertainty that sustains loneliness. Yet no existing scale specifically assesses the underlying social and local processes of these encounters. We developed and validated the Neighborhood Familiarity Scale using a multi-method approach to measure the impact of neighborhood encounters. First, eleven qualitative interviews using the “neighborhood go-along method” and five expert pre-tests were conducted to generate the items. Second, the scale was validated via an online survey. An exploratory ( n = 161) and a confirmatory ( n = 320) factor analysis confirmed two distinct factors: Social and local neighborhood familiarity . They represent the legibility of both social relations and the public space in the neighborhood. The scale was validated convergently using sense of neighborhood, place dependence , and place identity, and discriminatively using social dis-connectedness . Third, structural equation modeling ( n = 481) examined local mobility as a predictor for neighborhood familiarity. We found that cycling was significantly positively associated with local and social familiarity, sense of neighborhood, place identity, and negatively associated with social dis-connectedness. Notably, another mode of local mobility, being out and about with toddlers, predicted neighborhood familiarity, while driving or public transit showed no significant effects. We controlled for homeownership, length of residence, and age. These findings point to social correlates of local active mobility. The Neighborhood Familiarity Scale provides a validated instrument for urban planning and policy to capture the positive social psychological correlates of active mobility.

title: Exacerbating spatial inequity: Coupling physical barriers and social response in elderly accessibility under extreme floods in Shanghai
Balancing user logic and urban governance: Integrating shared e-scooters into a human-centred mobility paradigm
abstract: As European cities seek to reconcile sustainable urban mobility with the rapid expansion of light-electric vehicles, the integration of shared e-scooters raises critical questions about the transformation of human-centred mobility principles and the governance of urban space. This article examines how shared e-scooter systems reshape human-centred mobility principles in European urban transport systems, and explores the related tensions that emerge around equity, safety, and the regulation of public space through an international multi-actor qualitative analysis. A longitudinal qualitative design was employed, based on ten online expert focus groups conducted between December 2024 and February 2026 with fifteen purposively selected international stakeholders representing policymakers, city authorities, industry actors, research organisations, and user associations from five countries. Data were analysed using constructivist grounded theory with iterative coding and member checking, enabling the development of a conceptual model of human-centred shared e-scooter integration. The findings underscore that shared e-scooters advance human-centred mobility objectives only when governments coherently integrate and regulate them, aligning governance, spatial planning, lifecycle sustainability, and safety-oriented frameworks within car-dominant urban contexts. Placing mobility users’ needs at the centre of urban transport planning requires systemic transformation – through incremental, data-informed, and participatory governance approaches that embed shared e-scooters within multimodal frameworks aligned with equity, safety, and public space reallocation goals. Based on the findings, eight implication pathways are defined for research and practice, framing a governance-oriented agenda for operationalising human-centred e-scooter sharing system.

title: Exploring the interplay of sustainability and cultural values in urban design: Analyzing contemporary landscapes through machine learning (ML) insights modeling
Spatial non-stationarity in urban landscape perception: Decomposing feature contributions across distinct urban types
Mapping intra-urban transport equity through multiple justice lenses: A Berlin case study
abstract: Transport and urban decision-making are often guided by aggregate performance indicators and economic appraisal, even as it is increasingly recognized that transport systems distribute benefits and burdens unevenly across space and social groups. Transport justice research highlights these distributional concerns, yet many equity assessments embed implicit assumptions about what constitutes fair distribution and rarely compare alternative distributive principles. This paper asks how justice-theory choice alters intra-urban transport equity assessments and how distributive theories can be translated into quantitative metrics using spatial data. Rather than privileging a single perspective, we translate four prominent justice theories — utilitarianism, egalitarianism, prioritarianism, and sufficientarianism — into quantitative metrics and apply them to Berlin. We compute four transport currencies on 100 m × 100 m census grids and aggregate results to neighborhoods and districts using weighted and unweighted specifications. Currencies include 15-min walking accessibility to essential services, traffic noise, severe-injury and fatal road traffic crash density, and the proportion of car-dedicated street space. Egalitarian inequality metrics systematically diverge from other logics, sometimes reversing area rankings. Utilitarian, prioritarian, and sufficientarian metrics often converge because high mean burdens coincide with local hotspots and large shares exceeding minimum standards. Socioeconomic index ranking adds a social-ordering dimension and mainly reshapes interpretation at fine scales, distinguishing spatial hotspots from socially structured disadvantage. Overall, the study shows that equity metrics encode contestable normative claims and suggests that different transport outcomes may require different justice perspectives. For practice, we recommend either justifying the adopted principle or developing currency-specific evaluation logics alongside comparative reporting.

title: A cross-level diagnostic framework for spatial equity of public transportation services: Supply-demand mismatch and influencing factors in the Pearl River Delta
Polishing the perfect: The ambitions of smart urbanism
abstract: Cities are increasingly seen as agglomeration points for a vast range of contemporary challenges, and many advocate for developing and implementing transformative solutions at the city-level. Here, digitalization is presented as a silver-bullet solution, promising to yield sustainable, equitable and liveable futures through technological optimization and effectivization. In urban policy and planning, such ambitions are commonly articulated under the auspices of smart urbanism. While the transformative potential of smart city initiatives has been dealt with in existing literature, visions of ideal smart urban futures – and the transformative ambitions of these – have insufficiently been addressed. This paper interrogates the purportedly transformative potential of smart cities by developing an analytical framework that contrasts utopia with the end of history, applying this to an in-depth analysis of the smart city initiative in Stockholm. Utopia denotes a radical openness of the future, insisting upon the potential for alternative trajectories embedded within existing spatialities. In contrast, the end of history signifies a radical closure of the future, characterized by stasis and the absence of transformative possibilities. Empirically, the paper draws on interviews with key actors involved in Stockholm's smart city efforts, document analysis and participant observation. The findings suggest that the anticipations motivating smart urbanism rarely entail transformative ruptures with the status quo. Rather than exploring radically different urban futures, the utopias of the smart city in Stockholm aim for reinforcement of existing socio-spatial configurations, leaving us with a future that merely offers more of the same – with a technological twist.

title: Regulating thermal comfort via 2D and 3D urban morphology heterogeneity: Evidence from Beijing's local climate zones
Grassroots way of doing things – Creative reuse of an industrial heritage site in southern Sweden
abstract: Several ongoing societal transitions, including urbanization and digitalization, may entail adverse impacts to existing buildings and communities. One challenge is obsolescence caused by demographic shifts and deindustrialization. Adaptive reuse tackles building obsolescence and contributes to a circular use of the existing building stock. This study aims to establish how the creative reuse of an industrial heritage site impacts place-attachment and community social capital. As we explore a phenomenon in its real-life context, a qualitative case study method was deemed appropriate. Our case is a former ceramics factory in Southern Sweden, which has been adapted to an arts centre. Our data sources comprise interviews, written accounts, and observations during a site tour. We find three main processes 1) the preserved building and its characteristics contributing to place attachment; 2) empowerment developing through self-provision, and; 3) engagement and integration activities bonding social capital. First, the case employs immigrants and other individuals with difficulty entering the job market. Second, the focal actors have a do-it-yourself attitude and aspire to learn by doing, instead of procuring professional property management services. Finally, the case has enhanced the vitality of the small town and its inhabitants through art tourism and a street art gallery.

title: Measuring active school travel friendliness via big data and wearable biosensors: An evidence-based approach for child-friendly cities
Rethinking transit-oriented development in shrinking cities: Urban structure and life satisfaction in Tokyo metropolitan area
abstract: Shrinking metropolitan regions are already consolidating residents around railway stations under compact city and transit-oriented development policy, yet whether those residents report better lives has not been established. This paper examines how urban structure is associated with life satisfaction in the station catchment areas of the Tokyo Metropolitan Area. Combining an original survey of working residents with geospatial indicators of neighborhood walkability, the analysis employs ordered probit models and a recursive path model with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Residents of station catchment areas report lower life satisfaction than those outside them, and the difference persists after conditioning for leisure behavior and household type. Neighborhood walkability is positively associated with life satisfaction within station catchment areas, whereas housing conditions are the dominant correlate beyond them. The pathway linking walkability to well-being operates through the perceived quality of everyday life rather than its quantity: the indirect association through free-time satisfaction is significant, whereas the serial pathway through leisure quantity is not. Robustness tests show that work and family satisfaction carry comparable indirect associations, so leisure is the clearest instance of this mechanism rather than the only one. Furthermore, single-person households are concentrated in these areas and report significantly lower life satisfaction than other household types, though the pathway is not separately identified within that group. These findings challenge the assumption that accessibility and density inherently enhance quality of life, and suggest that compact city strategies in shrinking regions should prioritize the experienced quality of everyday environments rather than the intensity of concentration alone.

title: Public value and consumption transformation of shared spaces in community shopping centers: A comparative study of cases in Guangzhou
Mapping the relationship between accessibility and resilience in transportation: A systematic literature review
abstract: Over the past decade, transportation resilience has emerged as a central research priority, driven by increasing exposure of transport systems to natural, epidemic, and operational disruptions. Although frequently discussed alongside resilience in this growing body of work, accessibility is interpreted in diverse ways and has emerged as a prominent but conceptually unsettled concept in the literature. Despite their co-occurrence, the relationship between resilience and accessibility remains inconsistently defined and has not been systematically synthesized as the organizing focus of a review. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic literature review following the PRISMA framework, complemented by exploratory text-mining analysis. The review examines methodological approaches, application contexts, and the ways in which accessibility is positioned relative to resilience across the selected studies. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling and bigram analysis are used as supplementary tools to identify broad thematic patterns in the corpus. The review provides a structured synthesis of how resilience and accessibility are interrelated across studies. The findings identify five functional relationships: accessibility as a resilience outcome, a direct resilience indicator, a component of a broader resilience model, a vulnerability or inequality diagnostic, and a resilience-enhancement mechanism. These varying interpretations highlight significant conceptual and operational inconsistencies that limit comparability and hinder the development of integrated assessment frameworks. Based on this synthesis, the paper identifies relationship-specific and cross-cutting research gaps, including the limited representation of dynamic resilience, lack of hybrid approaches, and inconsistencies in both resilience and accessibility interpretations. The study concludes by outlining future research directions toward more holistic, data-driven, and integrated frameworks for resilient transportation planning.

title: Remote work and circular economy goals in municipal administration: paradoxical resource flows in Polish cities
Integrating Warsaw's Metro and Tram systems for spatial inclusion: Synergies in job accessibility
Why don't we walk? Exploring the environmental determinants of walking behaviour in Auckland
abstract: This study investigates walking behaviour in Auckland, New Zealand, focusing on environmental factors associated with pedestrian activity in a car-dependent urban context. Using mobile phone data and spatial analyses, the research examines the roles of road network connectivity, functional amenities, and natural environments in shaping walking patterns. As an initial framework, the study employs accessibility mapping based on the “15-minute city” concept to evaluate whether Auckland's urban structure supports walkability. While the mapping suggests that many areas align with the principles of walkable neighbourhoods, the analysis of actual walking trips reveals a significant misalignment between these urban structures and observed walking patterns. To explore this discrepancy, the study shifts the focus from static environmental conditions to an observed relationship by introducing a multidimensional framework comprising the Contextual Feature Index (CFI), Amenity Feature Index (AFI), and Nature Feature Index (NFI). The analysis identifies a critical misalignment primarily driven by inadequate pedestrian infrastructure, fragmented road network connectivity, and compromised micro-scale quality. Furthermore, the findings reveal that socio-economic context fundamentally shapes how people respond to their walking environments, distinguishing necessity-driven from discretionary walking. This research advances the understanding of walking behaviour in car-dependent cities, offering a scalable, multi-dimensional framework to inform equitable, context-specific urban interventions.

title: Making and governing a cross-boundary migrant settlement: State entrepreneurialism and migrant agency in Yanjiao, China
Spaces of life: Rethinking oncology departments as a fourth therapeutic space
abstract: Background Increasing evidence shows that healthcare environments influence physical and psychological well-being. However, the role of oncology spaces as social and relational environments remains underexplored. Methods Between February and April 2025, four approximately 90-min participatory meetings were held at the Oncology Department of Cannizzaro Hospital (Catania, Italy) with patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals, community representatives, and spatial design professionals. Participants shared experiences, needs, and expectations regarding the oncology care environment, generating qualitative and visual materials. These contributions were reviewed by the interdisciplinary team through an iterative process of synthesis and design translation, identifying recurrent experiential, relational, environmental, and functional needs and translating them into the “Spaces of Life” proposal and the “fourth therapeutic space” conceptual framework. Results The participatory process led to the development of the “Spaces of Life” concept, which reinterprets oncology environments as places where clinical care, social interaction, and everyday life converge. Key elements included integrating green spaces, increasing access to natural light in treatment areas, and transforming waiting areas into relational, community-oriented environments. Participants associated these proposed spatial characteristics with greater comfort, opportunities for social interaction, and a more supportive experience of time spent within the department. Conclusions The findings suggest that oncology departments can be reconceptualised beyond purely clinical settings, as relational environments that support patients' lived experiences. The concept of oncology as a “fourth therapeutic space” highlights the potential to integrate spatial, social, and clinical dimensions within a framework for more relational and patient-centred oncology environments.

title: From planetary urbanization to global scenarios of depopulation. A geographical perspective
A Dot-Product Gravity Model for predicting the evolution of population flow networks in cities along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor (NILSTC)
Social acceptability of public lighting reductions for light pollution mitigation: A regional, repeated cross-sectional study amidst the energy crisis in Wallonia (Belgium)
Safe, seen, and included: Understanding ethnic minority experiences of parks in a changing Polish City
abstract: Access to urban green space is a crucial determinant of urban quality of life, yet patterns of accessibility remain socially uneven. This qualitative study explores how ethnic minority residents in Wrocław, Poland, perceive and access urban parks. Sixteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with participants from South Asian, Middle Eastern, African, and East Asian backgrounds. Thematic analysis constructed four themes: safety and exclusion, park infrastructure and amenity provision, cultural and embodied barriers to comfort, and the emotional and social dimensions of belonging. Safety and discrimination emerged as the most consistently reported concerns, with experiences varying significantly according to the intersection of ethnicity, gender, and visible religious identity. Hijab-wearing women reported a compounded sense of exclusion, arising from being simultaneously marked as ethnic, religious, and gendered others within a predominantly white, secular public space. Limited access to free and clean toilet facilities, cultural unfamiliarity with public drinking norms, and the absence of inclusive programming further restricted park use and reinforced a sense of not belonging. Despite these barriers, participants consistently valued parks for their natural beauty and restorative benefits. Distance was never raised as a barrier; instead, participants' accounts indicate that social and cultural barriers, rather than physical distance, shape ethnic minority residents' use and non-use of green space. Specific recommendations are offered for safety improvements, amenity provision, and culturally sensitive programming to support Wrocław's growing ethnic minority communities.

title: Estimating the causal effect of extreme flooding on urban property markets: A case study of Porto Alegre, Brazil
abstract: The May 2024 floods in Porto Alegre, Brazil, triggered a pronounced spatial repricing of climate risk in the city’s housing market. Using a Bayesian structural time-series framework, we estimate an average causal impact of a 4.7% increase in sale prices and a 9.1% increase in rental price indices, driven primarily by price appreciation in elevated, flood-resilient neighborhoods. Our econometric approach accounts for nonlinear trends and macroeconomic controls, isolating the causal effect of the disaster. The findings highlight how climate shocks can exacerbate socio-spatial inequality, reshape urban investment patterns, and embed climate resilience into property valuations.

title: Temporality in urban heritage studies: A systematic thematic review of conceptual themes and research gaps
abstract: Temporality has become an increasingly visible concern in urban heritage studies, yet the field remains conceptually dispersed. Time related questions appear across discussions of collective memory, continuity, authenticity, integrity, place identity, adaptive reuse and the Historic Urban Landscape approach, but these concerns are rarely synthesised within a common analytical structure. This article systematically reviews how temporality has been conceptualised in urban heritage research and identifies the major thematic and theoretical patterns shaping the field. Using Web of Science as the primary database, the review combined one core temporality focused search with three supplementary searches on collective and urban memory, authenticity and change, and adaptive reuse, resilience and future oriented heritage. The search yielded 2294 records, reduced to 1666 unique records after duplicate removal. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 121 studies were retained for provisional qualitative synthesis, with 64 studies used for close thematic interpretation and theory building. The review identifies four recurring themes: temporality as memory, continuity and identity; authenticity, integrity and change; lived and perceived urban experience; and governance, layering and the management of urban transformation. These themes are further consolidated into broader theoretical families. The findings show that temporality is an underlying organising problem in urban heritage studies, but is often acknowledged in broad terms rather than translated into explicit analytical methods. Future research would benefit from more explicit temporal methods for addressing layered urban histories, present day inhabitation and contested heritage futures.

title: The densified city and the powerline right-of-way encroachment in Nigeria: Greening as an important intervention.
abstract: Urban densification is generally promoted as a strategy for sustainable development. However, it may also produce unintended consequences, such as exposure to environmental hazards. This study examines potential electrical hazard exposure in relation to the powerline right-of-way (ROW) encroachment in Port Harcourt Metropolis, a rapidly densifying oil and gas industry hub in southern Nigeria, using a mixed-method approach that combines geospatial datasets and social survey data. The Pressure and Release (PAR) framework is used primarily as an interpretive framework for organizing observed spatial conditions and respondents' reported reasons for and experiences in occupying buildings within the powerline ROW. The findings show that about 256 buildings are located within the powerline ROW. Among surveyed occupants, 58.3% reported access to infrastructure and 20.0% reported proximity to livelihood sources as reasons for occupying buildings within the ROW. No electrical accidents were reported, while 50% of respondents reported powerline sagging and 12.2% reported arc flash. The study suggests green infrastructure as a policy option for managing the powerline ROW by transforming it into a managed ecological corridor that could help reduce encroachment and provide environmental benefits. However, its effectiveness depends on the capacity of the relevant institution, maintenance, and community engagement. The paper contributes to ongoing debates on urban development by illustrating how densified development may be associated with potential exposure to powerline hazards and by highlighting green policy interventions as a possible option for managing powerline ROWs.

title: Governing climate neutrality through climate city contracts: Insights from twenty-five European cities
abstract: Mission-oriented innovation policy has become an influential framework for addressing complex societal challenges and is increasingly shaping urban climate governance through the European Union's Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities Mission. This paper examines how Climate City Contracts (CCCs) help cities address the principal governance barriers that constrain the transition to climate neutrality. A structured review of recent literature identifies seven recurrent governance gaps: institutional silos and systems integration; multi-level coordination; financing and institutional innovation; technical capacity and data; stakeholder participation and co-creation; ecosystem coordination; and climate justice and social acceptance. To examine how these challenges are addressed in practice, the paper analyses the Climate City Contracts of twenty-five European Mission cities. The results show that the main contribution of CCCs lies in their capacity to catalyse institutional innovation through governance arrangements designed to overcome systemic constraints. Across diverse urban contexts, six recurring families of governance instruments are identified: Mission Governance Structures, Portfolio Management Systems, Climate Finance Integration Instruments, Multi-Stakeholder Climate Platforms, Deliberative and Inclusive Participation Mechanisms, and Urban Innovation and Experimentation Platforms. Together, these instruments form an emerging governance architecture that enables cities to organise, finance, and implement climate-neutral transitions in systemic, adaptive, and socially legitimate ways. The paper contributes to research on urban sustainability transitions and mission-oriented innovation by showing how broad policy ambitions are translated into operational governance arrangements for climate neutrality at the urban level. • Climate City Contracts operationalize mission-oriented governance for climate neutrality. • Seven governance gaps shape the implementation of climate-neutral cities. • Twenty-five European cities reveal six recurring governance instrument families. • Climate City Contracts catalyse institutional innovation and systemic coordination.

title: Heat health risk assessment of major Chinese urban agglomerations considering inter-city interactions
From proximity to access: Childcare enrollment and accessibility in Brazil
authors: Samuel de Almeida Torquato e Silva
Fernanda Mara de Oliveira Macedo Carneiro Pacobahyba
abstract: This study examines walking accessibility to daycare facilities for children aged 0–3 in Brazil using a nationwide Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (2SFCA) approach. Accessibility is measured by combining teacher supply, child population demand, and Euclidean distance thresholds adjusted for network circuity. Using data from the 2022 Demographic Census and School Census for all 5,570 municipalities, the analysis relates accessibility to enrollment rates through compositional data analysis (α-transformation) and Geographically Weighted Regression. Results show that while proximity to facilities is associated with higher enrollment, improvements in service capacity generate substantially larger marginal effects than the mere expansion of spatial coverage. Accessibility effects vary substantially across municipalities and decline with higher levels of urbanization. A substantial share of the positive association between urbanization and enrollment is explained by accessibility, suggesting that urban advantages are largely associated with spatial conditions. At the same time, the weaker translation of accessibility into enrollment in more urbanized contexts indicates the presence of additional barriers not captured by spatial measures. These findings suggest that conventional distance-based accessibility measures may overestimate effective access when capacity constraints and local frictions are not considered. Accessibility emerges as a necessary but not sufficient condition for enrollment, highlighting the role of service capacity and contextual barriers in converting spatial access into actual use. Policies that expand coverage without addressing staffing constraints and local access conditions are therefore unlikely to achieve substantial gains in enrollment.

Governing urban AI responsibly: Public perceptions of ethical and practical challenges in local government
abstract: As AI becomes increasingly embedded in local government operations, public perceptions are a critical lens for evaluating responsible AI deployment. This study investigates how individuals' encounters with AI in local government settings relate to perceived benefits, risks, and understanding of AI, and how these perceptions are linked to the importance assigned to responsible AI characteristics. The study uses structural equation modelling to analyse survey data from 1220 respondents across Australia, Spain, and the US. The findings show that experience with local government AI is positively associated with perceived benefits and perceived understanding and negatively associated with perceived risks. Perceived risk is the strongest predictor of the perceived importance of responsible AI, while perceived benefits and understanding play supporting roles. This indicates that public prioritisation of responsible AI is linked less to optimism about AI's benefits and more to concern for safeguards and ethical governance. Country-specific models also showed variation in the relative strength and significance of these relationships across national contexts. These findings contribute to responsible AI scholarship by showing that public expectations for local government AI are shaped by both practical experience and governance concerns. The study highlights the need for context-sensitive AI governance strategies that build public trust, address perceived risks, and align AI deployment with public values.

title: Unveiling episodes of everyday informal politics in internationally funded slum upgrading programs
abstract: Politics permeates all facets of urban life in African cities. Yet research advancing inclusive slum redevelopment has not adequately illuminated its everyday intricacies and implications. This is particularly important, as supranational institutions are becoming central players through large-scale infrastructure investments. Consequently, this paper introduces the concept of ‘everyday informal politics’ to unpack the quotidian interactions among actors in two World Bank- and UN-Habitat-funded upgrading programs in Accra, Ghana's capital, and a politically significant swing-voting city. It asks: i) At what spatio-institutional scales did politics emerge? ii) How was power exercised in such politics? And iii) What inclusionary and exclusionary outcomes did they engender? To answer these questions, the article draws on rich empirical data (i.e., 40 semi-structured interviews and three focus group discussions). Results reveal three scales of everyday informal politics: a spatial scale of jurisdictional conflations and institutional scales involving state governance actors (e.g., Mayors) and non-state actors who simultaneously work alongside and parallel to the state planning apparatus (e.g., traditional authorities). A Foucauldian reading of such politics showed that, in some instances, state and non-state actors exercised power to exclusively capture resources and benefits, while residents exercised collective power productively and strategically to claim inclusion. The paper's findings establish the need for slum redevelopment programs to embed internal and external measures from the outset to curtail the exclusionary outcomes of everyday informal politics. Some recommendations are offered to advance a politically adaptive approach to slum upgrading.

Assessing the influence of urban morphology, vegetation, and topography on land surface temperature: A planning-support tool
abstract: Urban heat islands (UHIs) are intensifying under rapid urbanization and climate change, creating a need for interpretable tools that support climate-sensitive urban planning. This study develops a high-resolution urban climate assessment framework to quantify the effects of urban morphology, vegetation, and topography on land surface temperature (LST) in Clermont-Ferrand, France. Using 1 m thermal imagery and geospatial indicators aggregated across 8286 one-hectare cells, a multiple linear regression model explained 72% of LST variability. Statistical comparison of more than 106,000 grid cells confirmed significantly higher temperatures in urban areas, validating the UHI effect. Vegetation (NDVI) emerged as the dominant cooling factor, whereas road surfaces and Gross Floor Area (GFA) contributed to thermal amplification. Interaction analysis showed that vegetation provides greater cooling benefits in dense urban environments, while topography modifies the thermal influence of urban density. Mediation analysis further demonstrated that NDVI indirectly regulates LST through land-use composition, highlighting both direct and mediated thermal pathways. Sensitivity and scenario analyses illustrated how estimated LST varies across combined configurations of vegetation, development density, road allocation, and topographic conditions. To facilitate practical application, the regression framework was implemented as an interactive planning-support platform integrating scenario exploration, nomogram-based estimation, mediation visualization, and sensitivity analysis. The proposed approach bridges urban climate research and planning practice by providing an explainable framework for rapid urban heat assessment and climate-resilient urban design.

Spatiotemporal dynamics of informal settlements across argentine cities: A national-scale analysis
abstract: Informal settlements are expanding worldwide, yet global SDG 11.1.1 monitoring remains disproportionately focused on large metropolitan areas. This leaves a critical blind spot: the rapid growth of informal settlements in smaller urban areas. Using national-scale ReNaBaP data (2016–2023), this study quantifies, for the first time, the spatiotemporal dynamics of informal settlement growth across all Argentine cities above 2000 inhabitants. The analysis reveals that informal settlements are growing at an average annual rate of 1.79%. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, the largest total informal settlement area is found in extra-small urban areas (2000–50,000 residents; 267 km 2 ), exceeding even Greater Buenos Aires (216 km 2 ) despite its far larger population share. Between 2016 and 2023, the informal settlement areas in smaller urban areas expanded faster on average, i.e., small cities (50,000–200,000 residents) grew at 2.78% annually, compared with 1.44% in large metropolitan areas, and experienced sharper growth peaks (up to 5.06% in 2018). These findings reveal an emerging spatial shift in informal urbanization, where smaller cities, often absent from global datasets, are now critical frontiers of housing informality. Addressing this monitoring gap is essential for adequate housing, equitable resource allocation, and inclusive urban policy, both in Argentina and globally.
